title: Youth Citizenship, Digital Activism and Electoral Mobilisation Ahead of Nigeria's 2027 General Elections
abstract: Digital activism enables political participation beyond elections in Nigeria. This study examines how the #TinubuMustGo campaign on X connects youth citizenship, digital activism and electoral mobilisation ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections. Guided by connective action theory, it uses qualitative content analysis of public posts published between 1 and 30 June 2026. Findings identify political voice, accountability demands, rights claims and agency as constructions of youth citizenship. Digital activism involves hashtag amplification, information sharing, calls to action and protest coordination. Electoral mobilisation emerges when governance concerns are linked to voting, re-election and electoral choice. However, much of the campaign remains focused on accountability and political dissent without explicit electoral appeals. The study shows how personalised grievances circulate through hashtag-mediated communication and sometimes acquire electoral significance. It contributes to African political communication research by distinguishing networked political dissent from electorally oriented mobilisation between national elections.
bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

Digital media have transformed political participation across democratic and emerging democratic societies (Durotoye et al., 2026). Social networking platforms enable citizens to express political opinions, contest State policies, mobilise action and shape public discourse. In Africa, social media complement conventional political participation by enabling citizens, particularly young people, to organise protests, demand accountability and influence national conversations (Ajaegbu & Ajaegbu, 2024). In Nigeria, digital activism has characterised #OccupyNigeria (Uwalaka & Watkins, 2018), #BringBackOurGirls (Oriola, 2021), #EndSARS (Onayinka et al., 2026) and the #TinubuMustGo campaign.

Nigeria's youthful population has played a central role in digital political participation. Young Nigerians use digital platforms to discuss governance, economic conditions, insecurity and issues affecting their lives (Obia, 2025; Apata, 2025). Political participation occurs beyond elections and party activities through networked communication, hashtag activism and digitally coordinated civic action (Ugwuoke & Erubami, 2021). Through hashtags, posts, images, videos and other forms of online communication draw attention to political issues, challenge government actions, demand accountability and mobilise others (Uwalaka & Nwala, 2023). Such activism can sustain political discussion between elections and link governance concerns to future political participation (Odeyemi et al., 2022). Whether it develops an electoral orientation, however, requires closer attention.

Existing scholarship on digital activism in Nigeria has focused on protest mobilisation, online advocacy, misinformation, election campaigns and democratic participation (Obisesan, 2022). Studies of #EndSARS, have examined protest organizations (Akerele-Popoola et al., 2022), digital political narratives (Aboh, 2024), civic resistance (Adeniyi, 2022) and State responses (Dim & Chow, 2026). However, less is known about how governance and accountability concerns expressed through activism between elections connect with subsequent electoral mobilisation (Onayinka et al., 2026).

This study addresses this gap through the #TinubuMustGo campaign on X (formerly Twitter). It examines how the campaign constructs narratives of youth citizenship and political participation, the forms of digital activism evident and how governance concerns connect with electoral mobilisation ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections. It addresses three research questions: (1) How does the #TinubuMustGo campaign to construct narratives of youth citizenship and political participation? (2) What forms of digital activism are evident in the #TinubuMustGo campaign? (3) How does the #TinubuMustGo campaign connects governance concerns with electoral mobilisation ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections?

The study uses qualitative content analysis of posts containing #TinubuMustGo. Connective action theory provides a framework for examining how personalised political expressions connect through hashtag-mediated communication. The study links youth citizenship and digital activism to electoral mobilisation by examining political communication between electoral cycles.
## Conceptual Framework

This study examines three concepts: youth citizenship, digital activism and electoral mobilisation. They explain how youth participation in public affairs takes the form of digital activism and how governance-related activism may acquire an electoral orientation between elections.
## Youth Citizenship

Citizenship has traditionally been understood as the legal relationship between individuals and the State, encompassing rights, responsibilities and participation in public affairs (Marshall, 1950; Wood, 2022). Classical conceptions emphasised voting, political representation and civic obligations within formal democratic institutions (Dalton, 2008). Contemporary scholarship, however, extends citizenship beyond legal status to participation in civic and political life (Wood, 2022). Citizenship can therefore be practised through public deliberation, collective action, advocacy and engagement outside formal electoral institutions.

Youth citizenship concerns young people's exercise of rights and participation in public affairs (Vromen et al., 2016). Focusing on voting or party membership can overlook issue-based activism, advocacy, protest and community action. Youth engagement encompasses formal and informal political claims, public debate, accountability demands, agency and recognition (Staeheli et al., 2013). Despite formal rights, young people may have few opportunities to influence established decision-making (Harris et al., 2010). Alternative spaces let them voice claims, challenge decisions and act collectively (O'Loughlin & Gillespie, 2012).

Digital media extend youth citizenship into networked spaces (Bennett et al., 2011), where young people discuss public issues, scrutinise governments, organise around shared concerns, and circulate political information beyond traditional media and institutions (Loader et al., 2014). Using communication technologies to address public concerns can constitute citizenship (Choi, 2016), making it part of everyday political communication beyond elections (Bello & Kaufhold, 2023). However, digital citizenship is shaped by unequal internet access, misinformation, algorithmic visibility, and harassment, and does not necessarily lead to formal political action.
## Digital Activism

Digital activism involves using digital technologies to communicate grievances, organise campaigns, disseminate alternative information and coordinate protest activities (George & Leidner, 2019). It covers advocacy and political discussion, protest coordination, citizen documentation, and networked mobilisation (Treré & Kaun, 2021). Digital activism may operate through formal organisations, but social media also enable decentralised participation, allowing individuals to contribute to campaigns without belonging to a central organisation (Wang & Zhou, 2021).

Digital platforms lower barriers to political participation (Boulianne, 2020). Hashtags, livestreams, images, videos and user-generated content connect dispersed participants, circulate political claims and spotlight issues (Uwalaka and Nwala, 2023). Hashtags also aggregate contributions into searchable streams (Wang & Zhou, 2021). Digital resistance occurs when citizens use digital communication to challenge political authority, policies or dominant narratives and to organise opposition (Castillo-Esparcia et al., 2023). Digital activism also involves civic education, advocacy, information sharing, electoral discussion and mobilisation.

The political consequences of digital activism remain contested (Freelon et al., 2020; Santini & Carvalho, 2019). Low-cost forms of participation such as posting, sharing and hashtag use can expand opportunities for engagement, visibility and mobilisation, but do not necessarily lead to sustained participation or institutional change (Castillo-Esparcia et al., 2023). This study defines digital activism as digital communication for political expression, advocacy, accountability, and networked mobilisation.
## Electoral Mobilisation

Electoral mobilisation refers to activities that encourage citizens to participate in electoral processes through voting, political discussion, campaign engagement and other forms of participation (Vaccari & Valeriani, 2021). Traditional mobilisation strategies have relied on political parties, campaign organisations, community leaders and conventional media (Chadwick & Stromer-Galley, 2016). Digital communication has expanded mobilisation by allowing political information, appeals and discussion to circulate outside formal campaigns (Klinger et al., 2023).

Digital platforms also make the period between elections relevant to electoral mobilisation. Citizens can discuss public policies, assess government performance, exchange political information and debate political leadership before formal campaigns begin (Odeyemi et al., 2022). Such engagement can connect everyday political concerns with electoral (Kurniawan et al., 2024). However, political discussion or exposure to electoral information should not automatically be treated as mobilisation; electoral mobilisation requires an identifiable orientation toward electoral participation.

Protest-oriented participation and electoral participation are analytically distinct, but they may intersect when grievances about governance become linked to voting, voter registration, candidate evaluation, campaign participation or other election-related actions (Masunda, 2022). Digital activism connects dissatisfaction with current political conditions to electoral participation (Uwalaka et al., 2026). This study defines electoral mobilisation as digital communication that encourages, coordinates, or directs participation in elections, including voting, registration, political choice and other engagement.
## The Connective Logic of Digital Activism

Digital activism raises the question of how dispersed individuals participate in political causes without relying on formal organisations or shared collective identities (Bennett & Segerberg, 2012). Connective action theory explains this participation through personalised communication across digital networks (Bennett & Segerberg, 2023).

The theory distinguishes collective action, which generally relies on organisational coordination and shared identities, from connective action, which emerges through personalised political communication (Pond & Lewis, 2019). Bennett and Segerberg (2012) describe connective action through personalised action frames, in which participants adapt political claims to their own experiences, while remaining connected to a broader cause. Hashtags bring individual contributions into a common political discussion (Vromen, 2017).

Connective action theory is relevant to this study because #TinubuMustGo connects individual political expressions through a common hashtag. It explains how personalised posts on governance, accountability and political participation contribute to a wider digital campaign (Carson, 2021). The framework guides the analysis of how personalised grievances and political claims relate to youth citizenship and digital activism and whether these expressions acquire an electoral orientation ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections. An electoral orientation cannot be inferred from digital networking alone.
## Contextual Literature and Research Gap
## The #TinubuMustGo Campaign in Nigeria's Pre-2027 Political Environment

The period leading to Nigeria's 2027 general elections has been marked by debate over governance, economic conditions, insecurity and government accountability. Digital platforms have remained important spaces for political expression and mobilisation (Akamo, 2026). The #TinubuMustGo campaign examined in this study is situated within this pre-2027 political environment. The campaign provides a case for examining how governance-related digital activism between elections constructs narratives of youth citizenship and whether it acquires an electoral orientation ahead of 2027.
## Digital Activism and Electoral Politics in Nigeria

Research on digital political participation in Nigeria has grown alongside social media use for protest, advocacy and electoral communication (Obia, 2025). #OccupyNigeria linked online communication to protests against the 2012 fuel subsidy removal (Uwalaka & Watkins, 2018). #BringBackOurGirls sustained attention to the abducted Chibok schoolgirls and connected Nigerian advocacy with transnational publics (Onah, 2024).

Studies of #EndSARS examined youth-led digital activism (Akerele-Popoola et al., 2022; Uwalaka & Nwala, 2023), including protest coordination, information sharing and citizen documentation (Uwalaka, 2024); youth political expression (Olaitan, 2024); police accountability (Abioye, 2026); participatory governance (Omilusi, 2025) and digitally networked resistance (Ilesanmi, 2025). Electoral studies examine online campaigning, political information, candidate communication and citizen engagement (Morah & Nwafor, 2024). The Obidient movement linked digital activism with the 2023 elections (Egbunike, 2025; Onayinka et al., 2026).

Studies of protest activism and electoral communication have largely developed separately, leaving inter-election political engagement less examined. Digital platforms enable discussion of government policies, accountability and leadership after elections (Boulianne, 2020), while studies of Nigerian political parties document online communication and mobilisation between elections (Odeyemi et al., 2022). X has been used for digital activism in Nigeria (Ataguba, 2026; Obia, 2025), and its searchable hashtags allow researchers to examine how grievances, accountability demands and election-related messages intersect.

## Research Gap

Research linking Nigerian digital activism directly to subsequent electoral mobilisation remains limited. Studies linking protest activism to electoral engagement include research on #EndSARS and the Obidient movement (Onayinka et al., 2026). However, participation in digital protest should not automatically be treated as evidence of subsequent electoral mobilisation. Existing scholarship identifies three dimensions of Nigeria's digital political environment: social media facilitate protest and civic activism (Akerele-Popoola et al., 2022; Uwalaka & Nwala, 2023); young Nigerians are prominent participants in digitally mediated political engagement (Omilusi, 2025) and digital platforms support electoral communication (Morah & Nwafor, 2024; Onayinka et al., 2026). However, the electoral orientation of governance-focused activism between elections remains underexplored. To address this gap, the study examines how #TinubuMustGo constructs narratives of youth citizenship and connects governance concerns with electoral mobilisation ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections.
## Methodology

This study used qualitative content analysis to examine political communication within the #TinubuMustGo campaign on X (formerly Twitter). Qualitative content analysis enables systematic examination of texts to identify recurring meanings (Schreier, 2012). The analysis addressed youth citizenship and political participation, digital activism and electoral mobilisation.

The population comprised publicly accessible X posts containing the #TinubuMustGo. Posts published between 1 and 30 June 2026 were examined, situating the analysis ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections. Although a longer period could capture changes in political communication as the elections approached, the study focused on participation and electoral references in June 2026. Posts were retrieved using X search functions and date filters. X was selected because its public hashtag-based communication allows political messages, calls to action and electoral references to be examined together.

The #TinubuMustGo hashtag was selected as a case of digital activism centred on governance and political accountability. Its relevance lies in examining whether dissatisfaction with government performance also references electoral participation. Other political hashtags were excluded to retain focus on this campaign.

Purposive sampling was used to select publicly accessible, English-language posts relevant to the research questions (Campbell et al., 2020). Posts were included if they used #TinubuMustGo and addressed governance, accountability, citizenship, political participation, digital activism, or electoral issues. Duplicate content, advertisements, spam, identifiable automated posts and unrelated hashtag use were excluded. Quote posts and replies were retained when they provided substantive commentary or clarified an original post's political meaning, while reposts without commentary were excluded as analytical units.
The search retrieved 74 posts, screened against these criteria, yielding 18 for analysis. Each substantive post served as the unit of analysis.
![Figure 2](/images/articles/image16.png)

Posts were analysed using deductive and inductive coding (Kuckartz & Rädiker, 2023). Deductive categories covered three dimensions: youth citizenship and political participation, digital activism and electoral mobilisation. Initial codes included political voice, accountability, agency, digital resistance, information sharing, calls to action, personalised political expression, electoral references and electoral mobilisation. Inductive coding identified additional patterns. Codes were compared across the 18 posts and grouped into themes.
![Figure 3](/images/articles/image44.png)

Connective action theory (Bennett & Segerberg, 2012) guided analysis of personalised political expressions within hashtag-mediated communication. The analysis examined personalised action frames, the hashtag's connective role, digitally networked mobilisation and whether governance-related expressions remained protest-oriented or acquired an electoral orientation. The coding guide was refined through repeated readings and cross-post comparison. To strengthen trustworthiness, coding decisions were checked against the original posts to ensure themes reflected the language and political claims. Electoral mobilisation was coded only when posts contained textual or visual evidence linking political expression to electoral participation. Only public posts were analysed and usernames, profile photographs and other identifying information were removed from reported data.

## Findings and Analysis
## Youth Citizenship through Political Voice and Accountability

The analysis reveals youth citizenship as active political engagement expressed through political voice, accountability demands and claims about the State's responsibilities. These practices are evident in a post describing the #TinubuMustGo protest in Abuja:
"Nigerians are using their voices… In a democracy, protests remain one of the ways citizens make their feelings known."

The post constructs political voice as a democratic practice through which citizens communicate dissatisfaction. Through the #TinubuMustGo hashtag, this expression joins a wider stream of governance-related communication.
Political participation is also connected to political awareness. One tweet states:

"The fact that some people are still supporting Tinubu despite everything that's happening in Nigeria shows how messed up our situation is. There's a very huge awareness gap we need to bridge for us to have the country of our dream!"
The "awareness gap" frames political awareness as necessary for change, while "the country of our dream" connects individual judgement with a shared political future.
Accountability constitutes a second dimension. One tweet states that:
"20 killed in Kebbi. Another massacre. Another tragedy. Another reminder that the State is failing to protect its citizens. Nigerians deserve better."
The repeated "another" frames insecurity as an ongoing governance problem, while "Nigerians deserve better" expresses citizens' expectations of the State.
Another tweet broadens political authority:

"Seyi o, Must Go. Makinde, must go. Tinubu, must go. Useless, must go Enough of Playing politics with insecurity, the useless government that can't protect the people must leave. Be it president or governor. Be it IGP or COAS."
Naming different officeholders, the tweet distributes responsibility for insecurity across institutions and positions citizens to demand accountability from public authorities.
The discourse also connects citizenship with rights, evident in the assertion that:
"No prison is strong enough to silence the demand for justice. Freedom for the Nigerian people."

The language of "justice" and "freedom" constructs citizenship through rights claims, while "no prison is strong enough to silence" presents a political voice as persistent despite perceived constraints.
A further pattern concerns political agency:
"In case you missed this... #TinubuMustGo protest in Nyanya, Abuja. The day Nigerians decide to take back their country, all this political nonsense will end."

The phrase "take back their country" assigns agency to citizens, while its connection to the Nyanya protest links dissatisfaction with calls for political action. Overall, youth citizenship is constructed through political voice, awareness, rights claims, accountability and political agency.
## Digital Activism through Hashtag Amplification and Protest Mobilisation

The analysis reveals digital activism as a networked practice through which political messages are amplified, participation is encouraged and protest coordination is promoted. A tweet shows hashtag amplification directly:
"Hashtag tinubumustgo #tinubumustgo Push this hashtag guys"
The instruction to "push this hashtag" encourages users to increase campaign visibility.
A similar form of digital participation appears in another tweet:
"Everybody should #TINUBUMUSTRESIGN in the comments section it's take you nothing to re-tweet."
The expressions "everybody should" and "it's take you nothing to re-tweet" present commenting and reposting as low-threshold forms of participation.
Beyond amplification, the discourse uses digital platforms to mobilise participation in physical protest. One tweet states:
"Nigerians, when you wake up NATIONWIDE tomorrow, June 12 Democracy Day Action! TAKE CHARGE."
"NATIONWIDE" extends the call across locations, while "tomorrow" adds urgency to the appeal for protest participation.
More specific coordination is evident in another tweet:

"VDM said protests don't work - but last night, him and his "rats" proved otherwise. I love it. Join the movement: Abuja - join VDM Lagos - Friday, June 12, Ikeja Under Bridge No more silence. Demand accountability. End insecurity."

The tweet's date and location, along with the instruction to "join the movement", show how digital communication supports protest coordination across Abuja and Lagos. "No more silence" frames participation as a response to perceived government inaction.
Digital communication also circulates information about street-level action:
"Take It Back Movement protesters shut down Iwo Road, Ibadan this morning, demanding an end to insecurity and accountability over the ongoing kidnapping/abduction crisis."

Unlike the preceding calls to participate, this tweet reports an action. Sharing the Ibadan protest extends its visibility beyond those physically present and connects local action with the wider #TinubuMustGo discourse.
Another tweet uses the platform to recruit participants to an ongoing protest:

"Leave that club plan and meet us outside. Tinubu must go protest is on now in Abuja. We don't have a president and anybody occupying there who is clueless about running a nation, needs to get the hell out."
The informal instruction to "leave that club plan and meet us outside" redirects everyday activity towards protest. The phrase "protest is on now" adds urgency to the recruitment appeal.
## Electoral Mobilisation through Governance Evaluation and Electoral Choice

The analysis shows electoral mobilisation as a process that links dissatisfaction with governance to future voting decisions. The connection is evident in a tweet reflecting on the economic situation:
"Looking back at this tweet. I don't think Nigerians are angry enough now add another 4 years. to your age.
Re-tweeted: The difference between ₦1 and $1 is so wild that even if you earn ₦1 every day, you still won't have $1 after 4 years."
The phrase "add another 4 years to your age" projects economic dissatisfaction into another electoral term, encouraging reflection on the consequences of political choices.
Another tweet links dissatisfaction more explicitly to political change:
"Tinubu has successfully failed Nigerians and it's ripe for Nigerians to kick him out.
Re-tweeted:

ENOUGH IS ENOUGH Tinubu Must Go! Nigerians are suffering badly and we can't continue like this. The hardship is too much and the promises are all lies. We want our country back! APC Must Go! Time to take our power back. Share if you're tired too."

Perceived hardship and dissatisfaction with government performance support the call to "kick him out". The instruction to "share if you're tired too" connects this demand to wider digital circulation.
Voting emerges more directly as a means of exercising agency in another tweet:
"BAT and his cohorts want to add akara to the cassava (garri) and corn he promised us last election. Collect the akara chop but VOTE your conscience. Our future is in our hands"

The "last election" links past campaign experiences to future electoral judgement. The instruction to "VOTE your conscience" presents voting as an individual decision, while "our future is in our hands" gives it collective significance.
The discourse becomes explicitly oriented towards re-election in the repeated appeal:
"Dear Nigerians Stop supporting Tinubu's re-election stop supporting Tinubu's re-election Stop supporting Tinubu's re-election He has failed. APC has been failing Nigeria."
The repetition adds urgency to the call against re-election and links the poster's evaluation of government performance to a future electoral decision.
The 2027 election is invoked in another post:
"VeryDarkMan Just Post This: 'RATEL Don Land. The message is clear: Bola Ahmed Tinubu is a failure and should not come back in 2027.'"
The phrase "should not come back in 2027" connects dissatisfaction with current leadership to the forthcoming election as an opportunity for political change.
This relationship between present experience and future voting is reinforced in the tweet:
"You can't hear all this and still proceed to vote for Tinubu.
People are going through it mehnn"
The tweet makes hardship relevant to voting decisions, presenting electoral choice as a response to prevailing social and economic conditions.
Electoral mobilisation within #TinubuMustGo connects economic hardship, perceived government failure and dissatisfaction with leadership to re-election and voting in 2027.
## Discussion

The findings show how youth citizenship within #TinubuMustGo connects with digital activism and electoral mobilisation between elections. Youth citizenship is expressed through political voice, accountability demands, rights claims and political agency, while digital activism provides networked practices through which these expressions circulate. Some expressions take on an explicit electoral orientation by linking dissatisfaction with government performance to voting, re-election, and the 2027 general elections.

The campaign's construction of youth citizenship supports scholarship that conceptualises citizenship beyond voting and party membership (Vromen et al., 2016). Political participation within #TinubuMustGo is reflected in posts that discuss governance, demand accountability, assert rights and encourage protest. These practices position citizens as political actors who evaluate the State and articulate expectations concerning security, justice and government responsiveness.

Researchers have identified similar forms of digitally mediated citizenship outside conventional political institutions (Loader et al., 2014; Choi, 2016). Recent Nigerian studies link youth activism to civic agency, political expression and governance concerns (Apata, 2025; Omilusi, 2025). Within the campaign, citizenship expressed in protest and accountability discourse connects to electoral politics when governance evaluations inform electoral choices.

Digital activism connects these forms of participation. While hashtag amplification, reposting, sharing, calls to action and protest coordination enable participants to contribute at different levels (Wang & Zhou, 2021), digital platforms reduce organisational barriers and allow dispersed individuals to support political causes through flexible engagement (Bennett & Segerberg, 2012). Evidence from Nigeria's #EndBadGovernance protests shows that social media facilitated protest coordination through digitally networked participation (Uwalaka et al., 2026). The use of digital communication to publicise and coordinate protest within #TinubuMustGo reflects a broader pattern in Nigerian digital activism.

Connective action theory helps explain how these practices form a political campaign. Bennett and Segerberg's (2012) concept of personalised action frames is relevant because the posts do not reproduce a single organisational message. Participants articulate dissatisfaction through concerns about insecurity, economic hardship, justice, political leadership and government accountability. #TinubuMustGo connects these contributions without requiring identical motivations or organisational membership. However, connectivity alone does not establish electoral mobilisation.

Scholarship on digital activism cautions against assuming that posting, sharing or hashtag participation necessarily produces sustained participation (Boulianne, 2020; Castillo-Esparcia et al., 2023). Much of #TinubuMustGo remains centered on governance concerns, accountability and protest. Nevertheless, a distinct strand explicitly refers to voting, re-election, electoral choice and 2027. The campaign therefore contains both connective political dissent and electorally oriented mobilisation. This distinction between connective political dissent and electorally oriented mobilisation clarifies how connective action theory applies to governance-focused digital activism between elections.

Digital communication links personalised grievances, but these can remain protest discourse or become electorally oriented when hardship, insecurity and perceived government failure are tied to voting choices. Egbunike (2025) documents how digital media and deprivation-related grievances intersected with the Obidient movement's electoral activities in 2023. Onayinka et al. (2026) likewise link #EndSARS activism, the Obidient movement and youth electoral participation.

The findings have practical implications for civic organisations, political communication practitioners and researchers. Hashtag activity should not be treated as evidence of electoral mobilisation without examining the messages. Governance-related posts may encourage public discussion, accountability demands or protest, while others explicitly call for electoral participation. Distinguishing these forms of engagement can help practitioners assess whether online campaigns encourage public debate, protest participation or electoral action.

This study focuses on the period between national elections, when governance-focused activism may remain protest-oriented or acquire electoral meaning. The relationship should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously. Election-oriented messages within #TinubuMustGo does not demonstrate that digital participation will translate into voting behaviour or determine electoral outcomes. The findings identify electoral mobilisation at the level of political communication without inferring subsequent electoral behaviour.
## Conclusion

This study examined youth citizenship, digital activism and electoral mobilisation through the #TinubuMustGo campaign ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections. The campaign provides a networked space where citizens demand accountability, exercise political voice and circulate governance concerns through hashtags, reposts, calls to action and protest mobilisation. Some expressions move beyond protest by linking government performance to voting, re-election and electoral choice.

Digital activism does not automatically become electoral mobilisation, although the two can intersect. Governance-related activism can remain centred on protest, accountability and resistance without an electoral orientation. Within #TinubuMustGo, however, some personalised grievances become electorally oriented when economic hardship, insecurity and perceived government failure are connected to voting decisions. Connective action theory helps explain how hashtag-mediated communication links personalised grievances without necessarily giving them an electoral orientation.

The study contributes to African political communication research by identifying the period between elections as a site of political participation. During this period, citizens evaluate governments, contest policies and articulate expectations about subsequent elections. #TinubuMustGo illustrates how digital platforms can connect civic activism, protest mobilisation and electoral communication between electoral cycles.

The study has limitations. Its focus on a single hashtag and platform captures only a segment of the wider political conversation. The qualitative analysis identifies patterns in public communication but cannot establish participants' demographic characteristics, motivations or whether online expressions translate into voting or other electoral behaviour. Future research could examine the campaign across platforms, incorporate interviews or surveys and follow its development towards the 2027 elections to assess whether digitally networked engagement develops into sustained electoral participation.

title: Youthwashing as Political Performance in the Digital Age: Discursive Construction on X (Twitter), Instagram, and Facebook During Nigeria's 2026-2027 Electioneering
abstract: During the second phase of INEC's 2026 Continuous Voter Registration (CVR), 9,324,349 young Nigerians were newly registered. This period in the Fourth Republic marks an unprecedented democratic awakening, reminiscent of the #EndSARS protests and the 2023 Obidient Movement. While political elites acknowledge the electoral significance of youth demographics, much of their campaign messaging targets them. This study explored 'youthwashing' as a form of theatrical political rhetoric on X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and Facebook between 19 August and 30 October 2026, during Nigeria's 2027 election campaign preparations. Using multimodal discourse analysis and theories of mediated authenticity and performativity, it analysed how politicians and influencers portray "youth" as an electoral asset while marginalising them in policy engagement. A purposive sample of 60 public posts across Facebook, X, and Instagram was selected based on youth-oriented hashtags, visuals, and captions. The findings were examined against indicators such as hidden sponsorship, tokenistic youth imagery, hedged policy claims, and aestheticised politics, collectively revealing political elites' youthwashing. The study argued that these tactics foster an illusion of youth inclusion without genuine representation or accountability, influencing perceived legitimacy and potentially discouraging meaningful youth participation. Recommendations on campaign regulation, disclosure standards, youth, and media literacy will shape future electoral discourse in Nigeria.

bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

One enduring phenomenon shaping politics, polity, and policy is the internet's democratisation and its redefinition of political life, especially electioneering. The mass exodus of voters to social media platforms has reshaped political communication, including how it is framed and targeted. As digital natives grow, political elites match them with a vast supply of niche messages that mirror and resonate with them. This paradigm shift emboldens digital activism, social reengineering, and political manoeuvring. It is an unprecedented development for both encoders and decoders of digital semiotics. Incidentally, the forthcoming 2026-2027 Nigerian elections are set against a political climate in which youth have increasingly gained prominence in the country's democratic politics. One major sign of this trend was observed during the second round of the Continuous Voter Registration (CVR). According to INEC statistics, 9,324,349 young Nigerians were newly registered during the 2026 exercise (Akinwale, 2026). This increased visibility makes it possible to consider how political actors communicate with youth before elections.

Mustapha and Omar (2020) argued that Nigerian youths engaged in substantial online political activity during the 2019 elections and that social media use remained important even when other forms of civic and political engagement were controlled for the public good or for ulterior motives. Obisesan (2022) found that social media helped Nigerian youths build political agency, engage in debate, and develop socio-political networks during the 2019 elections. These studies collectively established that young Nigerians are both consumers and producers of political communication. This was evident during the youth-led #EndSARS protests against incessant police brutality in October 2020. The youths fiercely deployed social media such as Twitter (now X), Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and others to inform, document abuses, organise protests, and lobby for reforms. The protests highlighted the role that digital platforms might play in youth political participation and collective action (Adegbola et al., 2022; Uwalaka, 2022).

According to Dambo et al. (2022), Chiluwa (2023), and Awopetu and Chiluwa (2023), social media gave Nigerian youths opportunities to express grievances collectively and organise protests, while also revealing the systemic constraints facing digitally mediated activism. The political forces of #EndSARS also converged with the 2023 political environment, especially the rise of the Obidient movement. This indicates that young people's political activism in Nigeria increasingly occurs through digitally mediated collective identity and communication. As Ezeigbo (2025) demonstrates in his analysis of the 2023 elections, youths used social media for political advocacy, communication, and political activities.

However, this trend creates a major paradox. As young Nigerians' electoral importance grows, political elites have an incentive to recognise, respond to, and connect with youth. Meanwhile, youth are excluded from candidate selection, policy creation, political decision-making, and leadership. This distinction between visibility and agency lies at the heart of contemporary political communication aimed at youth. Ezeigbo (2025) notes that with the youth's high level of social media engagement during the 2023 elections, young Nigerians' participation has increased; however, this does not mean political institutions have given young people equal influence.

In this context, youthwashing serves as the organising framework for the current research. Viterbo (2025) defined youthwashing as a cynical practice that exploits young people without necessarily addressing their problems or engaging them. This definition helps us develop a conceptual approach to studying situations where the symbolism of youth inclusion does not align with youth activism. Accordingly, the current study adopts youthwashing as a relevant concept for analysing youth-oriented political communication in Nigeria, treating it as an analytical lens observable in practices such as tokenistic youth imagery, behind-the-scenes sponsorship, policy hedging, and aesthetic politics.
## Research Questions
The research questions that guide the study are as follows:
1. How is youth participation discursively constructed on X, Instagram, and Facebook during Nigeria's 2026-2027 electioneering?
2. In what ways are youth represented through textual, visual, and audiovisual features in selected political posts on X, Instagram, and Facebook?
3. In what ways can youthwashing be observed through sponsorship, tokenism, hedging in policy discourse, and the aesthetics of politics?
4. How do the constructions and manifestations of youthwashing vary across X, Instagram, and Facebook during Nigeria's 2026-2027 electioneering?
## Literature Review

This study reviews existing literature on social media, youth as a communication agency, and media advocacy as an intervention tool for the silenced voices. The review covers relevant concepts, theories, and empirical studies to help define the existing knowledge base and to lay the groundwork for the present study.
## Youthwashing as Political Performance

According to Viterbo (2025), youthwashing is the self-centred appropriation of youth that fails to adequately address their interests. Viterbo shows how organisations may invoke youth participation while retaining considerable discretion over whose voices they listen to and how they define participation. Youthwashing becomes relevant to political communication in electoral competition, and when politicians try to show their connection to young voters. The "washing" family of concepts highlights situations in which institutions, companies, or politicians strategically associate themselves with socially valuable causes or identities through communication, even when the link between symbolism and practice is minimal or even contradictory. For example, greenwashing refers to communication that can give audiences an overly positive image of an organisation's environmental practices (Delmas & Burbano, 2011; Lyon & Montgomery, 2015). The key message is that claims and performances need to be examined in relation to the practices they supposedly represent. In this study, youthwashing is defined as the strategic construction of youth inclusion in discourse and multimodal performance, whereby youth participation can be visible, linguistically or symbolically constructed, without any proof of actual youth engagement, representation, or political responsiveness. Youthwashing thus deliberately differs from normal youth-focused political communication. The presence of youth in a political campaign message cannot be considered youthwashing on its own. It becomes a possibility for analysing youthwashing only when youth inclusion is continuously constructed in political communication despite a lack of evidence of engagement, accountability, and policy specificity.

Mediated authenticity, the first theoretical point of reference, has become an important feature of modern political communication, as political actors must demonstrate sincerity, approachability, and relevance to citizens. In his definition of political authenticity, Luebke (2021) argues that it is a social construct developed and negotiated through political communication among politicians, the media, and the public. He distinguishes performed, mediated, and perceived authenticity and highlights the dimensions used to construct political authenticity. Similarly, Enli (2015) shows that mediation creates authenticity rather than simply transmitting a pre-existing quality. This mediation is intensified on social media platforms, where political actors can communicate directly with audiences by carefully curating the images, experiences, and interactions that shape their public identity (Enli, 2016; Marwick & Boyd, 2011).

Mediated authenticity is particularly relevant to youthwashing, as political actors may seek to perform sincerity in relation to youth politics. Casual images, youthful language, videos in direct address, popular cultural references, youth fashion choices, influencers, and spontaneous interactions can create an image of intimacy and shared identity. According to Marwick & Boyd (2011), social media users negotiate authenticity in relation to imagined audiences, while Luebke (2021) argues that politicians' authenticity is constantly constructed and negotiated through mediation. Therefore, youthwashing can be viewed as an attempt to perform a sincere connection with youth rather than to make explicit claims about youth inclusion.

The second theoretical frame is performativity, specifically the approaches of Goffman (1959) and Butler (1990). Goffman's (1959) dramaturgical theory focuses on the theatricality of social interaction, impression management, audience expectations, and the presentation of identity. This blend of mediated authenticity and performativity frames youthwashing as staged inclusion rather than genuine representation. A politician can repeatedly perform closeness to young people through photographs, videos, hashtags, and youth-centric speeches, while the communicative performance itself becomes evidence of their assumed inclusion. Symbolic visibility does not imply political agency.

This framework is salient to studies of Nigerian political communication. Most existing work has focused on how social media became a panopticon for youth engagement and political mobilisation. Aduloju (2016) argued that social media remained an effective avenue for youth political networking and discourse in the run-up to the 2015 elections. In contrast, Mustapha and Omar (2020) reviewed Nigeria's 2019 general elections and argued that young people's political participation was online rather than offline. Similarly, Obisesan (2022) argued that social media became influential in youth agency, political debates, and agenda-setting for the 2019 elections. Most recently, scholarship on Nigeria has focused on digitally mediated activism, identity construction, and political impact.
## Youth Political Participation in the Nigerian Fourth Republic

Youth political participation has become an increasingly salient feature of the Nigerian Fourth Republic- the current democratic dispensation that started on 29th May 1999, based on the constitution that was designed in the same year to favour the federal presidential system. Although youth numbers have not necessarily translated into equal representation in formal politics, statistics illustrate the rising importance of youth as an electoral constituency (Mustapha & Omar, 2020; Obisesan, 2022). INEC's preparations for the 2027 election continue to focus on maintaining and updating the integrity of the voter register, making youth registration and mobilisation especially relevant in the current electoral climate. Youth participation has not been limited to electoral processes; it has also become increasingly digital. The #EndSARS campaign underscored the role of social media in mobilisation, identity formation, resistance, and the dissemination of protest discourse (Bodunrin & Matsilele, 2024; Awopetu & Chiluwa, 2023). This meant the movement involved more than commentary on social media; it included both physical protest and calls for political accountability.

Furthermore, the 'Obidient' Movement- a socio-political and grassroots network that supported the presidential ambition of the Labour Party candidate, Peter Obi, in the 2023 general elections further highlighted another aspect of political participation through youth-mediated political activism, linking social media activism with electoral politics (Obisesan, 2022; Onayinka et al., 2026). According to Egbunike (2025), Twitter (now X) was particularly significant in mobilising young people within the movement, with identity formation and perceptions of economic disadvantage as key factors. More recent studies, such as those by Onayinka, Oluwasola, and Oyedele (2026), have also examined connections between the #EndSARS and Obidient movements through mediated political activism, as well as voting and political involvement.
## Political Marketing: Tokenism, Symbolic Politics and Concealed Promotion

The growing professionalism of digital political campaigns has also raised questions about the relationship between political marketing and political representation. Political marketing applies techniques to political actors, parties, ideas, and identities, which can lead campaigns to focus on image-building, emotional appeals, and audience segmentation (Lees-Marshment, 2001; Scammell, 2015). This suggests that symbolic politics will gain prominence, since political meanings can be conveyed without mentioning policies at all.

One example is tokenism, which uses particular groups symbolically to create the impression of involvement without real influence. In youth-oriented campaigning, images of young people, events targeting young people, youthful communicators, or the use of the term "the future" may signal inclusion of a generation. However, at the same time, they may not provide clear information about involvement in decision-making or how the needs of young people are translated into policy. This kind of communication should be studied multimodally, since meaning can be created through the interaction of written text, visual design, gesture, costume, music, editing, and platform norms (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006; Machin & Mayr, 2012).

Another issue is astroturfing, which involves organising apparently spontaneous grassroots support to mimic genuine public enthusiasm. Modern political influence campaigns may involve influencers, paid promoters, and secret relationships between politicians and communicators. In Nigeria, Uwalaka, Amadi, and Enyindah (2025) found secret influencer-based political promotion involving compensation, exaggeration, disguise, and public image management for politicians.

Cross-platform research shows that political campaigning often occurs behind the scenes, where large clusters of influencer accounts and compensation arrangements make it difficult to distinguish authentic political expression from strategically sponsored communication (Gaw et al., 2026). These practices apply to youthwashing, as youth voices can be used as political promotional material without audiences fully understanding the sponsorship and strategic nature of the messages.
## Literature Gap and Justification for the Study

Several previous studies indicate that young people in Nigeria play a prominent role in elections, activism, and political mobilisation (Aduloju, 2016; Mustapha & Omar, 2020; Obisesan, 2022; Egbunike, 2025). Previous research has analysed social media campaigns, political influence operations, and electoral communication dynamics on specific social media platforms (Ahmad et al., 2026; Uwalaka et al., 2025). Nevertheless, this literature tends to focus on youth as political participants, users, and mobilised audiences, without examining how political actors construct images and meanings of youth participation through multimodal political campaigning.

Further comparative work is needed on textual, visual, and audiovisual political communications aimed at youth on X, Instagram, and Facebook in Nigeria. Current scholarship usually focuses on individual platforms, political engagement, mobilisation, misinformation, or campaign efficiency. Less work examines how youth inclusion is represented in images, captions, videos, hashtags, influencers, sponsorship indicators, and policy statements.

This gap justifies the current research. By studying youth-oriented political posts through multimodal discourse analysis, the research goes beyond whether Nigerian youths engage in politics to examine how political actors portray, present, and perform youth participation. Tokenistic representation of youth, covert sponsorship, vague political statements, and aesthetic politics are ways to analyse how youthwashing manifests. The research, therefore, combines literature on youth participation, digital election politics, and political marketing with youthwashing, while also developing Nigerian political communication research from youth mobilisation to youth inclusion.
## Methodology

The study employs multimodal discourse analysis (MDA) as a framework to analyse how digital political communication constructs and represents youth participation across textual, visual, and audio-visual modalities (Kress and van Leeuwen, 2006; Machin, and Mayr, 2012). This approach is well-suited, given that political messages on contemporary social media platforms are multimodal and combine captions, hashtags, photos, videos, slogans, graphics, music, and other semiotic resources. As such, it enabled the study to go beyond what political actors say about young people and to examine how youth participation is rhetorically and visually performed.

The study used purposive sampling, and 60 political posts were publicly obtained from Facebook, X, and Instagram, with approximately 20 posts from each platform. The choice of Facebook, X, and Instagram was informed by their functionalities and the specificity of their users. Twitter/X is known for civic activism and public discourse (Obia, 2025); Facebook for its mass community and entertainment; and Instagram for visual branding and visibility. In addition, among Nigeria's young users, Instagram is estimated at 77%, Facebook at 94.7%, and X at 64% (Statista, 2026).

The posts were collected from Wednesday, 19 August, when INEC lifted the ban on political campaigns, through 30 September 2026, within the stipulated period for political campaigning ahead of the 2027 elections in Nigeria. Only posts containing youth-oriented hashtags, captions, images, slogans, or an explicit reference to youth participation, leadership, empowerment, mobilisation, and political inclusion were included. The selection focused on how young people are represented as voters, supporters, campaign volunteers, leaders, or agents of political change. The research used only publicly available social media information and anonymised data (Franzke et al., 2020) on regular users where necessary. This study is constrained by the purposeful sampling of 60 posts and its narrow scope on Facebook, X, and Instagram. Interpretive MDA (Machin and Mayr 2012) involves subjective researcher judgement, but systematic coding and intercoder checks enhanced analytical rigour.
## Findings and Analysis
In this study, the posts were analysed across four dimensions of youthwashing: hidden sponsorship, tokenistic youth imagery, hedged policy statements, and aestheticised politics.

This provisional distribution has aestheticised politics in the sample more often, especially on Instagram, where visual presentation, short-form video, and curated political imagery offer ample opportunities for stylistic performance among youth. Tokenistic youth imagery is also prevalent across the three platforms. Hedged policy claims are much more frequent on X and Facebook, where textual political messaging is more prominent. The cross-platform pattern shows that Instagram had the most prominent visual and aesthetic dimension, with 18 of 20 posts being aestheticised political statements and 16 posts featuring tokenised youth imagery. Hedged policy statements occurred more frequently on the X platform due to its relatively text-based political rhetoric. In turn, Facebook occupied the middle ground, combining visuals with text and community communication.
## Hidden Sponsorship: Unacknowledged Political Sponsorship Behind Alleged Spontaneous Youth Content

Hidden sponsorship was coded in 21 of the 60 posts (35%), making it the least common of the four codes. This lower frequency does not detract from its analytical significance, as sponsorship is often less observable than other elements, such as language and imagery. The coded posts contained youth-oriented content that appeared to come from individual youth, influencers, or supporters. However, their content showed features pointing to political coordination and sponsorship, without necessarily acknowledging the same level.

The coded data, therefore, indicate that hidden sponsorship may play a role in youthwashing when the political or promotional connection underlying the communication is not sufficiently disclosed. The coding did not establish hidden sponsorship based solely on stylistic similarity. In cases where sponsorship could not be proven with observable evidence, the post was treated as an indication of potential hidden political promotion rather than as proof of sponsorship. Thus, sponsorship through hidden channels could be confirmed by evidence of political financing, association, or coordination without disclosure, while sponsorship disclosure was not taken as sole evidence of such sponsorship.
## Tokenistic Youth Imagery: Youth as Backdrop vs Substantial Participation

Tokenistic youth imagery was observed in 42 posts (70.0%), making it the second most frequent indicator. The coding involved analysing how young people appeared in political pictures and videos and whether they appeared as political actors or merely as evidence of a political figure's popularity. A common theme was young people appearing around political figures at rallies, consultation meetings, empowerment programmes, and campaign meetings. The appearance of young people in political pictures and videos signals relevance, support, and inclusion, but the political figure remains the dominant political actor.
## Hedged Policy Claims: Ambiguous and Vague Policy Statements about Youth

There were 39 examples (65.0%) of hedged policy claims. These tended to use very broad statements about empowering young people, offering employment or entrepreneurship, encouraging youth participation in leadership or politics, and promoting innovation, education, and other policies, without clearly explaining how these would be implemented. Examples of this pattern of communication include statements such as "empowering the next generation," "giving young people a voice," "creating opportunities for young people," and "supporting young leaders." All these statements sound appealing, but might lack substance if the actual measures for implementation are not explained in the communication.
## Aestheticised Politics: Substance Under the Guise of Style in Campaign Materials Targeting Youth

Aestheticised politics had the highest frequency of use, appearing in 46 of the 60 posts (76.7%). This refers to the use of visual styles, including youthfulness, music, fashionable clothing, dynamic editing, contemporary cultural references, slogans, hashtags, stylish photography, and videos, to convey youthfulness and political substance.

The high frequency in this category underscores the importance of style in contemporary political communication aimed at youth. Social media platforms provide political actors with resources to construct their political identities through images, sound, typography, editing, and performance (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006; Machin & Mayr, 2012). The coded materials revealed that youthfulness might be expressed less through discussions of youth issues and more through aesthetic links to contemporary youth culture. This highlights a clear distinction between youth-centred political materials and youth-centred political aesthetics.
## Cross-Platform Comparison: X, Instagram, and Facebook

The coded indicators showed that youthwashing also occurred in different ways, depending on the affordances of the platforms. X was more closely linked to discursive and conversational performances, such as concise youth claims, hashtags, slogans, and impromptu youth political interactions. Instagram offered a suitable environment for visual performances, making tokenistic imagery and aesthetics more prominent. Facebook supported both visual and textual performances, as well as video performances.

These differences support Bossetta's (2018) thesis that platform architecture shapes political communication. Likewise, Kreiss et al. (2018) show how political actors tailor their communication to each platform's audience, affordances, genre, and timing. Accordingly, youthwashing should not be conceived as a single communication strategy. Performative modes vary with each platform's capabilities. X enables immediacy and conversational authenticity; Instagram enables visual intimacy, lifestyle, and politicised self-representation aesthetics; Facebook combines community-oriented interaction with text, visual, and audiovisual campaign communication.

Among the frequency distribution, aestheticised politics (76.7%) and hedged policy claims (65.0%) were the most common indicators, with tokenism of youth visuals appearing in 70.0% of posts and sponsorship hiding in 35.0%. Youthwashing involves the interplay of visibility, authenticity, ambiguity, and aesthetics. The present analysis does not claim that all youth-oriented messages were deceitful or that political actors intended to mislead their youth audience. Rather, it identifies a set of communicative patterns that enable the performance of youth inclusion in ways that may overshadow youth agency and specific politics.
## Discussion

The results suggest that youthwashing is not a single communication practice but a hybrid of discourses, images, and promotion. Hidden sponsorships, tokenistic youth visuals, ambivalent policy statements, and aestheticised politics operated at different levels to construct youth inclusion in the political discourse of Nigerian electoral communication as performance. It builds on Viterbo's (2025) conceptualisation of youthwashing as co-option without addressing youth concerns in the context of electoral communication in Nigeria, through authenticity, visibility, ambiguity, and aesthetics.

The first indicator, hidden sponsorship, concerns the creation of ostensibly authentic political communication. Messages targeting youth audiences, disseminated via influencers or supporters without any obvious political sponsorship, can appear as organic youth expression. This aligns with Uwalaka, Amadi, and Enyindah's (2025) study of Nigerian political influence operations, which identified remuneration, hyperbole, and concealment. It also supports Luebke's (2021) concept of political authenticity via media. Therefore, youthwashing can be used to create seemingly organic political communication from youth citizens.

Tokenistic youth imagery was the second indicator, highlighting the distinction between youth visibility and youth agency. The youth were depicted as crowds, supporters, or participants at events, or as visible proof of the generation's attractiveness, without participating in decision-making. This finding is especially important because young Nigerians have demonstrated their political agency through social media, elections, and digital activism (Aduloju, 2016; Mustapha & Omar, 2020; Obisesan, 2022). This contradiction is evident in the relationship between youth as political actors and symbolic capital. A multimodal approach accentuates this issue by showing that composition, salience, framing, and positioning define meaning in political images (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006; Machin & Mayr, 2012).

The third indicator, namely hedged policy claims, extends youthwashing into the linguistic domain. Mentions of youth empowerment, leadership, employment, and opportunities signal responsiveness but often omit details on implementation methods, beneficiaries, timing, or commitments in measurable terms. This finding is relevant to studies in political marketing on image, appeal, and audience-centred communication (Lees-Marshment, 2001; Scammell, 2015). Hedging is significant in this context because persistent vagueness allows politicians to connect with youth concerns without making concrete commitments.

The fourth indicator, aestheticised politics, synthesised the various dimensions aesthetically. Music, fashion, visual design, editing, cultural references, and format were among the elements that created youth and generational proximity. According to Kress and Van Leeuwen (2006) and Machin and Mayr (2012), political meaning arises from the interplay of linguistic and visual meaning. In this regard, youthfulness could become a political aesthetic that performs closeness to youth, particularly.

The implications of the indicators above for political legitimacy and youth political trust are that political legitimacy, in part, rests on perceptions of responsiveness, representation, and connectedness to citizens. When youth inclusion is largely symbolic, a gap may arise between perceived and actual inclusion. This research does not test political trust, nor does it imply causality. Nevertheless, a persistent disparity between symbolic representation and active participation over time might affect how young audiences perceive political sincerity. Luebke (2021) highlights that authenticity is negotiated by the audience, not solely controlled by politicians.

The results also suggest the possibility of demobilisation from politics. It might be assumed that youthwashing makes young people feel represented because of the prominence of their images, voices, and culture. In such a case, if visibility becomes equivalent to influence, some individuals may feel that participation is no longer necessary. Alternatively, awareness of the discrepancy between representation and responsiveness might lead to cynicism or demobilisation. These factors have not been examined, yet they matter, as social media is part of Nigerian youth political participation and political mobilisation (Aduloju, 2016; Obisesan, 2022; Onayinka et al., 2026).

The study's main theoretical contribution is to broaden the scope of mediated authenticity and performativity in the context of elections in Nigeria. The existing literature focuses on the idea that political actors increasingly use the media to demonstrate sincerity and credibility (Enli, 2015; 2016; Luebke, 2021), while performativity helps explain how identities emerge through acts (Butler, 1990; Goffman, 1959). The current study combines these approaches and demonstrates how youth inclusion can be performed as a political identity. Thus, youthwashing reveals the link between digital political communication and symbolism; youth visibility does not necessarily imply youth agency.
## Recommendations

Based on the study's findings, the following recommendations are proposed. First, campaign regulations and disclosure requirements should be strengthened to enhance transparency in digital political communication. Those engaged in political campaigns, including political actors, campaign groups, and influential figures involved in sponsored political communications, should disclose their funding, sponsorship, and promotional associations. Electoral commissions should also provide clear definitions of what constitutes political advertisements and organised campaign communications on social media channels.

Secondly, media and digital literacy programmes for young people should be strengthened. These programmes will equip young people with the skills to analyse political messages critically; spot tokenistic portrayals of youth, visual persuasion techniques, and policy promises; and distinguish between sponsored and independent political communications. This can be achieved through universities, civil society organisations, and media institutions.

Third, INEC must intensify its monitoring and civic-education efforts on digital politics, particularly in political advertising and sponsorship disclosure. Civil society organisations must be able to independently monitor political communication among young people and develop civic-education resources based on documented trends. Social media sites must also become more transparent about political advertisements by providing more information about sponsors and, where possible, making archived political content available on their sites.

Lastly, political campaign organisations must actively engage young people in consultations, policy formulation, and campaign management, rather than relying on symbolism in political campaigns. Researchers and journalists must continue analysing youth-related political claims, sponsorship, and political representations.
## Conclusion

The study explored youthwashing as a political performance in the digital age, specifically examining how youth participation in politics was discursively and multimodally constructed on social media platforms X, Instagram, and Facebook during Nigeria's 2026-2027 election campaign. The core premise of the study is that greater visibility of youth participation in political communication does not necessarily indicate youth agency or youth representation in that communication. Rather, youth-focused political communication uses specific linguistic and visual representations of youth participation in politics to create impressions of the inclusiveness of its content.

Further research should extend the study longitudinally through the 2027 elections to examine how youthwashing is produced and evolves across the stages of the electoral cycle. Multimodal discourse analysis could be combined with interviews, surveys, digital ethnography, and platform-use data to examine the relationship between political representation and audience interpretation and participation.

title: Framing Electoral Credibility on X: Public Discourse on Real-Time Result Transmission Ahead of Nigeria's 2027 General Elections
abstract: As the 2027 general elections in Nigeria approaches, real-time result transmission has become an important battleground for negotiating, building, and challenging electoral credibility. This study analyses how X becomes a platform where electoral transparency, trust, reform, and suspicion are discussed long before votes are cast. In addition to being seen as a legal and technological practice, the discussion of result transmission is also regarded as a political communication practice that emerges from elite framing, platform logic, news dissemination, and public response. Through a qualitative textual analysis of posts and reply threads shared by electoral agencies, political parties, civil society organisations, journalists, and influential individuals, this study uncovers the main frames in pre-election discussions on X. Rather than being an attempt to comment on the policies being discussed, the online debate on the issue actually becomes a source for setting public expectations regarding the integrity of the 2027 polls. Thus, this research contributes to the existing body of literature on platforms and political communication in Nigeria by analysing how electoral credibility is framed, amplified, and challenged through X. It becomes clear, then, that digital framing has become one of the most important preconditions for whether electoral results are going to be accepted, rejected, or contested in Nigeria.
