bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

The 2027 general elections in Nigeria are currently taking shape during the pre-election phase. Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has released a new schedule for conducting presidential and National Assembly elections on 16 January 2027 and governorship and State Assembly elections on 6 February 2027. Along with these early arrangements, there is ongoing discussion about real-time electronic result transmission, which has emerged as a major credibility issue in the election process. Reuters reported in February 2026 that the Nigerian Senate approved the real-time transmission of results despite reservations from some members about insecurity and unequal internet access. Such trends suggest that the credibility of elections is being challenged before the election process, not just afterward (INEC, 2026; Reuters, 2026).

Election credibility relies not only on regulations and procedures, but also on how they are framed and explained to the public. Ajaegbu and Ajaegbu (2024) found that social media has become a norm for political participation in Sub-Saharan Africa, while Fisher et al. (2024) noted that, in West Africa, digital media is now integral to political communication and party messaging. Therefore, debates about election procedures on social media are part of that process and shape how citizens view transparency and institutional effectiveness. The platform is examined not so much as a means of transmission as a place where legitimacy and visibility are mediated. As Naranjo-Vinueza et al. (2025) note, the dynamic nature of X influences how political communication on the platform constructs notions of authority and public meaning. This relates to the Nigerian example, where real-time result transmission is seen not only as an improvement in administrative processes but also as a way to verify and test the election process itself.

Research suggests that political discourse can undermine electoral trust before voting begins at polling units (Sinclair et al. (2018). Negative campaigns especially reduce trust where confidence in institutions is already lacking (Amakoh, 2025). This is relevant because debate about result transmission occurs in an environment already fraught with trust and legitimacy issues. While most discussions focus on administrative and legal aspects, less attention is given to discussions regarding electronic transmission of results on X. This study investigates how posts and comments have framed the transmission of results as a symbol of transparency and legitimacy ahead of the 2027 elections. This study addresses this gap by analysing discourse on X about the transmission of results before Nigeria's 2027 general elections, treating it as a communicative practice that shapes perceptions of electoral credibility. Two main objectives guide the study:
To examine how selected posts and reply threads on X frame real-time result transmission ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general election; and
Analyse how these frames shape public understanding of electoral credibility, transparency, and trust in the pre-election period.
## Platforms and the Public Construction of Electoral Credibility

Political communication research has evolved from merely studying digital media as channels for disseminating messages to recognising their role as spaces where platform-specific mechanisms create legitimacy, visibility, and power. As Naranjo-Vinueza et al. (2025) note, X has become a platform that puts political visibility and public authority at stake. This aspect is critical to this research, as a discussion of technical or administrative matters can swiftly become a symbolic battle over trust in institutions once taken up on X. This means the meaning of regulations is determined not solely by the regulations themselves but also by how they are framed.

Research suggests that electoral trust is sensitive to the overall communication context. According to Amakoh (2025), negative media reporting adversely affects electoral trust in contexts where institutional trust is weak. Similarly, Mauk and Grömping (2024) observe that online misinformation reduces accuracy and polarises beliefs about election fairness, whereas Cohen et al. (2024) note that electoral trust is contextual and depends on citizens' interpretations of elections. Overall, this research implies that procedures are not sufficient for credibility, but that credibility is constructed publicly through communication, interpretation, and exposure to rival claims. Therefore, in the present research, it is essential to view the debate over the real-time transmission of results on X as an integral part of the credibility process.
## Social Media and Election Communication in Africa

The debate around the role of social media in African elections research is no longer largely centered on whether social media is important. What is more crucial is the discussion of its relevance within particular political and media systems. According to Abboud et al. (2024), in their research on the 2022 presidential election, the influence of social media on politics is contingent on interactions among platforms, conventional media, and politics. This is relevant because it does not treat social media as an entity in its own right.

Research conducted in recent years on Africa suggests the same. According to Ajaegbu and Ajaegbu (2024), social media is now an everyday tool for political participation and discourse throughout sub-Saharan Africa. Fisher et al. (2024) illustrate how WhatsApp plays a pivotal role in the organisation and control of messages by the parties in Ghana and Nigeria. News and political conversations motivate people to participate actively in 30 African countries. Yet, the correlation is contingent on context (Adegbola & O'Neil, 2025). For instance, Omoniyi (2026) illustrates that the voter education programme run by INEC in Ondo City, Nigeria, was neither fully inclusive nor timely. The evidence above suggests that both social media and civic communication, whether effective or ineffective, can influence the pre-election information environment. That is why social media discussions of electoral procedures within the framework of the 2027 Nigerian elections are especially vital
## Electoral Credibility and the Pre-Election Information Environment

Electoral credibility would also need to address the disinformation problems that have characterised pre-election discourses. According to Hassan (2023), disinformation is a major element of political and electoral discourse in Nigeria, especially on social media platforms. Omilusi (2025) noted how election disinformation in Africa undermines not only the electoral process but also democratic values and people's rights. The significance of these studies is that they demonstrate that public discourse on transparency does not occur in a neatly organised information environment.

The recent studies from Nigeria support this notion. As shown by Okorie and Olagunju (2025), Lagos social media users encounter false information despite their high level of fact-checking knowledge. Additionally, Schwemmer and Riedl (2025) show how political influencers can sway elections by establishing specific structures of visibility and influence within networked environments. As shown by Uwalaka et al. (2025), secret influencer communities or "Data Boys" can be leveraged to advance and restore the reputations of political actors on social media, maintaining the façade of authenticity. In other words, these studies suggest that pre-election discussions on X encompass both sincere debate and organised efforts.
## Theoretical Framework

This research is based on the Framing Theory. Entman (1993) offered one of the best formulations of this framework, arguing that framing is a process of highlighting selected aspects of reality and making them more visible in a communicative text to diagnose problems and their causes, make moral judgments, and offer solutions. . In other words, public matters do not simply get into communication spaces, they get there after being chosen and highlighted in a particular way. It is also helpful because it connects media texts to public interpretation. As Scheufele (1999) states, framing is a process in which communicators create frames, audiences accept them, and public interpretations are formed. In the context of an upcoming election, this implies that rival posts, comments, and discussions on X will not only reflect public opinion but also help shape the interpretation of the election's credibility. Therefore, a discussion on the transmission of results can be framed as a technical necessity, an impossible expectation, an indication of weak institutions, or a means of protecting people from rigging.

According to de Vreese (2005), framing should be seen as an aspect of media production and of its effects on audience interpretation of messages. Chong and Druckman (2007) reinforce this framework by arguing that framing is important because people respond differently depending on which aspects are emphasised in the communication process. This is important to this study since X is not just a platform for communicating in the official language. It is also a place for responses by journalists, activists, political allies, opponents, and regular users to interpretations of events. This means that the transmission of results will not be decided by formal policy discourse alone. In most cases, public trust in elections depends on the first emphasis that attracts people's attention. For instance, if the dominant frame is about transparency, then the transmission of the results can be seen as an improvement in credibility. On the other hand, if the dominant frame is on technical problems or security issues, the same process can raise doubts among citizens.

In a nutshell, this framework works well for the study in two respects. First, it provides an ideal platform for identifying the patterns that define real-time discussions about result transmission on X. Second, it helps explain how these patterns can shape public perceptions of the credibility, transparency, and trustworthiness of the 2027 general election. This theory works well for the research because it enables the researcher to shift from describing patterns of result transmission to interpreting them.
## Methodology

This research uses a qualitative textual methodology to examine the meanings constructed in selected messages and reply threads on X about the real-time transmission of results before the Nigerian general elections of 2027. This qualitative methodology is appropriate because it explores debates and discussions about the credibility of the election in an increasingly rapid digital environment. Qualitative methodology is appropriate for exploring topics in which language, context, and the meanings of communication conveyed by the text are essential (Creswell & Poth, 2018; Tracy, 2010).

Purposive sampling identifies relevant messages and reply chains from publicly available messages related to the research objectives. Messages are included in the analysis if they directly discuss the transmission of election results, electronic result transmission, or similar topics related to the 2027 election in Nigeria. To explore different perspectives on the topic, the sample of messages is collected from categories of actors, including institutional actor (INEC), political actors (Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, Yunusa Tanko/Obidient Movement, Official PDP, Nasiru Ahmad El-Rufai), civic actors (EiE Nigeria, Nigeria Civil Society Situation Room), and media institutions (ARISE News, TheCable, The Sun. and THISDAY), were selected because they directly addressed real-time result transmission, electronic result transmission, IReV, BVAS, manual backup, statutory backing or related electoral credibility debates and because such actors occupy visible positions in Nigeria's pre-election information environment. The corpus comprised 14 original public posts and seven selected replies on X between January and May 2026. This period was selected because it captured the emergence and continuation of the public debate central to this study

The selection was also guided by public accessibility, traceability through post URLs, actor diversity, and clear framing relevance to transparency, institutional sincerity, technical feasibility, electoral preparedness, or public trust. Ethically, ordinary users were included only through selected replies that substantively accepted, extended, questioned or challenged the frames in the original posts. However, they were anonymised because they participated as private individuals rather than as official or organisational actors. This aligns with internet-mediated research ethics on participant confidentiality and identifiability, which recommend contextual ethical judgement and the careful handling of identifiable online data, even when such data are publicly available (Kaye et al., 2021; frannzke et al., 2020). Additionally, because political debate on social media can contain sensitive language, particularly in the context of pre-election.

The original posts and replies were selected purposively because the study sought information-rich texts that could illuminate how real-time result transmission was framed and contested within selected X discourse. This aligns with qualitative framing approaches that support analysis of purposively selected, meaningful, and manageable online-media samples rather than statistically representative datasets (Wachinger et al., 2025). The reply-thread sample was used as supplementary evidence of audience engagement with the frames identified in the original posts; it was not intended as a representative sample of all responses to the 14 posts, nor as a matched reply for every post. Replies were included only where they made substantive contributions by accepting, extending, questioning, or challenging the frames under analysis. This use of replies aligns with conversational framing research on X, which shows that replies can extend, challenge, or reframe meanings introduced in original posts (Zade et al., 2024). The six replies should therefore be read as information-rich examples within the selected X discourse, consistent with the qualitative framing purpose of examining how meanings were constructed and contested rather than measuring the volume or representativeness of responses across the platform.

Framing forms the foundation of thematic coding. The first step involves rereading the selected texts to identify patterns in framing and evaluation of real-time result transmission. This step focuses on problem identification, causal explanation, evaluation, and proposed solutions, following the structure of frame analysis (Entman, 1993). The second step involves organising the identified patterns of recurrence into broader interpretive frames. This allows us to determine how electoral credibility relates to the chosen topic. For this purpose, we used Braun and Clarke's (2022) approach to thematic analysis and Saldaña's (2021) principles of coding.

This research applies qualitative standards of rigour through coding notes, categorisation, and memo writing. Reflexivity is another crucial aspect because prior understandings of elections, media, and institutions may shape interpretations of political discourse. As Tracy (2010) claims, the credibility of a qualitative analysis relies on transparency, sincerity, and consistency in the methodological framework and the arguments raised by the researcher. These aspects shape the current analysis and allow frames to emerge from the data rather than being preconceived.
## Results

This section presents the key frames that emerged from selected public X posts and replies on the issue of real-time transmission of results in preparation for the 2027 general elections in Nigeria. Public entities, including individuals, media institutions, civic associations, and others, are named as they posted using public accounts. Regular users in the reply thread are represented using codes such as R1, R2, and R3, and so forth. The original posts are represented using codes such as P1, P2, P3, etc.

## Real-Time Result Transmission as a Transparency Safeguard

This frame presents real-time result transmission as a protection against electoral manipulation, and transparency during voting. From table 1, posts under this frame connected real-time result transmission to transparency, immediate access to results, reduced chances of manipulation, and increased public trust. Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi linked real-time transmission of results to election transparency and public trust before the 2027 elections (P1; P2). The discussion implies that the issue of real-time transmission of results reflects a lack of trust in the democratic process. EiE Nigeria demanded the mandatory real-time transmission of results to protect votes and ensure accountability in the elections (P10). Situation Room (11) framed real-time transmission of results as a civic accountability and vote protection issue by calling for the conference committee to adopt the house version that included real-time transmission,

The media organisations also propagated the transparency frame. THISDAY LIVE featured the Senate's move to mandate real-time electronic transmission of results (P4), while The Sun Nigeria and The Cable covered public and political reactions to the ongoing Senate debate (P5; P6). Meanwhile, ARISE NEWS covered the Senate's decision on electronic transmission and manual backup, taking the discussion further by explaining how electronic transmission works (P12). In the replies, X users supported the transparency frame by linking electronic transmission to protecting results from manipulation from the polling unit to the collation centre (R1; R2). Additionally, R7 extended this concern by suggesting that the conditional transmission clause could be exploited as a loophole for manual collation.
## Real-Time Result Transmission as a Test of Institutional Sincerity

In the second frame, real-time result transmission was seen as a way to assess the sincerity of political/electoral institutions. Posts in this frame focused on the implications of supporting or opposing electronic result transmission for the intentions of political leaders, legislators, and electoral administrators. In this respect, the official People Democratic Party (PDP) in Nigeria interpreted the Senate's stance on electronic result transmission as raising concerns about political commitment to credible elections (P7). Yunusa Tanko, from the standpoint of the Obidient Movement, found the failure to pass legislation on compulsory electronic result transmission unacceptable and called for civic engagement on the matter (P3). Both posts framed electronic transmission not just as a technical issue but also in terms of political trust and the integrity of the 2027 elections.

In addition, this frame included legal and civic discourses. The discourse provided by Barristerstreet in relation to Agbakoba's plea for statutory support for the electronic result transmission showed the significance of legal discourses in building public trust in the electoral process (P8). The replies to the tweets raised doubts about the motives of actors unwilling to back compulsory electronic transmission (R3). The responses suggested that resistance to electronic transmission would indicate a lack of commitment to transparency in the electoral process.
## Result transmission as a Technical and Infrastructural Risk

The third frame highlighted the need to disseminate results in real time, but this depended on infrastructure. Accordingly, posts and responses focused on implementation, network access, insecurity, rural connectivity, logistics, and election preparedness. Nasir El-Rufai's post discussed the link between electronic transmission and the Bi-modal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS), the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV), and electoral integrity (P9). In this regard, the post places this issue in the broader context of electronic transmission of results in Nigeria's election management system. ARISE NEWS added to this frame by reporting that the Senate had adopted electronic transmission with manual backup. Thereby raising the question of how the two processes could work together (P12). While some comments raised doubts about the effectiveness and adoption of electronic transmission across the country in terms of internet connectivity, poor infrastructure, or insecurity in particular areas (R4; R6), such comments did not oppose electronic transmission but rather expressed fear of technical failure or lack of universal implementation that would affect the credibility of the process. Similarly, INEC's posts on the draft regulations of 2026 and preparations for the 2027 general elections were framed in the same context, shifting focus to preparedness issues (P13; P14).
## Competing Interpretation in the Reply Threads

The fourth frame largely appeared in response threads, where people responded in different ways to posts about the real-time transmission of election results. For instance, some preferred mandatory electronic transmission, while others raised concerns about the political intentions behind the demand, its implementation, and the concept of manual transmission. In posts by Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, EiE Nigeria, and Official PDP Nigeria, some individuals suggested that real-time transmission could help stop result manipulation and build trust among people (R1, R2, R3). The language used here revolved around frames such as transparency, safeguarding of votes, and stopping rigging when collecting results. However, other responses questioned the political nature of the debate, as it seemed that politicians were using the demand for compulsory electronic transmission to mobilise people in preparation for 2027 rather than improve elections (R6; R7).

The third group of responses focused on implementation. In response to posts reporting electronic transmission with manual backup, respondents raised concerns about whether manual backup could interfere with the purpose of real-time electronic transmission (R6). Other responses also raised concerns about network coverage, the reliability of the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV), and the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System's (BVAS) ability to implement a uniform process in polling places (R4; R6). Later comments in response to posts from INEC discussed result transmission and other election-preparation issues, such as voter registration, regulations, the voter database, and organizational readiness (P13; P14).
## Discussion of Findings

The research results address the study's two objectives by showing how specific X posts and replies shaped the framing of real-time result transmission before Nigeria's 2027 general elections. They also show how this framing influenced perceptions of electoral credibility and transparency. The study identified four major frames: transparency as a shield, institutional sincerity, technical and infrastructural threat, and differing perceptions in replies. The study regarded real-time result transmission as an indicator of institutional trust, political sincerity, technological preparedness, and electoral credibility.

In the transparency frame, political and civic actors used real-time results transmission to support credible elections. For instance, Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, and EiE Nigeria mentioned real-time results transmission in connection with vote safety, verification, and protection from manipulation (P1; P2; P10). Situation Room's emphasis on conditional electronic transmission shows that public concern was on the procedure containing loopholes that could return the process to manual collation. This supports the first research objective by showing how selected X posts use real-time results transmission to ensure transparency and safeguard election integrity. This aligns with framing theory, since framing clarifies what is at stake by emphasising specific elements of the issue at hand (Entman, 1996). In the selected posts, the main concern was not just about moving results from one place to another. Instead, electronic transmission was seen as proof that the electoral process could be open, traceable, and less likely to be tampered with. This shows that electoral trust depends not only on formal institutions but also on how citizens and political actors see the fairness and openness of election procedures (Amakoh, 2025; Mauk & Grömping, 2024).

The technical and infrastructural risk paradigm challenges the idea that technology necessarily leads to trust in the election process. The messages regarding the BVAS, IReV, manual contingency, network problems, and INEC preparations indicate that, apart from the concerns related to the necessity for electronic result transmission, the concerns were related to the ability to implement it successfully across all polling stations (P9; P12; P13; P14; R4; R5). This addresses the second research objective by showing that public trust in elections is affected not only by support but also by fears about the effectiveness of technological measures. Network problems, unclear procedures, and inconsistent implementation create mistrust. This aligns with literature arguing that although digital political communication makes democracy visible, it also makes it ambiguous and open to multiple interpretations (Naranjo-Vinueza et al., 2025; Stremlau, 2025).

The discussion threads reveal that X was not just a platform for political communication but also a forum for negotiating meanings. While some participants subscribed to the narrative of transparency and regarded the electronic transmission process as a means of protecting themselves from manipulation (R1; R2), others challenged the reasons for making the results mandatory or raised feasibility and manual-counting issues (R4; R5; R6). This highlights that public discourse on electoral integrity is negotiated and contested. This finding resonates with recent literature on African political communication, where political parties, civil societies, media, politicians, and citizens communicate on the same platforms when discussing elections (Ajaegbu & Ajaegbu, 2024; Fisher et al., 2024).

However, the conflicting views in the reply threads reflect anticipatory distrust. Although some commenters used electronic transmission to demand for electoral transparency, others acted out of partisanship, institutional distrust, or technological failure. As a result, transmission of results became a focus for expectations, doubts and suspicions about the 2027 elections. This is consistent with research on election communication in Nigeria: digital platforms can generate uncertainty through conflicting stories, emotionally charged statements, and distrust of political institutions (Hassan, 2023; Omilusi, 2025; Okorie & Olagunju, 2025).

Overall, the findings indicate that this study achieved its two objectives. The research identified the frames used in some X posts and reply discussions to transmit real-time results, and how these frames shaped Nigerians' views on transparency, institutional trust, technological readiness, and electoral cynicism ahead of the 2027 elections. The study shows that the debate over real-time result transmission is not merely procedural, but ideological.
## Conclusion

This study examines the discourse frames surrounding real-time result transmission in selected X posts and threads before Nigeria's 2027 general elections, and how this discourse shapes perceptions of electoral credibility, transparency, and trust. The results show that real-time transmission of results on X has become a significant indicator of election credibility, rather than an election procedure. Specifically, the analysis identified four frames: transparency shield, institutional sincerity, technical and infrastructural risks, and competing interpretations. These frames show that public discussion of the process's technological, institutional, political, and verification aspects shapes trust in the upcoming elections.

Overall, real-time result transmission has become a symbolic indicator of electoral credibility in Nigeria's emerging digital political space. Beyond being an essential part of the election process, it symbolises transparency, institutional sincerity, and the need to verify results. To overcome distrust in electronic result transmission in Nigeria, it is important to consider features of its communication environment, including distrust in manual collation, inconsistent trust in BVAS and IReV technologies, concerns about network infrastructure, and X-based public expectations. Further research should compare X discourses with discourses on other communication platforms and track how those pre-election frames evolve during and after the 2027 general elections.

title: Digital Mobilisation vs Youth Apathy: A Documentary Analysis of INEC's Strategic Social Media Engagement Ahead of the 2027 Nigerian Election
abstract: Youth participation in Nigerian elections remains a persistent challenge: turnout fell from 69.08% in 2003 to 26.71% in 2023, although citizens aged 18 - 34 made up about 39.65% of registered voters. This study examined how the Independent National Electoral Commission's (INEC) Department of Voter Education and Publicity (VEP) has used social media to engage youth ahead of 2027. Anchored on Technological Determinism Theory, it used a qualitative documentary design with two data sets: scholarly studies (2014 - 2026), analysed thematically, and 19 news reports (1 January - 10 October 2026), analysed through qualitative content analysis. The scholarly studies show reliance on Facebook and Twitter/X and largely non-interactive content. The news reports show voter education reported mainly as community outreach (9 reports) and training and stakeholder meetings (11); social media featured in 6 reports, and none described interactive or platform-specific content. Reported challenges were misinformation (11 reports), apathy (10) and trust deficits (9); only one acknowledged limited digital access. VEP's reported engagement is audience-targeted but not platform-specific. The study recommends interactivity metrics, platform-specific content, youth-influencer partnerships and attention to access barriers.

bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

Elections confer legitimacy on leadership and let citizens choose leaders and hold government to account (Diamond, 2002). Since 1999, Nigeria's Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has been charged with organising elections and with voter registration, civic education and sustained engagement with the electorate (INEC, 2023). Yet turnout has eroded, particularly among youth: it fell from 69.08 percent in 2003 to 26.71 percent in 2023 (International IDEA, n.d.), even though citizens aged 18 - 34 formed about 39.65 percent of the 93.4 million registered voters (Okeregbe, 2023). Scholars attribute the 2023 slump to distrust in INEC, fraud, violence and hardship (Akindele et al., 2026), and youth apathy to corruption, marginalisation and broken promises (Mumuni & Abdulyakeen, 2024; Nyitse & Dogo, 2024; Putnam, 2020; Verba et al., 1995).

INEC's Department of Voter Education and Publicity (VEP) sits at the centre of addressing this. It has historically relied on advocacy visits, market outreaches and periodic media campaigns designed for an electorate reached through radio, television and town halls (INEC, 2026c). That sits uneasily against a youth electorate that turns to Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp, X and LinkedIn for information and community (Nyitse & Dogo, 2024).
## Statement of the Problem

Studies of INEC's social media practice point to a gap between presence and engagement. Ibanga et al. (2020) found that only 12 percent of INEC's Facebook and Twitter posts between August 2018 and January 2019 carried direct voter information and 78 percent were non-interactive. Nwoke et al. (2021) found INEC's large followings under-engaged, and Ayeni and Aweh (2025) reported follower growth between 2018 and 2023 but recommended more interactive, audience-specific content.

Yet apathy appears to respond to deliberate, platform-specific communication. Two quasi-experimental studies in South-East Nigeria found that structured engagement content on Facebook reduced youth apathy more than equivalent content on X (Achebe et al., 2025; Ngwu et al., 2025). They came from the same team, region and journal issue and tested constructed content rather than INEC's own, so they show what platform-specific engagement can achieve, not what VEP does.

Three gaps follow. Studies of INEC's practice end in 2023 and pre-date both the 2027 cycle and the 2026 call for voter education to become "continuous, strategic, targeted, and measurable" (Lashem, 2026). The experimental evidence has not been set against INEC's documented practice. And the INEC-focused work is largely descriptive and, where theory is used, draws on Actor - Network Theory (Ibanga et al., 2020) rather than a communication theory that explains why platform characteristics matter. This study therefore asks whether VEP's social media engagement ahead of 2027, as documented in scholarship and reported in the press, uses the technological characteristics of the platforms in ways that can counter youth apathy.
## Research Questions (RQ)
What primary communication channels does VEP use to engage voters, particularly youth?
In what style of communication has VEP packaged its youth-targeted messages?
To what extent has VEP's social media engagement been strategic and platform-specific, as opposed to generic and periodic?
What challenges limit VEP's adoption of sustained, platform-specific social media engagement?
## Electioneering, Elections and INEC

Elections are the central mechanism by which democratic societies confer legitimacy on leadership and are expected to be periodic, free, fair and inclusive (Dahl, 1971, as cited in Okafor, 2025). They are an intrinsic aspect of democratic rule (Khan et al., 2021) and are meant to be competitive, open and equal (Blokker, 2021). Electioneering, the campaigning and mobilisation of a nation's population (Adebayo et al., 2024), does not displace the electoral commission's own role (Akubor, 2020). INEC has organised federal elections since 1999 under the 1999 Constitution and the Electoral Act 2022, despite persistent electoral violence, vote buying and declining turnout (INEC, 2023; Okafor, 2025).

Nigeria's election management follows the independent model, with INEC responsible for federal and state elections and State Independent Electoral Commissions for local government elections (Akinduro, 2026; Namo et al., 2024). INEC is entrenched in Section 153 of the 1999 Constitution (INEC, 2026a), and voter and civic education is one of its eight core functions (Channels Television, 2019).
## The Roles of INEC's VEP in Audience Participation

VEP is the interface between the Commission and the electorate, charged with informing citizens of their rights and responsibilities to encourage participation and reduce apathy (Ibanga et al., 2020), and it works alongside the media, which, with voters, are indispensable to a credible election (Nigerian Guild of Editors, 2023). Its role covers disseminating accurate information through traditional and digital platforms (INEC, 2026c), countering misinformation, which INEC names as a central challenge ahead of 2027 (Omolaoye, 2026), and building audience participation through interactive content and trained social media staff (Ayeni & Aweh, 2025). VEP's role therefore extends from publicity, the broadcasting of messages, to engagement, interaction that invites the audience to respond.
## Youth Apathy and Social Media

Political apathy denotes disengagement from civic processes, often rooted in powerlessness (Achebe et al., 2025; Ekwenchi & Udenze, 2014), and in Nigeria it stems from disillusionment, corruption, violence and marginalisation (Nyitse & Dogo, 2024). Other causes cited include bad governance, unfulfilled campaign promises, rigging, thuggery and poverty, and in Ebonyi State the Resident Electoral Commissioner reported that only about 30 percent of eligible voters took part in the 2015 general elections (Ngene et al., 2024).

Social media are Web 2.0 applications that enable user-generated content and two-way interaction, unlike the one-way model of traditional mass media (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010, as cited in Ibanga et al., 2020), and in Nigeria platforms such as Facebook, X, Instagram, WhatsApp and TikTok are primary sources of political news among youth (Nyitse & Dogo, 2024).

Youth themselves rate these platforms highly: in a survey of 200 youths aged 18 - 35 in Kwara State, over 70 percent named social media networks as the tools with the greatest potential to mobilise young people, yet much of this activity stayed online and did not become offline participation, a pattern the study calls slacktivism (Maxwell, 2025).

Audience engagement refers to the depth and quality of interaction rather than mere exposure, a distinction between presence and engagement that anchors this study. Access conditions shape it: high data costs, poor connectivity, network fluctuations, inadequate electricity and the 2021 Twitter/X suspension limited online participation (Bassey et al., 2026; Maduagugbuo, 2026).
## Theoretical Framework

This study is anchored on Technological Determinism Theory, which holds that communication technologies are a primary force shaping how societies organise, perceive and act (McLuhan, 1964). It draws on Innis's (1951) idea that media carry biases and McLuhan's (1964) proposition that the medium, more than its content, shapes the scale and form of human interaction.

Applied to political communication, it directs attention to what a platform makes possible: its reach, speed, interactivity and format. Three ideas guide the study. First, the characteristics of a medium shape the form of the message, so the styles of communication VEP uses (RQ2) are partly a function of its channels (RQ1). Second, the benefits of a technology depend on whether its distinctive characteristics are used: a platform built for two-way interaction but used for one-way announcements delivers reach without engagement (Ibanga et al., 2020), the concern of RQ3.

Third, conditions such as connectivity, data costs, electricity and platform availability enable or constrain participation, which makes them central to RQ4 (Bassey et al., 2026; Maduagugbuo, 2026). A strong form of determinism understates human agency, so the study adopts a soft form, in which technology shapes what is possible but institutional choices determine how far possibilities are used. Trust, capacity and political context are treated as conditions that interact with technology.
## Methodology

The study used a qualitative documentary research design, in which existing documents are located, selected and interpreted to answer research questions (Bowen, 2009). Evidence came from three sources handled as two separate data sets: scholarly studies on INEC's social media practice, youth political apathy and platform-specific engagement, published between 2014 and 2026, and news reports on INEC's voter education and publicity activities, published between 1 January and 10 October 2026, the date of data collection.

INEC's own documents, such as its National Voter Education Manual and voter education guidelines, established the Commission's stated policy and were not coded (INEC, 2026b, 2026c). Scholarly studies were analysed thematically with Braun and Clarke's (2006) six-phase framework, and news reports through qualitative content analysis, a systematic method for describing the manifest and latent meaning of texts and drawing replicable inferences from them (Krippendorff, 2018).
The findings are reported separately and compared only in the discussion, so that news reports are not treated as research evidence.

Scholarly studies were purposively selected if they were journal articles, theses or academic manuscripts directly addressing voter education, youth political apathy or social media engagement in Nigeria; opinion pieces, blogs, irrelevant non-Nigerian studies and sources without clear authorship were excluded.

News reports were purposively selected through web searches combining "INEC", "voter education", "social media", "youth", "apathy", "misinformation", "manual", "radio" and "2027". A report was retained if it was published within the study period, reported an INEC official's statement or activity on voter education or publicity, and was a straight news report or interview. Editorials, opinion columns, non-news event write-ups and paid advertorials were excluded, and where several outlets covered the same event only the fullest account was kept. Of 30 reports screened, 19 were included.

The individual report was the unit of analysis, and the manifest statement referring to a channel, communication style, strategy or challenge was the coding unit, coded against a scheme derived deductively from the research questions and theoretical framework (Table 1). Coded statements were counted and grouped by research question. Statements were coded as stated, and no claim was treated as evidence of practice unless the report described an action rather than an intention.

Research Question Four: What Challenges Limit VEP's Adoption of Sustained, Platform-Specific Social Media Engagement?

The studies identify four kinds of constraint. At the trust level, youth often distrust official platforms and dismiss them as propaganda (Ekwenchi & Udenze, 2014; Nwoke et al., 2021). At the infrastructure level, poor connectivity, high data costs and unreliable electricity limit access, particularly for rural and low-income groups (Bassey et al., 2026; Maduagugbuo, 2026). At the capacity level, there is a lack of training, tailored content and paid promotion (Ayeni & Aweh, 2025; Okafor, 2025). At the political-environment level, the 2021 suspension of Twitter/X discouraged youth participation (Maduagugbuo, 2026).

## Discussion of Findings

The finding that INEC works through a mix of channels agrees with the scholarly record and adds to it. Earlier studies show a large but largely one-directional social media presence (Ayeni & Aweh, 2025; Ibanga et al., 2020; Nwoke et al., 2021), while the 2026 reports show social media as one channel among several, with the weight on community contact and partner networks. Community channels reach people who are offline but cannot supply the speed, scale or traceable two-way interaction of social media. That only 6 of 19 reports mention social media, and only one names a platform, suggests that platforms are discussed as places to be present rather than as technologies with particular capabilities, the presence without engagement identified by Ibanga et al. (2020). This fits the soft form of the theory adopted here: technology offers possibilities, but institutional choices decide how far they are used.

The reported styles of communication follow the same pattern. Offline activity reports were the largest category of INEC's posts in 2018 - 2019 (Ibanga et al., 2020), and the 2026 reports are themselves mostly accounts of workshops, meetings and events. No report described explainer videos, short videos, polls, live question-and-answer sessions or memes, the styles Ayeni and Aweh (2025) recommend and that Nwoke et al. (2021) found citizens using to amplify INEC's message. News reports are written about events, so their silence does not prove that VEP does not use such styles. What they show is that, in the public record of 2026, voter education is presented as institutional activity rather than content designed for a platform, whereas under Technological Determinism a platform that rewards short, visual and interactive content calls for content of that kind.

On strategy, INEC's reported approach is relational and targeted. Partnership appeared in 14 reports and audience targeting in 13, and the youth ambassador scheme (Adesina, 2026) is the clearest move towards the influencer-based communication that Nwoke et al. (2021) found effective when it came from citizens. The features that Achebe et al. (2025) and Ngwu et al. (2025) associate with reduced apathy (sustained, platform-specific, interactive content) were reported rarely or not at all: continuous education in 3 reports, evaluation in 2 and platform-specific content in none. The report that came closest set such aims as an expectation placed on officers (Lashem, 2026) and reported no results. By that benchmark the reported strategy is incomplete, and digital engagement appears only as an intention (5 reports), so presence can still be mistaken for engagement, as Ibanga et al. (2020) cautioned.

Trust is common ground between INEC and the scholars: 9 reports name a trust deficit or doubts about credibility, and Ekwenchi and Udenze (2014) and Nwoke et al. (2021) found the same barrier among youth. The difference lies in what is missing. Bassey et al. (2026) and Maduagugbuo (2026) found that network fluctuations, electricity, data costs and the 2021 Twitter/X suspension limited online participation, yet no report names any of these; the nearest is a Sokoto briefing urging officers to reach citizens with limited digital access (Lashem, 2026). INEC's account is attitudinal and informational, whereas the scholarly account adds technological and structural conditions. For Technological Determinism these are central, because a platform can shape participation only for those who can reach it.

Three limits qualify these points. The news reports are indirect evidence of what officials said and journalists chose to report. The sample was drawn by purposive web search and is not an exhaustive archive of 2026 coverage. And the scholarly studies cover 2018 to 2023 while the news reports cover 2026, so differences may reflect change over time as well as method. The comparison is between two records of INEC's practice, not two measurements of the same thing.
## Implications of the Study

Theoretically, the study applies Technological Determinism in its soft form to an institution's communication practice, showing the difference between a platform's presence and the use of its characteristics, and shows the theory's limit here, since the barriers that matter most (trust, capacity and access) are institutional and social. For policy, VEP should measure engagement beyond follower counts, publish platform-specific plans and results, and extend its existing staff training (John, 2026; Lashem, 2026; Osoteku, 2026) to interactive content design. For scholarship, the study adds a systematic content analysis of 2026 news reports tied to a communication theory; future work should analyse INEC's actual 2026 - 2027 posts and test whether the South-East experimental findings hold for INEC's own content and other regions.
## Conclusion

This study asked whether INEC's Department of Voter Education and Publicity has adapted its social media engagement to counter youth apathy ahead of 2027. The scholarly studies show a large but largely one-directional presence between 2018 and 2023. The 19 news reports from 2026 show an approach that relies on community outreach, training and partnerships, with social media mentioned in a minority of reports, no interactive styles of communication or platform-specific content described, and one passing acknowledgement of limited digital access. On the available evidence, the reported strategy is targeted but not platform-specific, though because the evidence is indirect this applies to what VEP has made public.
## Recommendations
The study makes six recommendations:

Adopt interactivity metrics, judging social media work by response rates, comment activity and completion of interactive content rather than follower counts, and publish the results (Ibanga et al., 2020; Nwoke et al., 2021).
Shift content towards direct voter information and interactive content such as short videos, live question-and-answer sessions and polls (Achebe et al., 2025; Ayeni & Aweh, 2025; Ngwu et al., 2025).
Formalise youth-influencer partnerships and evaluate the youth ambassador scheme (Adesina, 2026), building on citizen-led campaigns such as #GetYourPVC and #PVCisagoal (Nwoke et al., 2021).

Choose platforms by where young voters are. Facebook outperformed X in the South-East experiments (Achebe et al., 2025; Ngwu et al., 2025) and WhatsApp was among the most used in Akwa Ibom (Bassey et al., 2026), yet no 2026 report names WhatsApp, so VEP should pilot content on both.

Keep a hybrid outreach model and plan for access barriers, pairing digital work with radio, community and in-person channels (Lashem, 2026; Leonard, 2026; Osoteku, 2026) so that rural and low-income youth are not excluded (Bassey et al., 2026; Maduagugbuo, 2026).
Extend staff training to interactive content design and platform-specific strategy for those who handle social media (Ayeni & Aweh, 2025; John, 2026; Lashem, 2026; Osoteku, 2026).

title: Curated Media: Broadcast News Editors' Views of Political Media Briefings on 2027 Election Coverage in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria
abstract: Political media briefings are a common feature during election periods, bringing together journalists, who are expected to listen to political candidates, who in turn, take questions. It appears, however, that political media briefings are simply curated, with organisers controlling and gatekeeping the flow of information. This reality raises concerns about whether election reporting is increasingly being dependent on curated political communication. At the centre of this are broadcast news editors, whose duty includes probing proceeds of briefings. This study aimed to ascertain the views of broadcast editors in Akwa Ibom State on political media briefings regarding the 2027 general elections, paying particular attention to their perception; editorial disposition towards political briefings; the challenges and opportunities political briefings present for electoral journalism; and how they balance access to political sources with editorial independence. With the gatekeeping theory as a framework, the study adopted a qualitative approach, drawing respondents scheduled for interview from select broadcast outfits, including NTA Uyo, ADBN TV, and for radio, XL FM and Inspiration FM. A thematic analysis was employed for data analysis, with findings organised thematically, too. The findings showed that political press briefings were considered an important source of political information given during elections, but also lays a burden on news editors, who rely on diverse pillars to determine what is eventually broadcast. Hence, the study concluded that political press briefings, especially ahead of the 2027 general elections in Nigeria, presents a two-edged situation, but remains important for electoral journalism. It recommended that broadcasting organisations should strengthen newsroom protocols for handling political briefings, particularly through systematic verification, clear separation of paid political communication from editorial content, balanced sourcing and documentation of attempts to obtain competing perspectives.
