bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

Journalism - print or broadcast, in its purest form, takes the responsibility of informing society of events around it. In addition to information, other functions include education, entertainment, correlation, etc. Through these functions, Shi (2023) notes that journalism, within the context of public affairs, holds power to account. Yet, none of these functions is performed based simply on a journalist's imagination; they are characterised by reliance on sources, some of which could be human, while others are documents, all of which lend credence and trustworthiness to news reports and several other media contents.

Moreover, among the news sources are press statements and media briefings. According to De Semir, Ribas and Revuelta (1998), press statements serve as publicity materials for science journals, extending findings from scientific studies. Such is the case with political and electoral press statements; politicians and electoral bodies, such as Nigeria's Independent National Electoral Commission, make their activities public through press statements. The expectation, usually, is that journalists will write and publish news reports based on the content of the statements, and while at it, Mellado, et. al., (2020) observe that they express professional ideals into which they are socialised.

While Mellado, et al., (2020) further report gaps in the role conception and actual performance among journalists, Nwodu, Ekwunife and Ikegbunam (2025) opine that the image of journalism practice is long-damaged over gratifications. However, an even deeper question exists regarding how journalists - broadcast news editors in the case of this study - treat content of media briefings, which have been conceptualised as curated media. The concept, apart from underscoring the disablement of exclusivity to information (Nwankpa, Umoren & Utuk, 2021), highlights the reality of arranging journalists and supplying them with pre-arranged information that they are expected to publish, sometimes, with little or no questioning. This development makes the process more or less curated, given that organisers of media briefings direct the flow of events, and sometimes, tactically avoid probing questions from journalists considered unfriendly.

Similarly, this reality further manifests during electoral and political seasons, such as the pending 2027 election, with media briefings being a common feature. Political parties, aspirants and candidates, as well as electoral bodies at all levels frequently convene media briefings, usually designed as media relations. Moreover, Pang, Chiong & Hassan (2014, p. 273), citing other sources, conceive media relations as "all types of initiatives - including maintaining and updating media contacts, disseminating news releases, organising press conferences, offering content and responding to media queries". An important aspect of this mix is its identification of response to media queries as a component of media relations. It suggests that media briefings should, as a matter of principle, allow journalists to probe presentations made by political organisations, support groups, candidates and the Independent National Electoral Commission, rather than wholly absorbing and uncritically publishing proceeds of media briefings with little scrutiny.

However, it appears, from observations, that while regular press briefings aimed at promoting products, events, services, or an individual usually allow for robust interaction with pressmen, political press briefings are characterised by actors planted among journalists to deflect rather important issues through praise-singing and largely irrelevant questions. Often, situations also appear engineered to weary those who may have genuine questions to ask, thereby, protecting political actors from "difficult" questions, and leaving participating journalists with only pieces of information that are favourable to the media briefing organisers.

Whereas a journalist may proceed for further investigations, seeking to unearth further details (Ismail, Ahmad & Mustaffa, 2014), reference is usually made, primarily, to data realised from the press briefing, unintendedly yielding to the whims of the curators. This reality appears prevalent during electioneering and may put news editors in uncomfortable corners in view of how to deal with the stories, because according to Ibrahim, Pawanteh, Kee, Basri, Hassan and Mahmud (2011), the press always aims for news values, ethics and professionalism. This, however, could be argued otherwise owing to the findings from several Nigerian studies that report endemic bias within the Nigerian press.

Meanwhile, the 2027 general elections in Nigeria present an opportunity to interrogate this issue; how broadcast news editors perceive and treat political media briefings in their news production. The reality of the political landscape makes it quite interesting, particularly given the International Republican Institute (2026) statement of findings and recommendations, which suggested that Nigeria is bedeviled by a weakening opposition, economic hardship, insecurity, and declining confidence in political institutions. These situations, among other things, generate an avalanche of questions that should be answered.

Moreover, in Akwa Ibom State, where the government of the day has often repeatedly accused of opaqueness with the state's finances, silence over compensation disputes (Imukudo, 2026), and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) sued by the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) (Premium Times, 2026), political media briefings may be expected to address questions tied around these. Yet, the media - reporters and editors - do not determine the content of the briefings. They are, therefore, guided or believed to be guided by journalistic ethics, which could impinge on their perception and attitudes towards political media briefings, as well the treatment they give to information from the briefings in their production and dissemination of news.
## Statement of the Problem

With elections around the corner, political communication is heightened, with political actors including political parties, candidates seeking offices, electoral bodies, etc. interested in engaging with the electorates through the media. They take advantage of the several offerings of the media: from jingles on radio and television, newspaper and magazine adverts, online interactions, among others, they are afforded several means of communication through which they could reach the electorates. Among these, media briefings stand out owing to their amenability to interaction with journalists. They may also provide editors with direct access to political actors and their perspectives, thereby potentially broadening the range of information available for election reporting.

However, the increasing prominence of political media briefings during election periods raises important questions about their implications for editorial decision-making and the independence of news organisations. Understandably, political actors organise media briefings for diverse reasons including communicating particular issues, defending their interests, responding to opponents or influencing public discourse. This author's observation shows, also, that beyond arranging what they say at press briefings, there is a possibility of animating the engagement in ways that swing the tide to their favour, leaving several questions unanswered and grey areas uncovered. This poses a challenge to the media, who have the responsibility of reporting all sides of the story.

Thus, news editors occupy a critical position in the journalistic process, determining, among other things, the issues that receive attention, and how stories are framed for audiences. Consequently, the information supplied during briefings have the tendency to become part of the pool from which editorial decisions are made. Hence, a persistent issue becomes how editors interpret, select, verify and incorporate the data obtained from political media briefings into their bulletins. Editors are, therefore, left to determine whether a piece of information is publishable, and in what frame it should be published; also, whether it requires additional verification, and whether competing perspectives should be sought before broadcast amid meeting the news value of timeliness.

This issue is further exacerbated given the strange bed-fellow relationship between journalists, who seek access to political actors for the purpose of getting information, and the political sources, who want their interest continuously protected. This is because sustained access may create professional tensions, particularly where news organisations depend on political actors for information during periods when political events are unfolding rapidly, leaving editors to negotiate a delicate relationship between maintaining access and preserving the autonomy necessary to determine editorial priorities independently, which may appear in news editors' perception and treatment of such data. The study, therefore, leans on the foregoing to examine political media briefings from the perspective of news editors: understand editors' perception of them; and the extent to which data from political briefings may influence editorial decisions.
## Research Questions
The study was guided by the following research questions:
In what ways do news editors perceive political media briefings during election periods?
To what extent do political media briefings influence editorial decisions regarding election coverage?
What opportunities and challenges do political media briefings present for electoral journalism?
In what ways do editors balance access to political sources with editorial independence?
## Press Briefings as News Sources in Journalism

Unlike spontaneous encounters with political actors, briefings create a structured setting in which officials announce positions, explain policies, respond to criticism and answer journalists' questions. Hayek (2024) observes that government press conferences are principally designed to inform journalists and influence media coverage, even when they are simultaneously directed towards the wider public. Similarly, press conferences contribute to the salience of governmental issues in subsequent media discourse.

The news value of press briefings consequently derives partly from their ability to focus authoritative political information in a single journalistic encounter (Mañoso-Pacheco, 2020). At press briefings, political reporters and editors encounter announcements, explanations, quotations, clarifications and also have opportunities for follow-up questioning within a limited period. This makes the briefing a practical source for generating immediate stories. Yet, journalists, according to Cazzamatta (2026), still interpret, select, and verify the material.

Political actors, through press briefings, may determine the occasion, establish the opening narrative and decide which issues to foreground, while journalists retain some control through questioning, selection and subsequent framing. This interaction is evident in Sharra (2020), which reported that question time provided journalists with an opportunity to perform a watchdog function, but that political interests, inducements and unequal power relations could compromise journalistic independence.

The quality of briefing as a news source, therefore, is also affected by the behaviour of political actors. Shahbaz and Arif (2023) observe that journalists encounter evasive responses and, in some cases, are pressured to ask questions favourable to politicians. Hayek (2024) further notes that government actors have historically used press conferences as mechanisms for leading news coverage, with particularly strong effects where the subject matter is considered highly relevant.

Press briefings thus show usefulness, and perhaps, too, a trap to journalism. While they bring journalists close to politically consequential information, the risk of source dependence is also a possible outcome. A briefing can facilitate accountability when reporters ask probing questions, but can also become a vehicle through which political actors promote preferred narratives. Nonetheless, they are significant sites of news production, allowing journalists to seek information, while editors ultimately determine what deserves broadcast.
## Opportunities and Challenges of Political Media Briefings to Journalism

Political media briefings offer journalists access to political actors, official information, as well as the opportunity to clarify government policies and question decision-makers on issues of public concern. Damissah, Isiaka, Adejare and Ogunlana (2025) suggest that they could engender timely information gathering, provide explanations of government decisions and enable reporters to obtain responses to allegations or controversies. Also characterised by question-and-answer sessions, political media briefings make room for the strengthening of journalism's watchdog role through the challenge of official narratives. Ndukwu et al. (2024) observe that they also demand accountability and expose inconsistencies between political promises and actual performance.

While news editors may have valuable material for political reporting, particularly during election periods when public interest in candidates, parties, policies and governance intensifies, Waisbord and Guazina (2024) suggest that political media briefings may conversely present significant challenges, particularly because they are often organised to advance political interests, promote favourable narratives and manage public perceptions. Moreover, access to political sources can further create unequal power relations (Malling, 2021), where journalists may depend on continued invitations, exclusive information or privileged access, which may discourage critical questioning and encourage self-censorship, especially how they may shape editorial decisions and electoral news coverage in Akwa Ibom State ahead of the 2027 general elections.
## Theoretical Framework

The Gatekeeping Theory was adopted for the study. First postulated by Kurt Lewin in 1947 within the field of social psychology, it explains how information or items move through channels controlled by decision-makers. Lewin's original formulation was introduced into journalism by David Manning White in 1950, who applied the gatekeeping concept to the decisions of a newspaper wire editor. The major argument of the theory is that not all available information reaches an audience. Information encounters points at which decisions are made concerning selection, exclusion, modification, prioritisation and presentation.

In journalism, these decisions are at the foundation of which events become news and how they are presented to the media audience. Gatekeeping, therefore, places considerable importance on the actors who control these decisions. Bro and Kristensen (2024) describe contemporary gatekeeping as involving multiple interconnected forms and actors, reflecting the transformation of journalism from the relatively linear model associated with the traditional editor to a more complex digital environment. Yet, Scheffauer, Goyanes and Gil de Zúñiga (2024) found that audiences continued to value professional journalistic selection, demonstrating that editorial judgement remains important even in the face of increasing algorithmic selection.

Moreover, the continuing importance of the editor is particularly significant. Political media briefings are an important source of information for the newsroom, but the information supplied by political actors does not automatically become election news. The onus lies on editors to consider a briefing newsworthy, perhaps, based on its provision of timely information, direct access to political sources or capability to generate further stories. Editors may equally question its value because political briefings can represent carefully constructed attempts to promote particular interests, interpretations or political narratives.

From the foregoing, the Gatekeeping Theory makes it possible to understand the editor's intermediary role as a process of editorial judgement, a process that allows them to accept, reject, modify, verify, contextualise or use the briefings as a starting point for independent reporting. Meanwhile, present-day applications of the theory further suggest that editorial decisions are shaped by both organisational and professional environments. In light of this, Ndukwu et al. (2024) found that editorial policy influenced political reporting, while ownership interests could also affect the application of editorial policy; this reinforces the argument that gatekeeping is understood as an individual's personal decision, and also embedded in organisational and institutional structures.

The theory provides a framework for examining whether political information is reproduced largely as supplied, subjected to additional scrutiny, balanced with competing perspectives, or transformed into independent journalism, thus accommodating both the opportunities and challenges presented by political briefings to broadcast news editors.
## Method

The qualitative design was considered appropriate and, therefore, adopted for the study, given its nature, which "seeks to understand and interpret the meanings and experiences of individuals in their natural settings" (Regmi, 2024, p. 37). The study involved collecting interview data from broadcast news editors' lived experiences, particularly on how they perceive and treat political media briefings in their production of news in Akwa Ibom State ahead of the coming 2027 elections.

News editors covering the political desk were purposively sampled in the following broadcast outfits in Akwa Ibom State: NTA Uyo, ADBN TV, and for radio, XL FM, and Inspiration FM. In addition to balancing the number of television and radio stations, these stations were selected because of their concentration on news content rather than other types of programmes. The editors and heads of news units that interviewed have interfaced with several political media briefings ahead of the upcoming elections, and possessed sufficient knowledge to attend to the questions. In total, six (6) respondents participated in the study, consisting of three heads of news and three editors.

Data were collected through structured physical interviews, where the objectives of the study were explained to each of the participants following the instructional guide of Millum & Bromwich (2021). In addition, the questions were well-explained to the participants to ensure that they understood them before responding. Consequently, follow-up questions were asked, where necessary, to substantiate or clarify some of the comments made by the respondents.

To complete the data analysis, the Braun and Clarke six-phase framework was adopted, allowing a thematic analysis that according to Naeem, Ozuem, Howell & Ranfagni (2023), yields itself to identifying and reporting patterns hidden in a dataset. The analysis was, therefore, presented in themes that make clear the direction of thoughts of the participants in the study. Consequently, the interview data were transcribed, followed by the identification of keywords, selection of codes, development of theme, review of themes, and eventual expression of the codes. Based on these, the findings were determined and discussed.
## Thematic Data Analyses
Theme One: Editors' Perceptions Of Political Media Briefings During Election Periods

The interviews reveal that respondents generally perceive political media briefings as important platforms for political communication, electoral enlightenment and access to political information. However, this positive perception is accompanied by an awareness that briefings are also strategic instruments through which political actors promote themselves, their candidates and their parties.

OEO described political briefings as "very, very key", particularly because they provide opportunities for electorates to understand candidates, interact with them and question their plans. He associated the briefings with creating an interface between political actors and the people they seek to represent. The respondent particularly put it this way: "Press briefings are good, providing opportunities for the electorate to make informed decisions where they know what to do, how to vote, and who they want to vote for." Similarly, DFI considered political briefings "critical to 2027 elections", explaining thus "I think political media briefings are critical to 2027 elections because they provide opportunities for political parties to inform citizens on issues; agendas that the political parties are promoting to the masses… in such a way that once candidates emerge, they manifest those ideologies that they sold out to the people." DFI said they enable political parties to enlighten citizens about their agendas and proposed programmes.

For BBI, political briefings provide an avenue through which parties can "sell and educate" voters about their candidates and programmes. OO, however, placed greater emphasis on the promotional dimension, describing briefings as occasions through which political parties and support groups "market or sell" the candidates they support. Thus, "When I'm invited to a political press briefing... I just know, okay, this political party or this support group has a candidate and they want me to launder the image or to project the image of the candidate... it's basically PR..."
## Interpretation

The respondents, therefore, perceive political media briefings as legitimate and potentially valuable sources of electoral information, but they also recognise their strategic character. The briefing is simultaneously an information encounter and an opportunity for political actors to promote particular candidates, programmes and narratives.
Theme Two: Political Media Briefings Influence on Editorial Decisions

Data show that the briefing does not automatically determine the content of what is eventually broadcast by the outfits. Rather, its material is subjected to editorial selection, verification and, in some cases, further contextualisation. Hence, editors engage in editorial gatekeeping and selection.

BBI explicitly described the media as the "gatekeeper", explaining that political information should be assessed before being transmitted to the public. They particularly emphasised the need to avoid propaganda, hate speech and statements capable of "heating up the polity," adding "The NBC code has given us a direction to what should be done, what should be aired, and what shouldn't be aired... Information given out must be factual. Information given out must address issues and not personalities. It must not be propaganda. They must not contain hate speech... they must not contain inflammable statements that are capable of, you know, heating up the polity." Similarly, DFI explained that partisan claims are expected during political periods but indicated that the newsroom attempts to avoid material that could be defamatory or damaging.

Furthermore, data show that verification appears as a determinant of editorial treatment; a major mechanism through which briefing information is converted into news. Thus, BBI noted that political actors sometimes "overpromise", suggesting that their claims require scrutiny before being presented as factual information. Likewise, DFI maintained that information is checked before transmission and that journalists should hold a story where reliable confirmation cannot be obtained. OO similarly indicated that information found to be inconsistent with reality could be excluded following fact-checking. However, the respondent also added another angle, noting "...if it's not a good story per se, there has to be a reason we are indulging in the first place, and that's where the financial parts come in... where you work on it because the station has been paid for it." But, OEO emphasised comparing political claims with evidence and authoritative sources.
## Interpretation

The data indicate that political briefings influence the pool of information available for editorial consideration without necessarily determining the final news product. Their influence is mediated through gatekeeping processes such as selection, verification, contextualisation and editorial judgement.
Theme Three: Opportunities and Challenges Presented by Political Media Briefings for Electoral Journalism

The third theme brings together the positive and negative consequences of political briefings identified by the respondents, with the opportunities largely centering on access and information, while the challenges involve commercialisation, propaganda, misinformation and deadline pressure. BBI described direct interaction with political actors as a "big opportunity for electoral journalism in Akwa Ibom". He explained that journalists could use the opportunity to ask questions, seek clarification and obtain information about candidates and their programmes. In a similar response, DFI emphasised the opportunity to obtain information "firsthand" and establish relationships with political actors. This respondent said journalists could exchange contacts with political actors and subsequently invite them for interviews or other programmes.

While OO highlighted another dimension of access, noting that informal conversations outside the formal briefing can enable journalists to obtain additional information and develop useful source relationships, data nonetheless, indicate commercialisation and political promotion as challenges, with respondents highlighting that access may be accompanied by commercial considerations. Thus, OO described political briefings as essentially "PR" and stated that briefings involving electronic media are "normally paid for". BBI likewise acknowledged that many political briefings are paid for, although they maintained that payment does not eliminate the newsroom's responsibility to verify information. Furthermore, the challenge of political influence was also expressed by OEO, who warned that resources received from political actors can "shape your opinion and shape the way you think and the way you want to act on the job".

Further challenges have to do with time pressure and verification. Respondents acknowledged that deadline pressure constitutes another challenge. DFI said that information emerging from briefings may be time-sensitive but maintained that it should still be verified before transmission. BBI expressed the same principle through the maxim, "when in doubt, leave out".
## Interpretation

Political media briefings produce a dual effect for electoral journalism. They make political information more accessible, facilitate interaction with sources and generate story opportunities; at the same time, they expose journalists to political promotion, commercial pressures, misinformation and the practical constraints of broadcast deadlines.
Theme Four: Negotiating Political-Source Access and Editorial Independence

In the fourth theme, the study's final research question is answered, as interviews reveal different perceptions of the extent to which relationships with political sources affect editorial independence. Firstly, source access is considered a potential influence, as OO acknowledged that political access and resources can influence reporting. The respondent's account suggests that where political communication becomes financially connected to media production, the distinction between editorial content and political promotion may become less clear. OEO similarly acknowledged that political resources "can influence" reporting, although they maintained that journalists' professional conscience should determine how they ultimately perform their responsibilities.

DFI introduced another dimension: unequal access, explaining that where one political party is accessible and another is unavailable, the difference in access can affect what the newsroom is able to publish. Hence, journalists may have to indicate that attempts were made to obtain the other side.

Moreover, editorial safeguards and professional independence further emerged as an intersecting negotiation point, with BBI presenting a stronger position on editorial independence. The respondent maintained that political access does not determine editorial decisions because stories are considered at editorial meetings and are guided by professional standards and Nigeria Broadcasting Commission (NBC) requirements. Furthermore, they indicated that the newsroom attempts to provide opportunities for different political parties, including less influential ones.
## Interpretation

The interviews data suggest that editorial independence is not experienced as an absolute condition but as something that editors and journalists must actively negotiate. Access to political sources is professionally valuable, yet excessive dependence on particular sources, financial relationships or unequal access can create pressures that potentially affect editorial judgement. Professional ethics, editorial meetings, verification, balance and regulatory requirements consequently function as mechanisms for maintaining independence. ## Discussion

Taken together, the interviews reveal a considerably more complex picture than a simple perception that political media briefings are either useful or problematic. The respondents largely recognise their informational and access value, particularly their ability to connect journalists directly with political actors and provide information about electoral developments. This is in tandem with findings in the study of Sparks & Wagner (2025), who reported the perceived credibility of elite and government sources in news reports, in addition to having a higher information adequacy than other sources. At the same time, they recognise that briefings are often strategic political communication, as equally underscored by Macnamara (2025), who described this strategy as linear; and in some cases commercially organised activities, a position that is not widely recognised by Minggirovna (2023) and Olariu, I., & Nichifor, B. (2015), but introduces questions about propaganda, source dependence, verification and editorial independence.

The most significant finding for the study is the tension between access and autonomy. The respondents' accounts suggest that political briefings can simultaneously strengthen journalism by improving access to sources and complicate journalism by introducing political, commercial and relational pressures. This tension is recognised by Malling (2021), who agrees that political news sources have some influence on journalists and journalism, although the author classifies interaction with political news sources into formal invisible and informal invisible, with the former serving as gatekeepers and the latter as agenda setters. Furthermore, some respondents' description of strong safeguards based on objectivity, editorial meetings, professional ethics and NBC regulations, is indicative that broadcast news editors still recognise the guardrails of journalism. However, in line with Charles (2025), others acknowledge that access, payment and source availability can affect the eventual publication of political information. Charles identifies, among other things, commercial pressures and an outfit's leaning as part of factors responsible for media bias in political coverage.

Data's consequent pointing towards a central interpretive proposition tilts towards a clear deduction: political media briefings are perceived as valuable sources of electoral information, but their journalistic value is mediated by editorial gatekeeping, verification practices, commercial considerations and the newsroom's attempt to preserve professional independence.
## Conclusion

The findings of the study indicated several related points, showing that political media briefings ahead of the 2027 elections in Akwa Ibom State are considered veritable sources for information from which broadcast editors could generate interesting news stories that are expected to answer questions that would help the electorates make informed decisions. This takes root in the interactions with political actors that cut across parties, candidates, support groups, and even the electoral body. Hence, the respondents generally perceived them as useful for political communication and public enlightenment, but not as neutral information channels. Political media briefings' value to journalism largely depends on post-briefing activities, including the selection, verification and contextualisation of information that become news.

Moreover, the findings revealed a tension between access to political actors and editorial independence, feared to attract political and financial relationships, unequal access to competing political actors, partisan claims, misinformation and broadcast deadlines create pressures that can complicate editorial judgement. However, journalistic significance of political media briefings lies in the editorial processes through which that information is negotiated before it reaches the electorate.
## Recommendation

Consequently, the recommendation in this study follows that news organisations should strengthen newsroom protocols for handling political briefings, particularly through systematic verification, clear separation of paid political communication from editorial content, balanced sourcing and documentation of attempts to obtain competing perspectives.

title: Singing Truth to Power: Musical Skits, Digital Performance, and Political Accountability in Nigeria's Media Society
abstract: As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 General Elections, digital media have become increasingly important sites for political participation and democratic accountability. Among the most influential yet underexplored forms of online political expression are short musical skits and satirical performances disseminated across platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, X, and YouTube. This paper argues that such performances constitute an emergent form of participatory political communication, enabling ordinary citizens, comedians, musicians, and digital creators to scrutinise political actors, expose governance failures, and influence public discourse in ways that often rival conventional news media. The study's theoretical orientation draws on participatory culture (Henry Jenkins), affective publics (Zizi Papacharissi), and performance as political communication; it examines how musical skits function as alternative media within Nigeria's digital public sphere. Methodologically, this study uses qualitative digital ethnography and multimodal discourse analysis of selected viral political performances produced before the 2027 elections; the paper investigates how rhythm, lyrical composition, satire, visual symbolism, and platform affordances combine to construct narratives of accountability, mobilise civic engagement, and shape political consciousness. It pays particular attention to how these performances circulate across multiple social media ecosystems and how they generate public debate, challenge official narratives, and sustain political memory beyond the news cycle. The study contends that short musical performances represent more than entertainment; they are emerging forms of digital civic intervention that blur the boundaries between journalism, artistic expression, and political activism. In a society increasingly characterised by declining trust in traditional institutions and growing digital participation, these performances provide netizens with innovative spaces for scrutinising political leadership, contesting official narratives and negotiating the meaning of political accountability.

bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

Digital platforms increasingly shape Nigeria's political communication environment, where citizens encounter, interpret, and respond to political issues. While conventional news media remain important to electoral communication and public accountability, social media have expanded the range of actors and expressive forms through which political discourse is produced and circulated (Jacobs, 2016; Bruns et al., 2026). TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, X, and YouTube have enabled comedians, musicians, skit makers, and other digital creators to participate in political conversation alongside journalists, politicians, and established media organisations. Within this expanding digital public sphere, short musical and satirical performances have emerged as particularly accessible ways to translate political concerns into humour, parody, music and performance. Such content complicates conventional distinctions between entertainment and political communication because performances produced primarily for popular consumption can simultaneously comment on political leadership, governance failures and the conduct of public officials. Thus, this article argues that political commentary in Nigeria's media society increasingly takes culturally familiar, entertaining forms. The study examines these performances as an emergent form of participatory political communication and asks how their aesthetic and platform-specific characteristics enable political critique to circulate beyond conventional journalistic spaces. It contends that musical and satirical skits create an alternative communicative space in which political dissatisfaction can be rendered visible, emotionally resonant and culturally intelligible. Through rhythm, lyrics, parody, characterisation, gesture and visual symbolism, creators can transform complex political grievances into performances that audiences can watch, interpret, comment upon and share (Rose, 2025; Garg & Rai, 2025).

This circulation can extend political discussion beyond the immediate performance and allow particular political narratives, jokes, and criticisms to gain persistence within popular digital culture. Such performances raise an important question for scholarship on digital political communication: It draws on Henry Jenkins's concept of participatory culture, Zizi Papacharissi's theorisation of affective publics, and scholarship on performance as political communication, conceptualising these performances as affective participatory interventions. It examines how musical skits combine participatory and affective dimensions with platform circulation to produce alternative forms of political visibility and accountability. Through a qualitative multimodal analysis of selected digital performances, including the Facebook videos that form the article's primary empirical corpus, the study considers how music and performance mediate political criticism and how audiences are incorporated into its circulation.

The research questions that animate this study ask: how do Nigerian musical skits use music, humour, parody and multimodal performance to construct political critique and narratives of accountability? It also examines how social media platforms facilitate the circulation, visibility and audience engagement of these political performances. Together, these questions enable the study to examine both the representational strategies through which political meanings are constructed and the digital infrastructures through which those meanings acquire visibility, circulate across networked publics, and generate engagement. This dual focus positions musical skits simultaneously as multimodal cultural performances and as digitally mediated forms of political communication within Nigeria's evolving digital public sphere
## Thesis and Argument

Nigerian musical and satirical skits constitute an emergent form of participatory political communication in which humour, music, performance, and platform affordances transform political dissatisfaction into affectively charged and highly shareable forms of civic discourse (Ajaegbu & Ajaegbu, 2024; Toumaras, 2025). This argument challenges conventional distinctions between political communication and entertainment by recognising that political critique need not occur exclusively through journalism, electoral campaigns or explicitly political speech. Within Nigeria's increasingly platformised media environment, comedians, musicians and digital creators can enter political discourse through cultural forms that are simultaneously entertaining and politically expressive. Musical skits can therefore expose contradictions in political leadership, ridicule official narratives and articulate popular grievances while remaining accessible to audiences who may not ordinarily engage with conventional political content. The political significance of these performances lies not simply in what they communicate, but in how political meanings are produced, experienced and circulated. Humour can make political authority available for ridicule; music introduces rhythm, repetition, and emotional intensity; and performance enables political figures and behaviours to be impersonated, exaggerated, and reimagined (Rai, 2015; Salukvadze, 2026).

Once disseminated through social media, these performances become potentially participatory texts whose meanings can be extended through commenting, sharing, remixing and response. The audience is consequently not merely a consumer of political messages but can become part of the process through which political meanings acquire visibility and circulation. Nevertheless, one should avoid equating participation or virality with political efficacy. A widely circulated skit does not necessarily produce political mobilisation, alter voting behaviour or generate institutional accountability. Its democratic significance is better understood through its capacity to make political critique memorable, affective, participatory and publicly discussable. This distinction matters because digital political satire operates within commercial platforms structured around attention, engagement and visibility. The same affordances that enable creators to challenge political narratives can also encourage prioritising humour, spectacle, and emotional intensity. Digital satire consequently occupies a productive but contested space between civic intervention and entertainment, political critique and commodification, and participation and platform dependency. The article therefore conceptualises Nigerian musical and satirical skits as affective participatory interventions: cultural performances that make political critique emotionally resonant, publicly visible, and capable of networked circulation. Their significance lies not in virality alone, but in how performance and platformed participation create alternative spaces for political interpretation, public discussion, and accountability discourse.
## Social Media and Nigerian Political Communication

The expansion of social media has fundamentally altered the communicative environment within which Nigerian politics is produced, circulated and contested. Political communication, once mediated predominantly through newspapers, radio and television, now operates within a more decentralised and interactive digital ecology in which political parties, journalists, activists, influencers and ordinary citizens can participate in producing and circulating political discourse. Research on Nigeria's 2023 General Elections, for example, identifies Facebook, X, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp as important spaces for disseminating political messages, mobilising supporters, countering competing narratives and facilitating real-time audience engagement (Aideloje et al., 2024; Okon et al., 2025; Chukwu, 2025). This transformation, however, extends beyond substituting one set of communication channels for another. Social media alter the conditions under which political visibility, participation and public discourse are produced. This shift has encouraged a more participatory conception of political communication. Citizens can respond to political claims, produce counter-narratives and circulate interpretations without requiring access to institutional media organisations. Recent scholarship consequently identifies social media as creating more decentralised and interactive forms of civic engagement in Nigeria, while also acknowledging persistent limitations, including misinformation, digital exclusion and forms of online participation that do not necessarily translate into sustained civic action (Iloh et al., 2026; Onayinka et al., 2026).

This latter qualification matters: increased digital expression should not automatically be equated with democratic empowerment. Indeed, the apparent disjunction between high levels of online political activity and offline electoral participation during the 2023 elections demonstrates the limits of assuming a straightforward relationship between digital engagement and political action. The contemporary Nigerian digital political sphere should therefore be understood as simultaneously participatory, affective and contested. Social media provide opportunities for political actors and citizens to shape public agendas, but they also intensify emotional appeals, polarisation and competing claims to political legitimacy. In this unsettled communicative environment, musical skits and political satire take on new significance. Their importance lies not simply in providing another channel for political messages, but in introducing popular cultural performance as a mode of political expression. By combining entertainment with commentary, such performances can expand political discourse beyond conventional news formats and create alternative routes through which political grievances become visible, affectively experienced, and publicly circulated.
## Participatory Culture

Henry Jenkins's concept of participatory culture provides an important starting point for understanding how digital audiences have moved beyond the conventional position of passive media consumption (Jenkins, 2006; Jenkins, Ito & boyd 2016). For Jenkins, participation is not reducible to the technical interactivity enabled by digital technologies; rather, it is a cultural practice through which people acquire the capacity and confidence to create, circulate and attach meaning to media (Jenkins, 2006). He distinguishes participation from interactivity precisely because the latter describes a technological property, whereas participation describes a cultural relationship to media. Jenkins's formulation is particularly significant for political communication because it recognises civic engagement as one domain in which participatory culture can operate (Jenkins, Ito & boyd 2016). Participatory cultures are characterised by relatively low barriers to artistic expression and civic engagement, support for creating and sharing content, and a sense among participants that their contributions matter (Jenkins, 2006).

Applied to Nigeria's digital media environment, this framework shifts one's attention away from the political message as a finished product and towards the social processes through which political meaning is produced and circulated. A musical skit, for example, does not conclude its communicative life when its creator uploads it. Its subsequent trajectory may involve users commenting on its political implications, sharing it with their networks, reproducing its jokes, quoting its lyrics or catchphrases, creating responses and parodies, tagging other users, or incorporating elements of the original performance into new content. In this sense, the audience becomes part of the communicative infrastructure through which political discourse acquires visibility. Jenkins and his collaborators' later concept of spreadability is useful here because it replaces the relatively passive notion of distribution with a model of circulation in which audiences make active decisions about what content to pass along, how to frame it and which networks it should reach (Jenkins, Ford & Green 2013).

This perspective is particularly productive for understanding the political potential of entertainment. Participation does not necessarily require membership of a political organisation, attendance at a rally or direct engagement with formal political institutions. Within platformed environments, political participation can occur through apparently mundane cultural practices: sharing a satirical video, adding a political interpretation in the comments, reproducing a politician's caricature, or using a creator's catchphrase to comment on a subsequent political event. Such practices can be understood as forms of vernacular political expression, in which citizens appropriate popular cultural forms to interpret political realities (Papacharissi, 2015; Howard, 2011). The musical skit's significance therefore lies partly in its ability to lower the symbolic and cultural barriers separating political discourse from everyday entertainment.

However, Jenkins's participatory model requires critical qualification when transferred to the Nigerian platform environment. Participation should not be romanticised as an automatic redistribution of communicative power. The ability to produce or circulate content does not mean all participants have equal visibility, influence, or access to audiences. Platform algorithms, commercial incentives, moderation practices and unequal digital resources continue to structure whose contributions become visible and whose remain marginal (Gillespie, 2018; Noble, 2018). Indeed, Jenkins's later account of spreadability recognises that contemporary circulation involves a mixture of bottom-up and top-down forces rather than a simple displacement of institutional power by empowered users (Jenkins, Ford & Green 2013). The Nigerian context therefore requires understanding participation as enabled but also conditioned by platform infrastructures.

This qualification is crucial to the present study. The political significance of a musical skit cannot be inferred simply from the number of views, shares or comments it attracts. Nor should every act of sharing be interpreted as evidence of political commitment. A user may circulate a skit because it is humorous, because it expresses an existing frustration, because it is culturally recognisable, or because sharing it strengthens a social relationship. Political meaning may consequently emerge indirectly through practices whose immediate motivation is entertainment. The focus should be on how entertainment-oriented participation can create conditions in which political interpretations, emotions and criticisms are collectively produced and circulated. Furthermore, it complicates the conventional opposition between consumer and producer. In the context of Nigerian musical satire, the creator may produce the initial political performance, but audiences shape its subsequent cultural life. They can reinforce its interpretation, contest it, detach its language from the original context, or transform it into a reusable cultural reference. A catchphrase can become political shorthand; a comic character can become a way to interpret real political actors; and a musical refrain can acquire meanings beyond the original performance. What circulates, therefore, is not simply a political message but a culturally adaptable resource for political interpretation (Jenkins, 1992; Jenkins, Ito & boyd 2016).

Participatory culture thus provides this article with more than a description of social-media engagement. It offers a way of reconceptualising political communication as a process of collective cultural production and circulation. Nigerian musical and satirical skits are significant precisely because they bring political discourse into forms of participation already embedded in everyday digital culture. This provides the conceptual bridge to the article's central concern with musical skits as affective and potentially consequential forms of digital civic intervention. Jenkins's framework is valuable here because it enables an examination of how audiences participate, what they do with political performances after encountering them, and the technological and cultural conditions under which those practices become forms of political communication. It provides the conceptual bridge to the article's central concern with musical skits as affective and potentially consequential forms of digital civic intervention.
## Political Satire as Alternative Media

Political satire has a long intellectual and cultural lineage as a mode through which power can be questioned, mocked and rendered open to public scrutiny (Gray, Jones & Thompson 2009; Test 1991). By relying on irony, parody, exaggeration, humour and indirect expression, satire creates a communicative space in which political authority can be challenged without necessarily adopting the formal language of political journalism or institutional criticism (Day 2011). Its significance therefore lies in its ability to make political actors, institutions and practices available for reinterpretation and ridicule. In this sense, satire has historically operated as a form of alternative political communication, particularly where direct criticism may be constrained or where conventional media fail to capture the vernacular ways through which citizens experience political life (Hariman & Lucaites, 2007; Baym, 2015).

Digital platforms, however, alter the communicative conditions within which satire operates. In conventional performance contexts, the relationship might be understood relatively simply as performance → audience: a satirical performance is produced and presented to an audience whose principal role is to watch, interpret and respond. Digital satire introduces a more complex and recursive structure: performance → platform → audience → comments → sharing → remix → renewed circulation. The platform therefore becomes part of the communicative process through which the meaning, visibility and subsequent life of the satirical performance are negotiated (Jenkins, Ford & Green 2013; Gillespie, 2018).

This distinction matters for understanding Nigerian musical and comedic skits. Once uploaded, a performance can acquire communicative trajectories beyond those anticipated by its creator. Audiences may comment upon its political implications, tag other users, reproduce its phrases, create responses, modify its audio or visual elements, or circulate it across different platforms. The audience consequently becomes implicated in the ongoing production and redistribution of political meaning. Satire becomes networked and recursive, rather than transmitted from performer to spectator (Jenkins, 2006; Baym, 2015). The political significance of this transformation should nevertheless not be equated automatically with democratic empowerment. Participation can expand the circulation of political critique while remaining shaped by platform algorithms, commercial incentives and unequal visibility (Noble, 2018; Gillespie, 2018). Digital satire is therefore best understood not simply as satire relocated online, but as a form of networked alternative media in which political critique can be continually reproduced, reframed and contested through participatory circulation (Jenkins, Ito & boyd 2016; Highfield, 2016).
## Affect and Political Communication

The relationship between emotion and political communication is particularly important to understanding the circulation of digital satire. Rather than treating emotion as the opposite of rational political communication, this article treats affect as one means through which political communication acquires social force. (Papacharissi, 2014) Papacharissi's concept of affective publics is useful here because it highlights digitally networked publics that emerge and sustain themselves through shared feelings, expressions, and storytelling. (Papacharissi, 2014; Papacharissi, 2015) Affective publics do not necessarily form around stable political organisations or coherent ideological programmes; rather, they can materialise through the circulation of emotionally charged expressions that allow individuals to "feel their way" or "vibe" with political events and issues.

This perspective is particularly relevant to musical skits, where political meanings are rarely communicated through propositional argument alone. Humour, rhythm, gesture, facial expression, parody and repetition can generate amusement, anger, frustration, recognition, embarrassment, solidarity, cynicism or hope. These effects can make political commentary socially memorable and give audiences reasons to respond to, reproduce, or circulate particular performances. Papacharissi's work on networked storytelling similarly demonstrates how digital political communication can combine information, opinion and emotion, making their separation analytically less useful than approaches that recognise their hybridity (Papacharissi, 2012; Candon, 2016).

Affect can therefore be constitutive of the communicative process itself. A humorous performance may transform frustration into laughter; recognition may prompt a viewer to tag another person; anger may motivate commentary; solidarity may encourage sharing; and embarrassment may make a satirical representation particularly memorable. In this sense, affect can make political communication socially sticky: it gives users reasons to remain attentive to, respond to and circulate particular messages. However, effective circulation should not be equated automatically with political mobilisation or democratic change. A widely circulated performance may generate laughter without producing sustained political engagement. The analytical significance of affect lies in examining how particular feelings facilitate the movement of political meanings across networked publics. Digital musical satire can thus be understood as an effective form of political communication in which feeling becomes part of the infrastructure through which critique travels, connects audiences and acquires public visibility.
## Methodology

This study adopts a qualitative multimodal digital analysis of selected digitally circulated Nigerian political performances; it examines how political meanings are constructed through the interaction of musical, visual, verbal and performative elements within digital environments. The approach draws on multimodal discourse analysis (MDA), a concept that investigates how multiple communicative codes construct meaning beyond language (Jones, 2012), while remaining attentive to the platform contexts through which performances are encountered, circulated, and discussed. The analysis focuses on selected political musical skits and satirical performances circulated on social media platforms, with particular attention to their use of lyrics, rhythm, humour, parody, gesture, costume, visual symbolism and characterisation. It also considers the digital contexts surrounding these performances, including audience comments, sharing practices and observable patterns of recirculation. These elements are examined not as separate communicative components but as interconnected resources through which political critique is produced and made meaningful.

The study therefore treats the performances as networked cultural texts whose significance extends beyond their original moment of production. Attention to circulation is particularly important because digital platforms allow audiences to respond to, reinterpret, reproduce and redistribute performances. The methodological objective is to examine how their multimodal and affective characteristics create possibilities for political commentary, audience participation and public discussion. The selected performances are analysed comparatively to identify recurring patterns in the representation of political authority, governance, accountability and citizen experience. This approach enables the study to connect the formal characteristics of musical satire with the broader communicative conditions of Nigerian digital media, while recognising that visibility, circulation and participation remain shaped by the affordances and constraints of platforms themselves.
## Empirical Analyses

The participatory possibilities of musical satire are particularly visible in the two Facebook performances examined in this study. The first skit, Skit 1 - Facebook video, features a reggae artist whose performance uses reggae's musical conventions to comment on President Bola Tinubu. The lyrics question aspects of the President's educational background, identity, wealth and age. These claims are presented through musical performance rather than conventional political commentary, transforming potentially complex and contentious political questions into an accessible, performative form. The post attracted 224 comments, sparking exchanges between users who supported the President, opposed him, or were drawn primarily by the performance's musical quality.
The comments demonstrate that participation extends beyond simply viewing the performance. One commenter describes the political leadership in highly critical terms, stating that:
"A criminal cartel hijacked the country's leadership and the masses are paying for it" (sic).
Another commenter, apparently defending the President, invokes the 2022 election campaign and argues that, despite previous criticism, Tinubu:
"floored all his opponents and the naysayers" and is now "globally recognised and respected" (sic).

The significance of these contrasting responses lies less in determining which position is correct than in demonstrating how the musical performance becomes a discursive object around which competing political interpretations are articulated. The skit therefore does not end when the song ends; its political meaning extends and is contested through the comment section.

The second performance by a musical artist called Big Lion (Skit 2), spelt as Biqlion, offers a somewhat different form of political musical intervention. Here, Biqlion uses song to enumerate the problems and anxieties Nigerians face, including insecurity, hunger, inadequate infrastructure, and limited access to basic amenities. The performance drew 196 comments, many praising both the musical quality and the political message. One commenter succinctly observes:
"Great music, great message, good job."
Another expresses admiration for the performer while simultaneously voicing concern about his safety:
"I love your courage…I am afraid if this guy will not send assassins for you…but really don't want to lose you please be careful somehow" (sic).

This latter response is particularly revealing because it demonstrates the affective complexity of political participation. Admiration, fear and concern coexist within a single response to the performance. The commenter's apparent reference to being "assassinated" indicates that political musical expression is perceived not merely as entertainment but as potentially consequential dissent. At the same time, the response constructs a relationship between performer and audience based on recognition and emotional attachment. Taken together, the two skits illustrate the recursive structure of digital political satire identified earlier: performance → platform → audience → commentary → contestation → renewed circulation. Their comment sections function as spaces in which political meanings are affirmed, challenged and emotionally negotiated. Importantly, the volume of comments should not itself be treated as evidence that the performances produced political mobilisation or changed political attitudes. Rather, the exchanges demonstrate a more specific form of participation: audiences use the performances as prompts for political expression, disagreement, affiliation and affective response. Musical satire thus becomes a participatory form of political communication, in which entertainment provides the cultural form through which political questions enter everyday digital conversation.
## Analytical Framework

The analytical framework for this study develops five coding dimensions that bridge theory and the empirical analysis of Nigerian musical skits, grounding abstract concepts in the concrete practices visible in the two cases‑study performances. Firstly, political representation examines how politicians and state institutions are depicted, focusing on the symbolic and narrative strategies that frame, contest, or ridicule authority. In Skit 1, for example, the reggae performer's lyrical references to President Bola Tinubu's alleged lies about his education, identity, and wealth foreground satire as a mode of political scrutiny, while audience comments such as "A criminal cartel hijacked the country leadership…" reveal how viewers extend and reinterpret these representations.

Secondly, performance attends to multimodal features: music, rhythm, gesture, vocal style, parody through which it produces political meaning. Both skits rely heavily on musical form: Skit 1 uses reggae beats to animate political critique, while Skit 2 deploys a melodic lamentation to catalogue insecurity, hunger, and infrastructural decay. These aesthetic choices shape how audiences perceive and emotionally engage with political content.

Thirdly, affect analyses the emotional textures mobilised by the skits, recognising how humour, frustration, recognition, ridicule, or fear contribute to the social force of political commentary. The comments on Skit 2, including expressions of admiration ("Great music, great message") and fear ("…am afraid if this guy will not send assassins for you"), demonstrate how affective responses can amplify or complicate political interpretation.

Fourthly, platform circulation investigates how sharing, commenting, tagging, and cross‑platform movement shape the visibility and iterative reproduction of meaning. The 224 comments on Skit 1 and 196 on Skit 2 exemplify how audiences become active participants in the communicative process, transforming satire into a networked, recursive form of political discourse.

Finally, civic intervention examines how these skits facilitate accountability, awareness, critique, or political memory. Audience discussions about Nigeria's political future, concerns about dissent, and reflections on governance indicate that musical satire can create conditions for civic reflection even when motivated by entertainment. Together, these dimensions provide a coherent methodological structure for analysing how musical skits operate as culturally embedded, affectively charged, and digitally mediated forms of political communication.
## Performing Political Accountability

Digital musical satire in Nigeria performs political accountability by transforming political critique into humorous, affective, and participatory practices that circulate widely across social platforms. Across the skits analysed, humour, performance, affect, circulation, and civic intervention converge to produce a distinctive communicative form that differs markedly from conventional political journalism. Rather than presenting political information through formal reporting, these skits make power laughable, emotionally resonant, and socially shareable, enabling audiences to participate in political discourse through everyday cultural engagement.

Humour is central to this process. Satire destabilises authority by reversing the symbolic order through which politicians ordinarily maintain seriousness, ceremony, and respectability (Gray, Jones & Thompson, 2009; Day, 2011). Characters such as Governor Amuneke (Kevinblak) exemplify this reversal: through exaggeration, caricature, and comic incompetence, Amuneke embodies the stereotypical Nigerian politician boastful, corrupt, and performatively inept. Skit 1 deploys similar mechanisms. The reggae performer mocks President Bola Tinubu by singing about alleged lies concerning his education, identity, and wealth. The humour lies in the juxtaposition of reggae's relaxed rhythm with accusations of political dishonesty, producing a comic incongruity that destabilises presidential seriousness. Audience comments extend this humour into explicit critique: "A criminal cartel hijacked the country leadership…" reframes the skit's satire as a broader indictment of governance. Laughter here becomes a civic resource, enabling critique that is emotionally accessible and socially distributed in ways conventional journalism rarely achieves (Hariman & Lucaites, 2007).

Music and performance intensify this political critique by transforming political information into affective experience. In Skit 1, rhythm and repetition embed political accusations within musical pleasure, allowing audiences to internalise critique through melody rather than argument. Tone, facial expression, gesture, and comic timing further shape the performance's emotional texture, making political meaning felt rather than merely understood (Auslander, 2008). Skit 2 operates through a different affective register: its plaintive melody and sombre tone evoke frustration, sorrow, and recognition of Nigeria's hardships. The singer's strained voice and expressive gestures communicate emotional burden, while lyrics listing insecurity, hunger, and infrastructural decay produce a shared affective landscape. Audience responses reflect this intensity, admiration ("Great music, great message") coexists with fear for the performer's safety ("…am afraid if this guy will not send assassins for you"), revealing how effective engagement can generate protective publics. Drawing on Papacharissi's concept of affective publics, these skits demonstrate how political issues become emotionally charged events: political issue → aesthetic performance → emotional response → circulation (Papacharissi, 2014; Papacharissi, 2015).

Platform circulation further shapes how these skits perform accountability. The 224 comments on Skit 1 and 196 on Skit 2 illustrate how audiences become active participants in meaning‑making. Sharing, tagging, remixing, and cross‑platform movement turn satire into a recursive communicative process in which users continually reframe political critique. Platforms are not neutral channels; they are infrastructures that amplify certain voices, intensify affective responses, and enable dialogic exchanges that extend the life of the performance (Gillespie, 2018; Jenkins, Ford & Green, 2013). The comment threads reveal political disagreement, humour, fear, and speculation about Nigeria's future, demonstrating how circulation produces publics that are emotionally and politically invested.

Ultimately, these skits facilitate civic intervention by enabling informal forms of accountability, awareness, and political memory. Audience discussions about governance failures, concerns about dissent, and reflections on Nigeria's political direction indicate that musical satire can prompt civic reflection even when motivated by entertainment. This aligns with scholarship on everyday political engagement, which argues that informal media practices can contribute meaningfully to civic awareness and democratic critique (Highfield, 2016; Dahlgren, 2009). The skits do not necessarily mobilise political action, but they create conditions in which critique becomes visible, memorable, and collectively negotiated. Through humour, affect, performance, and circulation, digital musical satire becomes an alternative mode of political communication, one that renders authority laughable, makes political issues emotionally resonant, and invites audiences to participate in the ongoing production of political meaning.
## Discussion of Findings

The findings reveal several tensions that complicate the democratic possibilities of digital musical satire. The relationship between virality and political efficacy remains uncertain. A skit may attract hundreds of comments, shares, and cross‑platform circulation, yet such visibility does not necessarily translate into behavioural change or sustained civic engagement. As Jenkins and Shresthova argue elsewhere, participatory visibility can create "thin" forms of engagement that feel politically expressive without producing institutional impact (Tufekci, 2017). Virality may amplify critique, but it can also dissipate into fleeting affective attention.

Digital satire must also balance entertainment with political seriousness. Humour makes politics accessible, lowering the cognitive and emotional barriers to participation, yet it also risks trivialising complex issues. Scholars of political comedy note that satire can oscillate between critique and entertainment, producing what Baym elsewhere calls "discursive integration," where political information is blended with humour in ways that may obscure structural analysis (Jones, 2010). The skits analysed here demonstrate this tension: audiences laugh, comment, and share, but the comedic framing may soften the gravity of corruption, insecurity, or economic hardship. Furthermore, the skits reveal a tension between participation and algorithmic dependence. While creators appear autonomous, opaque platform logics shape their visibility. As Bucher notes, algorithms act as "sensory infrastructures" that determine what becomes perceptible online (Bucher, 2018). The circulation of Skit 1 and Skit 2 is therefore not solely a function of audience engagement but also of algorithmic amplification, ranking, and recommendation. Moreover, digital satire exists within the creator economy, producing a tension between civic intervention and monetisation. As Abidin's work on influencer cultures shows, creators often navigate commercial pressures alongside expressive or political goals (Abidin, 2018). Political critique may coexist with revenue generation, sponsorship, or platform incentives, complicating the authenticity or independence of civic messaging.

Finally, satire risks partisan appropriation. Political actors may court, co-opt, or weaponise popular creators to harness their visibility. As Marwick and Boyd argue, networked influence is vulnerable to strategic manipulation (Marwick & Boyd, 2011). The same affective publics that enable critique can also be mobilised for partisan ends. These tensions underscore that digital musical satire is neither inherently emancipatory nor trivial; it is a contested communicative form shaped by humour, affect, platforms, and political interests.
## Conclusion

Political communication in Nigeria increasingly unfolds through cultural and entertainment forms, where citizens encounter political issues not only through news media but through music, humour, and everyday digital creativity. Musical and satirical skits exemplify this shift by transforming political critique into affective, participatory, and highly shareable performances that invite audiences to laugh, feel, debate, and reinterpret political authority. Their democratic significance lies in their capacity to create alternative spaces of visibility, interpretation, and accountability, spaces where political behaviour becomes open to scrutiny through vernacular, emotionally resonant modes of expression. As Nigeria approaches the 2027 elections, these skits offer an important lens for understanding how citizens may engage with political issues within an increasingly platformised electoral environment. Rather than predicting their impact, this article suggests that musical satire will remain a meaningful cultural interface through which Nigerians process, negotiate, and make sense of political life. The paper recommends greater scholarly and institutional attention to digital performance as an important component of Nigeria's evolving democratic communication ecology. Researchers, media organisations, and civic institutions should recognise musical skits and other forms of participatory digital expression not merely as entertainment but as significant spaces in which citizens interpret political events, contest official narratives, and negotiate accountability

title: Electorates' Responses to AI-Generated and Human-Created Campaign Messages in South-South Nigeria Ahead of the 2027 General Elections: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how political campaigns are produced and circulated. In Nigeria, parties, candidates, and supporters now rely heavily on digital tools to create adverts, images, and voice messages, yet little is known about how ordinary electorates in South-South Nigeria read such content. This exploratory study therefore examined how registered voters in South-South Nigeria distinguish AI-generated from human-created campaign messages, explain their trust or distrust in them, and describe their emotional responses and possible voting intentions ahead of the 2027 elections. A qualitative exploratory design was used. Nineteen registered voters aged 18 - 40 who actively use social media were purposively selected for maximum variation. Data were collected through online semi-structured interviews using six campaign messages, along with observation notes, and analysed with reflexive thematic analysis. Participants identified AI mainly through unnatural movement, implausible settings and contextual inconsistencies. Human-created messages were generally trusted more, although emotionally relevant AI content could also appear credible. Emotional reactions included humour, hope, confusion and worry, but these rarely translated directly into voting intention. Within this sample, recognition, trust and voting responses depended on realism, relevance, prior knowledge and candidate credibility. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger, representative studies.
