bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping political communication by enabling campaigns to produce persuasive text, images, audio and video quickly and cheaply (Hassim & Nasir, 2025; Beacken et al., 2026). Globally, experiments show that large-language-model messages can shift political attitudes, but effects vary by issue, audience, and message design; persuasive capacity, therefore, does not automatically imply greater influence than human communication (Bai et al., 2025; Jungherr et al., 2026). Research further shows that citizens judge deceptive AI uses more negatively than routine campaign applications, while many people struggle to distinguish AI- from human-generated information (Jungherr et al., 2026; Stefkovics & Gere, 2026).

Across Africa, digitally networked elections combine wider participation with greater exposure to misleading political content (Gadjanova et al., 2022; Abboud et al., 2024). However, literature has largely examined social-media campaigning, misinformation, digital literacy and the wider democratic consequences of internet use rather than directly comparing electorates' responses to AI-generated and human-created campaign messages (Cariolle et al., 2024; Muringa & Adjin-Tettey, 2024; Mustapha et al., 2024). Emerging research has begun to document the use and risks of generative-AI propaganda in African elections (Wack & Parry, 2025; Wack & Prochaska, 2026), including Nigeria (Uzuegbunam, 2026; Beacken et al., 2026), but remains primarily concerned with disinformation threats, governance and countermeasures rather than how electorates recognise message origin, form trust judgements, experience emotional responses or translate such responses into voting intentions.

The studies reviewed above leave three specific gaps. First, on recognition, Nigerian studies have examined WhatsApp campaigning (Fisher et al., 2024), influencer-led influence operations (Uwalaka et al., 2025) and campaign responses to disinformation (Ibrahim & Ekdale, 2026), but none asked electorates to distinguish AI-generated from human-created messages. International evidence on this question is mixed: AI messages can persuade (Bai et al., 2025), people often cannot tell AI-generated from human-written content (Stefkovics & Gere, 2026), and deceptive AI use attracts public disapproval (Jungherr et al., 2026). Second, on trust, the Nigerian studies closest to this topic examined consumer trust in AI-generated advertising (Ekanem & Nwagbara, 2024), the role of AI-generated videos in one candidate's social identity (Nwaoboli & Ojete, 2025) and South-South voters' trust in algorithm-curated political messages (Abdulazeez et al., 2026); none compared trust in AI-generated and human-created campaign messages from the electorate's perspective. Third, on emotions and voting intention, Nigerian evidence comes from a single university's students (Ngoka et al., 2026) or from campaign actors rather than voters (Ibrahim & Ekdale, 2026), and does not address AI-generated content. Because the phenomenon is new and these questions have not been mapped in this region, an exploratory approach that builds in-depth understanding and generates propositions for later testing is more appropriate than a confirmatory one (Stebbins, 2001).

Given these gaps, this exploratory study examined how electorates in South-South Nigeria perceive and respond to AI-generated and human-created campaign messages ahead of the 2027 general elections. Specifically, it sought to:
Identify the cues electorates use to distinguish AI-generated from human-created campaign messages.
Explore the reasons electorates give for trusting or distrusting each type of campaign message.
Describe the emotional responses that the campaign messages evoke among electorates.
Explore how electorates perceive the campaign messages as shaping their voting intentions for the 2027 general elections.
## Conceptual Clarification: Electorates, Responses and Campaign Messages

In legal terms, electorates are people qualified to vote; in Nigeria, these are citizens aged 18 or above who have registered with the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). Beyond this legal status, digital-election research treats electorates as audiences whose readings of campaign messages are shaped by identity, experience, media exposure and prior attitudes, rather than as uniformly persuadable voters (Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2019; Venus et al., 2025). In this study, electorates are registered voters resident in the six South-South states (Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa, Cross River, Delta, Edo and Rivers) who actively use social media and belong to Generation Z (born 1997 - 2012; aged 18 - 29 at the time of the study) or the Millennial cohort (born 1981 - 1996; aged 30 - 45). Electorates' responses are broader than persuasion: exposure to a campaign message may produce recognition, scepticism, humour, distrust or emotion without any change in voting preference (Conrad et al., 2025; Gondwe, 2025; Gallegos et al., 2026). Responses are therefore operationalised as electorates' recognition, interpretations, trust judgements, emotions and stated voting intentions following exposure.

AI-generated campaign messages are better conceptualised by production process, not falsity: generative systems can create or substantially transform political text, images, audio and video, whether truthful, satirical or deceptive (Goldstein et al., 2024; Łabuz & Nehring, 2024). Operationally, they are study stimuli generated or materially synthesised using generative-AI tools.

Human-created campaign messages cannot simply mean "authentic": humans also manipulate, selectively frame and strategically persuade. Their analytical value is therefore comparative authorship rather than presumed truthfulness, especially because AI labels themselves can alter credibility judgements (Gallegos et al., 2026; Goldstein et al., 2024; Schiff et al., 2025). In this study, they are campaign stimuli produced through conventional human recording, photography or design without generative-AI synthesis.
## Recognition and Interpretation of Campaign Messages

Experimental research suggests that the key question is not whether electorates can "spot AI", but which cues they rely on to assess authorship and meaning (Groh et al., 2022; Stefkovics & Gere, 2026). Groh et al. (2022) observed, in five experiments, that audio-visual cues, more than content alone, determined whether deepfake political videos were recognised. In contrast, across 27 European countries, Stefkovics and Gere (2026) found little difference in how respondents reacted to human- and AI-generated headlines when authorship was undisclosed, suggesting that text-based synthetic content is hard to distinguish. This is further complicated in Africa by fragile information environments, as evidenced by high levels of perceived exposure to disinformation and low trust in social and national media in Kenya (Wack & Prochaska, 2026), Nigeria (Ngoka et al., 2026) and South Africa (Mtsweni et al., 2023). Thus, in Sub-Saharan Africa, recognition is likely to occur under general suspicion rather than confident, positive identification. During the 2023 presidential election, misinformation in Nigeria involved the dissemination of fabricated information, as well as the use of "fake-news" labels, prebunking and debunking terms to challenge rival statements by campaign actors (Ibrahim & Ekdale, 2026). Thus, South-South electorates might use partisan identity, pre-existing beliefs, language, platform cues, and perceived authenticity, rather than just the technology being used, to interpret a message as AI-generated.
## Trust in AI-Generated and Human-Created Campaign Messages

Trust is shaped less by whether a message is objectively AI-generated than by what voters believe its source and production process imply. In US - UK experiments, Altay and Gilardi (2024) found that an "AI-generated" label reduced perceived accuracy and sharing intentions even when content was true or human-written. Further, internet use has been associated with lower institutional trust and weaker perceptions of democracy, suggesting that digital distrust predates generative AI and may condition reactions to it (Wang et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2025). Adeleke (2025) documents the circulation of deepfake audio during the 2023 elections, showing how synthetic media can weaken confidence not only in false content but also in authentic recordings. More locally, Abdulazeez, Anthony and Iwegbue (2026) found that South-South voters' trust in algorithm-curated political messages varied with exposure and demographic factors. However, their cross-sectional design cannot establish causality. This exploratory study therefore attends to whether participants distinguish distrust of AI authorship from distrust of parties, platforms, candidates and Nigeria's political information system.
## Emotional Responses and Voting Intentions

Evidence cautions against technological determinism, even though AI-generated campaign messages can engage voters through emotional and personalised persuasion. Conrad et al. (2025) note that politically produced AI images may be more likely to induce attention and emotional processing, and reactions to them may be largely attributable to their perceived humanness and trustworthiness. But emotional arousal does not necessarily lead to lasting change in voting behaviour; most experiments report shifts in attitudes rather than behaviour at the polls. In Africa, the 2024 South African election offers a warning: Gondwe (2025) analysed 22,384 messages from politically engaged WhatsApp groups and found that AI-generated deepfakes interacted with emotional manipulation and group ideology to construct false narratives, showing that AI content works relationally through partisan communities, platform dynamics, and grievances.

However, such results cannot be transferred wholesale to Nigeria, where ethnic, religious, regional and party identities shape political choice. Nigerian studies of the 2023 presidential election show that religion and party politics influenced candidate choice alongside social-media engagement, with variation across regions (Morah & Nwafor, 2024; Salahu, 2023; Baba & Jibril, 2023), while Ngoka et al. (2026) reported that WhatsApp campaigns affected the turnout of University of Nigeria students, although this single-university study has limited transferability. The open question for South-South Nigeria is whether AI shapes emotional intensity and voting intention beyond source identity, partisanship, and social-media exposure.
## Theoretical Framework

Source Credibility Theory, developed by Hovland et al. (1953) from Hovland and Weiss's (1951) experiments on communicator credibility, holds that messages influence audiences more when the source is perceived as knowledgeable (expertise) and honest (trustworthiness). It has since been widely applied in advertising, journalism, health and political communication, although a review of five decades of evidence shows that credibility effects are conditional: they weaken when audiences are highly involved with the issue, hold strong prior attitudes, or learn the source only after the message (Pornpitakpan, 2004). Two further limitations matter here. First, credibility is perceived rather than fixed and can be distorted by beliefs, partisanship and context. Second, the theory assumes an identifiable human communicator. Generative AI unsettles this assumption, because audiences may judge a message by cues about the technology itself, sometimes applying a "machine heuristic" that treats machine-made content as more objective (Sundar, 2008), even as AI labels can lower perceived accuracy (Altay & Gilardi, 2024). Consistent with the exploratory design, the theory is used as a sensitising rather than a testing framework: it directs attention to how participants judge the expertise, honesty and authenticity behind AI-generated and human-created messages, and whether these judgements relate to their trust, emotional responses and voting intentions, while leaving room for explanations the theory does not anticipate.
## Method

This study adopted a qualitative exploratory design. Exploratory research suits new phenomena about which little is known, where the aim is to discover how people understand an issue and to generate propositions for later testing, rather than to measure prevalence or test hypotheses (Stebbins, 2001). Because AI-generated campaign messages are new in Nigerian elections and no prior study had examined how South-South electorates read them, the study did not seek to estimate how the region's millions of registered voters respond, which would require a large probability-based survey. Instead, it sought an in-depth account of how electorates understood, trusted and emotionally responded to AI-generated and human-created campaign messages, allowing participants to explain why particular messages appeared credible, artificial or persuasive (Braun & Clarke, 2022; Keen et al., 2022).
## Participants and Sampling

Nineteen participants (see Table 1) were purposively recruited from active political groups across social media. Inclusion criteria were that participants were aged 18 or above, were registered voters with INEC, resided in one of the six South-South states, used social media daily and were regularly exposed to political content online. Participants were spread evenly across all six states, with three or four from each. Maximum-variation sampling was used to capture differences in age, gender, occupation and experience with AI-generated content. Online recruitment and interviewing made it possible to reach participants across the region, a recognised strength of virtual qualitative research (Keen et al., 2022). Sample size was guided by information power rather than statistical representativeness: a focused aim, a specific participant group, rich dialogue and an established analytic strategy reduce the number of participants needed (Malterud et al., 2016), and empirical tests show that interview studies with relatively homogeneous groups often reach saturation within 9 - 17 interviews (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022). Participants are identified by letter codes.

## Data Collection

Data were collected through online semi-structured interviews. Each participant was presented with six campaign messages, labelled CM1 to CM6, comprising both AI-generated and human-created materials in video and still-image formats. The researcher observed participants as they watched the materials and noted immediate reactions such as laughter, hesitation, surprise and confusion. Follow-up questions explored what they noticed, believed, trusted, felt and whether the messages could affect their voting intentions.
## Data Analysis

The data were analysed using Braun and Clarke's (2022) six-phase reflexive thematic analysis, an approach suited to exploring patterns of meaning in small, in-depth datasets. First, transcripts and observation notes were read repeatedly for familiarisation. Second, relevant statements were coded. Third, related codes were grouped into possible themes; thus, the themes emerged from the data rather than being predetermined. Fourth, the themes were checked against the full dataset. Fifth, they were refined and clearly named. Finally, the findings were written using representative quotations. Consistent with the exploratory design, the analysis aimed at transferable insight and theoretical propositions rather than statistical generalisation.
## Results

Three themes were developed from the data. Consistent with the exploratory design, they describe patterns within this sample of 19 participants and are not intended to estimate how widely these views are held among South-South electorates.
## Theme 1: Recognition and Interpretation of Campaign Messages

Among the 19 participants, recognition of AI-generated campaign materials was largely anchored in perceived departures from normal human movement, facial expression, voice, setting and political reality. QR, for instance, claimed complete confidence, identifying "a watermark in the video that clearly shows that it was made with an AI tool… the body movements, they were not realistic". Similarly, AB rated his ability 10/10 because "AI itself, no matter how good it is, currently doesn't capture [human behaviour and tone] to its best." CM, CD and AC also cited appearance, body movement, intonation, video quality, facial expression and background as diagnostic cues.

The most frequently identified example was CM1, the politicians' race. FG judged it artificial because "I don't think our president is young enough to be sprinting", DD pointed to the exaggerated leg split, and AP, PM and MN to unnatural speed and movement. MN was particularly attentive to behavioural consistency, noting that "Peter Obi was laughing to the end and Tinubu wasn't laughing from the beginning to the end… there should be signs that shows that there is something going on." Recognition was thus not only technical: participants compared what they saw with their knowledge of normal bodies and of the candidates.

Contextual plausibility also shaped interpretation. The communion video was repeatedly challenged: TA described "different celebrities receiving communion from a presidential aspirant as a priest" as an obvious impossibility, while CG stated simply: "I have not seen a Muslim in church taking Holy Communion before." These accounts indicate that participants identified AI not only through visual aberrations, but also through breaches of social, religious and political norms.

In contrast, CM3 and CM6 were typically seen as human-made because they resembled familiar campaign environments in Nigeria. AY explained that CM3 "shows the normal campaign settings… many, many voters and then she's talking to the crowd," while RA described CM3 and CM6 as "natural… realistic." For CG, CD and AC, visible crowds, recognisable campaign practices and spontaneous reactions signalled human production, while NA looked for correspondence between voice and emotion, and CF for source credibility and factual traceability.

Yet recognition was not universal. FG, AY, QB, PG, TA, RA, AC and CF all struggled with at least one static image, particularly the flag image, suggesting that static AI imagery was harder to classify than moving video. CF captured this ambiguity: "the picture was not factual… there were faces on the Nigerian flag, and we all know there are no faces on the Nigerian flag." Likewise, NA rated himself only 6/10 because "sometimes AI… looks more real," while RA rated herself 4/10 due to the increasingly advanced generation. For these participants, recognition was a layered process that became less reliable as the technology improved.
## Theme 2: Trust and Credibility of Campaign Messages

Participants' perceptions of authenticity, realism, source plausibility, emotional connection, and perceived human presence were primary drivers of trust, and human-created materials were generally trusted more than AI-generated ones. PG expressed this clearly: "the human-generated political material… looked real, authentic, I could easily connect to it", whereas the AI materials appeared "very fake… it did not look real." DD similarly trusted the human-created videos because "you could actually relate to what was happening." Credibility was thus often established by perceived human realism rather than by the message itself.

This preference was especially noticeable for CM3 and CM6. AY trusted CM3 because "it shows a normal voting system, normal election process, normal campaign settings", RA trusted CM3 and CM6 simply "because they are real", and CD explained that CM3 "looked so real and the environment was very natural."

However, trust did not depend solely on human production. AP found AI-generated CM4 convincing because "the message passed through that material is very genuine and clear" and spoke directly to Nigeria's present circumstances. PM trusted CM4 because it conveyed grief and sadness, while CF trusted the same content because of its emotional resonance: "it kind of told a story… it was emotionally connecting… I was moved by it." These responses blur a clear-cut division between AI and human content: where AI content depicted recognisable social realities, its message could outweigh its production method.

Distrust of AI nonetheless remained common. QA questioned the race material because "it looked very unreal and untrue", while TA stressed that looking believable did not mean political acceptance: "Credible in terms of, do I, would I vote for these people? No." NA doubted even CM2 and CM3, showing that realistic-looking scenes could prompt verification rather than automatic acceptance.

Several participants also linked credibility to AI's distortion of known reality. QR rejected CM2 because "we all know Tinubu is a Muslim… that would be unbelievable," while CG similarly distrusted the communion scenario. CF further distinguished emotional believability from factual credibility, noting that some materials were "believable, but… not factual." Overall, credibility was built from visual realism, familiarity, emotional appeal, factual consistency, perceived source authenticity and alignment with participants' experience of political life.
## Theme 3: Emotional and Behavioural Influence of Campaign Messages

The campaign materials produced markedly different emotional responses, which did not always translate into voting intentions. Humour, confusion, hope, interest, worry and indifference were all evident, with AI-generated materials more often provoking amusement or scepticism, and human-created materials more often eliciting interest and connection. PG described the AI-generated race video as "very funny because it's not something I would usually see", but the human-generated campaign event produced "a little bit of excitement" because of the visible turnout, suggesting that some AI content functioned more as political entertainment than as persuasion.

Yet humour could weaken behavioural influence. DD said that if a candidate used AI-generated videos, "I would take the person as not being serious", because elections should involve "bringing people together for a common purpose." CG asked: "why not do it real time?" For these participants, artificiality signalled insufficient political seriousness.

Other participants experienced more substantive emotions. AP felt hopeful because CM4 addressed current national conditions: "if we do what is right, we elect, we vote for the good candidates, there will still be hope in our country." AC also felt hopeful, while RA said the materials increased her "interest in politics because of the way the APC campaigned." CF was moved by the bloodstained flag, indicating that even AI-generated material could generate affective engagement where its symbolism resonated with participants' understanding of national hardship.

Conversely, confusion and worry arose where messages were ambiguous or exaggerated. MN said CM1 left him confused because "the campaign portrays everybody to be active", making it difficult to determine "who is good for the job." PM doubted the campaign's sincerity: "I don't want a situation where they will make all these things and still turn their back on us." NA worried that images of candidates pushing one another suggested political hostility.

However, emotional engagement did not uniformly produce persuasion. TA remained "indifferent" because "if this is a campaign video, there should be a message. There was no message," adding that the materials made the candidates appear "not very serious." QR said the materials had no political effect because "they are not persuasive," and CF explained: "videos will not change my view"; she would instead assess candidates through "the way you speak and your past performances."

In contrast, AY, QB, AB, RA, AC and CD indicated that campaign materials could influence their electoral judgement. AY said a meaningful manifesto delivered before a crowd would make her "listen… and be looking forward to seeing what you accomplish when you get into the office." AB acknowledged that even AI-generated portrayals influenced his perception of President Tinubu because they "draw a parallel line to what we are facing in Nigeria." Within this sample, behavioural influence depended less on emotion alone than on whether emotion was reinforced by message relevance, perceived authenticity, candidate credibility and prior political judgement.
## Discussion

On the first objective, the findings suggest that recognition was contextual and embodied rather than purely technical. Participants flagged unnatural movements, mismatched laughter and breaches of known religious or political facts, as when CG questioned a Muslim aspirant administering Communion. This aligns with Groh et al. (2022), who showed that audio-visual anomalies, not just content, drive deepfake detection. It appears to contrast with Stefkovics and Gere's (2026) 27-country survey, which found little difference in judgements of undisclosed AI and human content; however, their stimuli were text headlines lacking the embodied cues participants here relied on. Consistent with this, participants such as CF struggled most with still images, suggesting that recognition confidence declines as AI content offers fewer cues to check against lived experience.

On the second objective, participants generally trusted human-created content more, rejecting AI content as unreal (PG, DD). This echoes Altay and Gilardi (2024), whose participants discounted content labelled as AI-generated even when it was accurate. However, AP and PM judged the AI-generated CM4 credible because it reflected Nigeria's current challenges. This complicates reliance on labelling: where the source is unclear, emotional relevance can act as a credibility cue. In terms of Source Credibility Theory (Hovland et al., 1953), source characteristics appeared to matter most when the source was clear, while relevance substituted for them when it was ambiguous. Moreover, whereas Abdulazeez et al. 's (2026) cross-sectional data could not separate believability from willingness to vote, TA explicitly distinguished distrust of AI from distrust of politicians.

On the third and fourth objectives, AI-generated content more often evoked humour or scepticism (as in DD's reaction to the race video), while human-generated content evoked interest or excitement (PG, RA). Emotion seldom translated into voting intention: TA, QR and CF reacted emotionally yet found the material unpersuasive, consistent with Conrad et al. (2025), who warn that increased emotional processing does not necessarily produce lasting behaviour change. This differs from Gondwe (2025), who found AI deepfakes actively spread through partisan WhatsApp groups in South Africa. The contrast may reflect method rather than context: Gondwe examined organic network diffusion, while these interviews captured reflective judgement within a Nigerian identity politics in which religion and party already shape choice (Morah & Nwafor, 2024; Salahu, 2023; Baba & Jibril, 2023).

Taken together, these exploratory results suggest an extension of Source Credibility Theory, which assumes an identifiable source: participants first determined whether a human source was present, then evaluated its honesty and expertise. Recognition, trust and emotional response therefore appear sequential rather than parallel, a layering that the literature on AI and African elections, largely concerned with disinformation risk (Wack & Prochaska, 2026; Ibrahim & Ekdale, 2026), does not fully theorise. These are propositions to be tested in larger, representative studies rather than conclusions about South-South electorates as a whole.
## Implications

Although exploratory, the findings suggest that AI-generated political campaign content can influence electorates, even when they are aware of its artificial nature. This is relevant to Nigeria's 2027 elections, particularly for young electorates, political parties, electoral bodies, journalists and fact-checkers. Participants detected AI content through errors, unrealistic behaviour and violations of familiar political or religious contexts, but these cues will become less reliable as AI improves. Convincing synthetic videos or images could damage reputations, erode trust and deepen existing political and religious divisions. Political parties should therefore use AI transparently, while INEC, media organisations and civil society groups should strengthen voter education and fast fact-checking.
## Limitations and Directions for Future Research

As an exploratory qualitative study, this research has limitations that define how its findings should be read. The sample of 19 purposively selected, social-media-active registered voters aged 18 - 40 is not statistically representative, and the findings should not be generalised to all South-South electorates; they offer transferable insights and propositions instead. The participants also responded to selected campaign materials in an interview setting rather than during an actual campaign, where party allegiance, peer pressure and repeated exposure may shape responses differently. Future research should test the propositions generated here through larger, probability-based surveys of registered voters across all six states, experiments comparing AI-generated and human-created messages, and studies conducted during the campaign season.
## Conclusion

This exploratory study suggests that the South-South electorates interviewed did not judge campaign messages by technology alone. They recognised AI through embodied and contextual cues, trusted messages that felt real and relevant, and rarely allowed emotional reactions to override prior political judgement. As AI-generated content becomes harder to detect, these patterns warrant confirmatory research ahead of the 2027 general elections.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the 2027 Elections: Comparing Urban and Rural Voters' Responses to AI-Generated Campaign Messages in Abia State, Nigeria
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Nigerian electoral communication ahead of the 2027 general elections, raising concerns about authenticity, trust and misinformation. This exploratory study examined how voters aged 18 - 40 in Abia State, Nigeria, understand, feel about and respond to AI-generated and AI-assisted campaign messages, and how urban/semi-urban and rural voters compare. Method: A qualitative exploratory design was adopted. Twenty voters (ten urban/semi-urban and ten rural) were purposively selected from communities across Abia State and interviewed individually using six AI-generated or AI-assisted campaign materials (CM1 - CM6), supplemented by observation notes. Data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted with the Elaboration Likelihood Model. Findings: AI familiarity varied within both groups rather than simply between them. Participants separated emotional appeal from credibility, and realistic fabrication caused more concern than obvious satire. The messages stimulated attention, discussion and verification more readily than candidate support, and rural participants relied more on interpersonal and community verification networks. Conclusion: Within this sample, AI-generated campaign messages shaped electoral judgement through credibility, emotional appeal, realism and verification conditions rather than automatic vote conversion. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger studies.

bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

Nigeria's 2027 general elections are scheduled for 16 January 2027 (presidential and National Assembly) and 6 February 2027 (governorship and State Houses of Assembly). Under the revised timetable of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), campaigns for the federal elections began on 19 August 2026 and those for the state elections on 9 September 2026, and all campaigns must end 24 hours before polling day (Oliji, 2026). The 2027 campaign is therefore the first Nigerian general election campaign to unfold while generative AI tools are cheap and widely available.

AI is increasingly being integrated into electoral communication, giving political agents tools to quickly and cost-effectively tailor text, images, audio and video content while posing fresh challenges of authenticity, accountability and trust (Juneja, 2024; Chowdhury, 2024). In Nigeria, the 2023 elections marked a visible entry point: a viral audio clip purporting to capture Atiku Abubakar, Ifeanyi Okowa and Aminu Tambuwal plotting to rig the election was found to be a doctored deepfake (Shibayan, 2023). In West Africa, OpenAI (2025) reported an AI-generated influence operation that produced partisan articles and comments ahead of Ghana's 2024 election. Technical capacity, however, does not guarantee a uniform impact. In experiments around elections in the United States, Canada and Poland, Lin et al. (2025) found that dialogues with AI significantly shifted candidate preferences, while Neyazi et al. (2025), who studied 1,627 people in India, did not find a boost in affective polarization after reading about campaign deepfakes. These results challenge deterministic claims about the persuasive effects of AI-generated political messages. The distinction is particularly relevant in Africa, where political information does not travel only through the Internet: Gadjanova et al. (2022) show how misinformation spans digital divides through interpersonal and socially mediated communication in northern Ghana, and Hassan (2023) found that electoral misinformation in Nigeria moves through social and traditional media.

This study is set in Abia State, south-east Nigeria, which has 17 local government areas, 4,069 polling units and over two million registered voters (Okoronkwo, 2023). The state combines urban commercial and administrative centres, notably Aba and Umuahia, with semi-urban towns and rural farming communities. The study focuses on voters aged 18 - 40, a group heavily exposed to political content online (Mustapha & Omar, 2020). This group is not homogeneous. In Nigeria, where mobile internet spread mainly after 2010, younger voters grew up with smartphones and social media and can be regarded as digital natives, whereas older voters in the bracket adopted digital technologies later and resembled digital immigrants (Prensky, 2001). Such differences, together with uneven internet access between urban and rural areas (Conroy-Krutz et al., 2024; Kemp, 2024), may shape how AI-generated messages are understood.

Existing scholarship does not adequately capture how such messages are understood and acted upon in Nigerian communities. First, influential experimental studies are geographically limited to North America, Europe and India, and their results cannot be assumed to apply to Abia State (Lin et al., 2025; Neyazi et al., 2025). Second, Nigerian studies have found that misinformation can affect voter attitudes, trust in the electoral process and democracy, but they focus on misinformation generally rather than on generative-AI campaign content or on comparing flyers, synthetic audio and short videos (Hassan, 2023; Akinola et al., 2024). Third, African studies show differences in access to, and verification of, information, but there is little evidence on whether these differences lead to different reactions to AI-generated electoral messages among urban, semi-urban and rural voters (Gadjanova et al., 2022; Azeez et al., 2026).

Because the phenomenon is new and these questions have not been examined in Abia State, an exploratory approach is appropriate: rather than measuring effects across the electorate, it seeks in-depth understanding and propositions for later testing (Stebbins, 2001). The study contributes to scholarship by providing early evidence from a Nigerian state on AI-generated campaign messages ahead of the 2027 elections, by comparing urban/semi-urban and rural voters, a contrast largely absent from AI-persuasion research, and by extending the Elaboration Likelihood Model to AI-generated political content in a hybrid online - offline information environment. Practically, it offers INEC, parties, journalists and civil society insight for voter education during the campaign.

This exploratory study therefore explores how voters aged 18 - 40 in urban, semi-urban and rural Abia State comprehend, feel about and react to AI-generated political campaign messages delivered as flyers, audio recordings and short videos. Specifically, it sought to:
examine how voters aged 18 to 40 in Abia State understand AI-generated campaign messages;
explore how voters feel about AI-generated campaign flyers, audio messages, and short videos;
examine how AI-generated campaign messages influence voters' willingness to seek more information, discuss a candidate, or support a candidate;
compare the responses of urban and semi-urban voters with those of rural voters to AI-generated campaign messages.
## Conceptual Clarification

In this study, AI-generated campaign messages are political flyers, audio clips or videos whose content is produced wholly or substantially by generative AI, such as synthetic images, cloned voices or fabricated scenes. AI-assisted campaign messages are human-designed materials in which AI performs supporting tasks such as editing, image enhancement or drafting text (Nobel et al., 2026). Urban areas are the state's main administrative and commercial centres (Umuahia and Aba); semi-urban areas are smaller towns with mixed urban and rural features (such as Ubakala, Olokoro and parts of Isiala Ngwa); and rural areas are farming and trading communities with more limited infrastructure and internet access (such as communities in Bende, Ikwuano, Isuikwuato, Ohafia and Umunneochi).
## Voters' Understanding of AI-Generated Campaign Messages

Studies by Lee and Yuan (2025), Nobel et al. (2026) and Chae and Tewksbury (2026) suggest that voters' understanding of AI-generated campaign communication relies on more than identifying the term "AI"; it involves assessing authenticity, credibility and communicative intent. This is important because politically generated AI content ranges from innocuous design help to fabricated speech. In five preregistered experiments with 2,215 participants, Groh et al. (2024) showed that individuals distinguished political deepfakes from real speeches better than chance, but not perfectly, and that audio-visual information aided recognition more than transcripts. Younger voters cannot be assumed to recognise synthetic content easily either: Dozier (2026) reported that 80% of 18 - 34-year-olds could only correctly identify AI images 50% of the time, and White (2025) reported that more than half of 13 - 18-year-olds could not determine whether AI content was true. Disclosure further complicates understanding. Harff (2026) found that labels on AI-generated images improved recognition but also lowered source credibility, and Nobel et al. (2026) found that when source credibility was low, fully AI-generated political advertisements were rated less favourably than AI-assisted ones. These studies, however, were conducted mainly outside Africa, leaving open how Nigerian voters with uneven AI exposure understand such messages.
## Feelings Towards AI-Generated Flyers, Audio and Videos

Attitudes to flyers, audio and short videos are likely to be modality-specific and should not be analysed as a single attitude to AI. Flyers allow more time to consider wording and visual anomalies (Farooq & de Vreese, 2026), while audio can capitalize on familiar voices and passive listening (Groh et al., 2024). Short videos include facial expressions, body movement, emotional cues and voice, which could enhance both perceived authenticity and deceptive potential (Groh et al., 2024; Hameleers et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026). Groh et al. (2024) also found that state-of-the-art synthetic speech was harder to identify than actor-voiced fakes, so audio-visual cues do not guarantee detection. Similarly, evidence of the persuasive power of some AI messages should not be extended to all formats. Among 4,829 respondents, Bai et al. (2025) found that LLM-generated messages changed attitudes as effectively as human-authored ones, but Hewitt et al.'s (2024) archive of 146 campaign experiments shows that the effects of political ads are small and variable. How Nigerian voters feel about each format remains largely unexamined.
## Behavioural Responses: Information Seeking, Discussion and Support

Behavioural responses may also vary. AI-generated messages can prompt information seeking when they seem novel, uncertain or manipulative, whereas distrust can lead to avoidance. Mustapha and Omar (2020) found that Nigerian youths were more politically active offline than online, a caution against equating online exposure with participation. Discussion, information seeking and candidate support should therefore be distinguished; a campaign message may stimulate discussion precisely because recipients doubt it. At a larger scale, a US$8.9-million digital campaign experiment reaching two million Americans had no effect on turnout (Aggarwal et al., 2023), showing that exposure reveals little about how content is processed. Evidence on these behavioural responses among Nigerian voters exposed to AI content is lacking.
## Urban - Rural Differences in Responses

The urban - rural comparison is particularly significant in Africa. Conroy-Krutz et al. (2024) found that 65% of people in 39 African countries regularly get news from radio while 47% do so via social media or the Internet, with digital use concentrated among urban, younger, better-educated and wealthier citizens. Nigeria is digitalising fast but access remains uneven: Kemp (2024) estimated that 103 million Nigerians used the Internet in early 2024 and that 54.6% of the population was urban. These figures caution against assuming social homogeneity in internet contact.

In Nigeria, WhatsApp is used for text, photos, voice notes and videos in both urban and rural areas, but Ogbodo et al. (2023) warn that digital literacy alone does not prevent sharing misinformation. Among 1,200 Nigerian youths, Azeez et al. (2026) found that urban youths were more likely to be exposed to misinformation, while rural youths were more likely to change their electoral preferences, especially when the message came from a trusted community or religious intermediary. Rural voters should therefore not be viewed as simply "less digital"; they may interpret AI through more socially mediated channels, while urban and semi-urban voters might have more exposure to AI and more scepticism or verification. No study has yet compared how these groups respond to AI-generated campaign messages.

In sum, the literature leaves four gaps that correspond to this study's objectives: limited evidence on how Nigerian voters understand AI-generated campaign messages; little attention to how they feel about different formats; scarce evidence on behavioural responses beyond persuasion; and no direct comparison of urban/semi-urban and rural voters. The question for Abia State's young voters is, therefore, not whether AI-generated messages 'work', but how format, disclosure, trust, digital access and community validation affect their processing and behavioural responses.
## Theoretical Framework

The Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) holds that persuasion follows two routes (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986). Through the central route, people who are motivated and able to process a message scrutinise its arguments, producing stronger and more lasting attitudes. Through the peripheral route, people with low motivation or ability rely on cues such as source credibility, emotion, familiarity and presentation, producing weaker and less stable attitudes. Whether elaboration is high or low depends on motivation, such as personal relevance, and ability, such as knowledge, time and freedom from distraction (Petty et al., 1981).

Each ELM component is linked to a study variable. First, ability to elaborate corresponds to voters' AI familiarity, digital literacy and confidence in detecting synthetic content (Objective 1). Second, peripheral cues correspond to the emotional appeal, realism, recognisable political figures, religious symbols and format of the flyers, audio and videos (Objective 2). Third, central-route processing corresponds to voters' scrutiny of claims, such as checking whether a depicted alliance is real or weighing a candidate's record, while elaboration outcomes correspond to information seeking, discussion and candidate support (Objective 3). Finally, motivation and ability are shaped by context: access to data, verification opportunities and trusted community intermediaries differ between urban/semi-urban and rural settings (Objective 4). Consistent with the exploratory design, the ELM is used as an interpretive lens rather than a set of hypotheses to be tested.
## Method

The study adopted a qualitative exploratory design. Exploratory research suits new phenomena where the aim is to understand how people make sense of an issue and to generate propositions, rather than to measure prevalence or test hypotheses (Stebbins, 2001). The study therefore does not claim to represent Abia State's more than two million registered voters, which would require a large probability-based survey; its urban - rural comparison is analytical rather than statistical. The design enabled participants to explain why certain messages seemed authentic, dubious or persuasive (Braun & Clarke, 2022).

Individual semi-structured interviews were preferred to focus group discussions for three reasons. Political preferences are sensitive, and group settings can produce conformity to dominant partisan views; the study needed to observe each participant's immediate, unprompted reaction to the materials; and individual interviews allowed participants with low AI familiarity to speak without being overshadowed by more digitally confident peers. Focus groups are recommended for future studies of how voters negotiate AI content collectively.
## Study Area, Participants and Sampling

Twenty voters, ten urban/semi-urban and ten rural, were purposively selected from communities across Abia State. Urban participants were drawn from Umuahia and Aba, semi-urban participants from towns such as Ubakala, Olokoro and Isiala Ngwa, and rural participants from communities in Bende, Ikwuano, Isuikwuato, Ohafia and Umunneochi local government areas. Participants were aged 18 - 40, eligible to vote and resident in the study area. Gender, occupation, educational level, smartphone ownership, social-media usage and previous awareness of AI were considered as they may influence interpretation. Purposive sampling was appropriate for selecting information-rich cases (Ahmad & Wilkins, 2025). Sample size was guided by information power rather than statistical representativeness: a focused aim, specific participants, rich dialogue and an established analytic strategy reduce the number needed (Malterud et al., 2016). Twenty participants, ten per setting, therefore suited an exploratory comparison, although the findings are not generalisable to all voters in the state.

## Data Collection

Semi-structured individual interviews were used to gather data. Participants were shown six campaign materials (CM1 - CM6), which included AI-generated or AI-assisted flyers, audio recordings and short videos (Table 2). The researcher noted immediate reactions such as laughter, hesitation, surprise and uncertainty. Follow-up questions explored what participants observed, understood, trusted and felt, and whether the messages could prompt them to seek information, discuss or support the candidates. Using identical stimuli for all participants aided comparison.

## Data Analysis

Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse the data. Transcripts and observation notes were read many times for familiarisation; statements were coded and related codes were formed into themes. Themes were reviewed against the data set, refined and named, and representative quotations were selected. Coding was mostly inductive. The Elaboration Likelihood Model was then used as an interpretive lens to examine how careful evaluation compared with rapid credibility, familiarity and emotional cues, without forcing the data into predetermined categories (Braun & Clarke, 2022; Byrne, 2022).
## Ethical Considerations

Participation was voluntary, and participants gave informed consent after the purpose of the study was explained. They were assured of confidentiality and are identified only by codes (U01 - U10 for urban/semi-urban and P2 - P11 for rural participants).
## Results

Two themes, one for each setting, were developed, each organised around the study objectives. Consistent with the exploratory design, they describe patterns within this sample and do not estimate how widely these views are held among Abia State voters.
Theme 1: Urban and Semi-Urban Voters' Perceptions and Responses to AI-Generated Political Campaign Messages

The study found that none of the ten urban and semi-urban participants accepted or rejected AI-generated political communication outright. Instead, answers depended on their knowledge of AI, the message's structure, emotional intensity, perceived authenticity, and whether synthetic manipulation was disclosed.
## Understanding AI through recognition, uncertainty and disclosure

Participants' understanding of AI-generated political content varied widely. The more tech-savvy urban participants exhibited more developed notions of AI. U01 (female, 19, urban Umuahia, student, high AI familiarity), for example, understood that AI could alter multiple layers of communication: "AI-made means software generated or changed some part of the content. It may be the picture, the voice, the face, the wording, or all of it." Yet she conceded that "AI is getting better, so... you can still be fooled." U02 (male, 22, urban Aba, student, high AI familiarity) similarly identified "funny fingers", stiff faces, lip-sync problems and unnatural voices, but admitted that professionally produced AI required verification rather than visual guesswork.

This contrasted with U07 (female, 33, semi-urban Ubakala, teacher, low AI familiarity), whose prior knowledge centred mainly on ChatGPT: "I thought it was mainly for writing and answering questions." She added: "It may be difficult for me... if it is neat I may accept it." U10 (male, 40, semi-urban Isiala Ngwa, artisan/trader, low AI familiarity) similarly asked, "If it is very fake I may see it, but if it is clean, how will I know?" AI literacy thus depended less on urban residence than on prior exposure and occupational experience, as evidenced by U04's professional experience with generative design technologies.
## Emotional appeal versus credibility and authenticity

Participants clearly differentiated between attention-grabbing and credible information. The politically neutral satire race, CM1, amused most urban participants (U01 - U05, U07 and U08) but persuaded few. U04 (male, 27, urban Aba, graphic designer, high AI familiarity) described it as "political meme content", noting that disclosure reduced deception: "Because it says AI, I can enjoy it as satire; if the same clip removed the label and pretended to be real, I would see that as deceptive."

CM4 struck a different emotional register. The shattered Nigerian flag, distressed faces and disaster imagery brought sadness, tension and unease to U02, U03, U04, U05, U07, U08 and U09. For U04, "The visual metaphor is much heavier than ordinary campaign flyers. There is no candidate, no policy, just national pain concentrated into one image." U07's reaction was more visceral: "The faces in the flag... [pauses] that one is not easy to forget." Recognising synthetic production did not neutralise emotional impact.

CM5 raised the greatest credibility concerns. Its portrayal of an unconfirmed Obi - Kwankwaso partnership, using real political figures and official-looking design, worried U01, U03, U04, U05, U06, U08 and U09. U03 (female, 24, urban Umuahia, online retailer, moderate AI familiarity) explained: "I felt confused first, then suspicious. I would ask, is this ticket real? Because a fine graphic can make something look official when it is not." U09 (female, 38, semi-urban Olokoro, public servant, moderate AI familiarity) regarded CM5 as more dangerous than emotional imagery because it could manufacture political certainty around something that might not exist.
## Attention and verification rather than automatic political support

The messages appeared more capable of stimulating attention, conversation and verification than determining vote choice. U01 explained: "It can affect my attention, not my final vote. A strong video may make me search the candidate, but I still need policies, track record and debates before support." U03, U05, U06, U07, U08 and U09 likewise prioritised competence, integrity, governance records, economic conditions and policy over campaign aesthetics.

Nevertheless, dismissing persuasive influence altogether would be misleading. U04 observed that "Repetition, colour, music and emotional framing can make a candidate feel credible before you analyse anything," and U09 argued that "Repeated exposure can influence salience and emotional orientation, even when a voter thinks he or she is being rational." For these participants, the key question was how AI was used: disclosed creative assistance was generally accepted, while synthetic impersonation, fabricated events and AI-made claims presented as political fact raised concerns about trust.
## Theme 2: Rural Voters' Perceptions and Responses to AI-Generated Political Campaign Messages
The discussion draws on ten rural participants (P2 - P11).
## Limited AI familiarity complicated by convincing realism

Rural participants' knowledge of AI, and their confidence in spotting it, was inconsistent. P2, P3, P7, P8, P10 and P11 had no prior substantive knowledge of AI-generated political content, while P4, P5, P6 and P9 had seen or used AI through social media, ChatGPT, synthetic images or cloned voices. For P2 (female, 21, Bende, trader, no prior AI awareness), AI had seemed remote from everyday politics: "I did not know ordinary political pictures and voices on phone could be made that way." P7 (male, 27, Umunneochi, farmer, no prior AI awareness) admitted that he might already have encountered synthetic material without recognising it.

This uncertainty persisted even among participants with prior awareness. P4 (female, 20, Isuikwuato, student, prior AI awareness) could inspect "mouth and voice, hands, eyes, shadows, writing on posters", yet conceded: "I won't boast that I can always know - these things are improving." P5, P6 and P9 expressed the same caution. Awareness of AI, therefore, did not guarantee detection. P2 captured the vulnerability: "But if it is well made, I can believe it."
## Emotion, familiarity and community context shaped credibility

Some rural participants interpreted messages through familiar cultural and religious cues. CM2, which placed a politician at a Catholic Mass, was more troubling to them than obviously artificial content. P2, P3, P4, P5, P6 and others challenged the use of religion to transfer moral currency to a politician. P5 (male, 24, Ikwuano, artisan, prior AI awareness) argued that "Church attendance and good government are not the same thing." Such a familiar religious scene could circulate through WhatsApp, church networks and interpersonal discussion without immediately appearing suspicious.

CM4's damaged Nigerian flag and suffering faces generated strong emotional responses across P2 - P11. P10 (female, 30, Ikwuano, trader, no prior AI awareness) stated: "It made me sad and a bit angry. You start remembering food prices, roads, unemployment... even though the video did not name them." AI imagery thus activated genuine economic grievances without evidence linking them to a candidate. Yet participants generally resisted equating emotional truth with evidential truth: hardship might be real, but the generated image did not establish responsibility.

CM5 produced suspicion rather than sadness. P2, P3, P8 and P11 were struck by the apparently official Obi - Kwankwaso pairing and the threatening hook/noose imagery. P2 explained: "My first question was, 'Did these two really announce this ticket?' The hook and noose also make me uneasy because they are telling me to fear the pairing before I even know whether the pairing is real."
Here, the danger lay in manufacturing apparent political facts from recognisable people rather than in obviously fantastic imagery.
## Messages stimulated discussion and verification more readily than vote conversion

Across P2 - P11, the messages were more likely to provoke curiosity, interpersonal discussion and verification than immediate support. The more digitally engaged P5 and P9 checked official pages or news sources, while P2, P3, P7, P8, P10 and P11 combined WhatsApp or Facebook searches with asking relatives, traders, farmers, community members or other trusted people. This reflects a hybrid rural information environment rather than mere digital exclusion. P8 explained that information could arrive through "WhatsApp forwarding, radio, church, market, family or one person's phone", so a convincing clip could circulate widely before its source was examined.

Nevertheless, participants repeatedly separated attention from vote choice. P8 (female, 26, Ohafia, trader, no prior AI awareness) acknowledged that grassroots footage could make a candidate appear serious, but maintained that "voting would still depend on record, policies and whether I trust the people behind him." P10 expressed the same position, while P5 stressed that even real footage could exaggerate support.

Rural participants, therefore, did not automatically believe AI-generated campaign messages. Rather, their vulnerability centred on verification conditions: limited data, uneven AI literacy, familiar religious and community cues, trusted interpersonal circulation and highly convincing synthetic material. Accordingly, P11 called for labelling, simple verification procedures and quick corrections from "Radio stations, community leaders and journalists". For these participants, hidden manipulation, such as fake alliances, voices, crowds or religious scenes, was the most alarming threat to political trust.
## Discussion of Findings

Regarding the first objective, comprehension of AI-generated campaign messages was shaped less by location than by prior exposure, digital experience and confidence in verification. Some urban participants (U01, U02, U04) were well versed in synthetic images, voices and video manipulation, whereas some semi-urban participants (U07, U10) were not, and even rural participants with AI awareness (P4, P5, P9) doubted their ability to spot it. The most AI-literate urban participants were among the youngest (U01, 19; U02, 22) and the least familiar semi-urban participants were older (U07, 33; U10, 40), consistent with the distinction between digital natives and digital immigrants (Prensky, 2001); however, young rural participants such as P2 (21) also lacked AI awareness, suggesting that access matters as much as age. These patterns align with Groh et al. (2024), Dozier (2026) and White (2025), who show that even young users struggle to identify AI content. In ELM terms, low ability to judge authenticity may push voters towards peripheral cues such as visual realism, source familiarity and presentation quality (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986).

On the second objective, participants separated emotional response from perceived credibility. Emotionally intense content such as CM4 evoked sadness, anxiety or anger but did not necessarily produce belief, consistent with Hameleers et al. (2024), Groh et al. (2024) and Guo et al. (2026), who note that audio-visual cues can evoke emotion and create opportunities for manipulation. More concerning to participants was CM5, whose recognisable politicians and 'official look' lent it apparent political reality. Realistic fabrication may therefore be more democratically consequential than disclosed satire such as CM1, extending Harff (2026) and Nobel et al. (2026) on disclosure and credibility. In ELM terms, recognisable politicians, official design conventions and evocative symbols acted as peripheral credibility cues before substantive claims were scrutinised.

On the third objective, AI-generated messages prompted attention, verification and discussion more than candidate support. Participants in both settings distinguished curiosity from voting intention and emphasised policy, competence, integrity and record. This is consistent with Hewitt et al. (2024), who show that political advertising effects are small and variable, and Aggarwal et al. (2023), who found no turnout effect from extensive digital exposure, but contrasts with Lin et al. (2025) and Bai et al. (2025), who found measurable attitude change. The difference may be methodological: experiments isolate persuasive impact, whereas interviews capture reflective judgement, and self-reports may underestimate unconscious influence, as U04 and U09 suggested. Within this sample, influence appeared indirect, operating through attention, salience and later information seeking, which in ELM terms reflects motivation to elaborate rather than immediate attitude change.

On the fourth objective, rural participants were not less sceptical, but their verification relied more on interpersonal and community networks: relatives, churches, markets, radio and WhatsApp. This supports Gadjanova et al. (2022) and Hassan (2023) on misinformation spreading through hybrid online - offline systems, and partly supports Azeez et al. (2026) on rural vulnerability to messages from trusted intermediaries. However, rural participants often challenged political claims rather than accepting them, so the better explanation is unequal verification conditions, not rural gullibility. In ELM terms, limited data, lower AI familiarity and socially trusted cues may make the peripheral route more influential without removing critical judgement. Because the sample is small and self-reported scepticism may not predict election-day behaviour, these are propositions for larger studies rather than population-level differences.
## Conclusion, Limitations and Recommendations

This exploratory study suggests that the electoral risk of AI-generated communication in Nigeria lies less in automatic vote conversion than in attention, emotion, credibility and verification. This is especially relevant as campaigns for the 2027 general elections run until January and February 2027. Interventions should therefore go beyond generic digital-literacy campaigns to verification strategies that reflect how information circulates through WhatsApp, radio, churches, markets and interpersonal networks, involving INEC, journalists, civil society groups and community leaders. Political parties should also disclose AI use in campaign materials.

The study has limitations. The sample is small, purposive and limited in scope, so the findings cannot be generalised to Abia State's electorate, and self-reported scepticism may not reflect campaign behaviour. The study focused on selected materials (CM1 - CM6) rather than long-term or repeated exposure, and did not fully explore partisanship, ethnicity, religion, gender, education, algorithmic amplification or the difference between AI-assisted content and deepfakes. Future research should test these exploratory propositions through larger surveys, experiments, focus group discussions and longitudinal designs covering all 17 local government areas.

title: Electoral Propaganda and Public Opinion Formation in Nigeria's Fourth Republic: A Conceptual Analysis
abstract: Electoral propaganda has become a structural feature of democratic competition in Nigeria's Fourth Republic (1999 to present), systematically shaping how citizens perceive candidates, parties, and democratic processes. This paper conceptually examines the relationship between electoral propaganda and public opinion formation in Nigeria, deploying Agenda-Setting Theory, the Propaganda Model, and the Spiral of Silence as an integrated analytical framework. Using a qualitative documentary approach based on the synthesis of scholarly and institutional sources, the study is organised around three thematic concerns: the structural machinery and media dimensions of electoral propaganda; the digital and AI-driven transformation of propaganda practice; and the implications of propaganda-saturated communication environments for democratic consolidation. The analysis demonstrates that electoral propaganda in Nigeria operates through coordinated information management, media capture, digital influence networks, and identity-based emotional appeals, producing public opinion climates that reflect elite preferences rather than deliberative citizen judgment. The findings further indicate that digital platforms, computational propaganda, organised disinformation networks, and emerging artificial intelligence applications have expanded the scale and sophistication of opinion manipulation in contemporary electoral politics. By integrating classical communication theories with emerging scholarship on digital influence, the study contributes a conceptual framework for understanding how propaganda shapes democratic participation and public opinion in Nigeria's Fourth Republic. The paper recommends strengthening media independence, digital platform regulation, information literacy, and fact-checking infrastructure as systemic correctives.
