bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

Elections constitute the most consequential arena of democratic governance, representing the institutionalised mechanism through which citizens exercise sovereign authority and signal policy preferences. Yet elections are also the primary space in which state actors, political parties, and contracted communication networks deploy sophisticated propaganda strategies to shape public opinion in ways that serve strategic rather than deliberative ends (Bernays, 1928; Lasswell, 1927). In contemporary democracies, including emerging ones such as Nigeria, the management of electoral perception has become as politically consequential as the formal conduct of the election itself.

Nigeria's Fourth Republic, inaugurated on 29 May 1999 following the transition from military rule, has provided a sustained democratic context in which electoral propaganda has evolved from rudimentary mass messaging to digitally coordinated influence operations. Across seven general election cycles from 1999 to 2023, successive administrations and opposition formations have employed increasingly refined communication strategies, including mass media campaigns, disinformation, ethno-religious identity appeals, digital astroturfing, and platform-based influence operations. The 2023 presidential election demonstrated the extent to which these strategies have become institutionalised features of electoral competition, with disinformation deployed at scale against candidates, institutions, and the electoral process itself (Madueke and Enyiazu, 2025; Anaukwu and Obiozo, 2025).

Recent studies suggest that this transformation is not confined to campaign messaging alone but extends to broader processes of public opinion construction. Examining the post-2015 electoral environment, Okolie, Enyiazu and Nnamani (2021) show that propaganda strategies increasingly function as instruments for shaping electoral narratives and legitimising political actors. Scholarship on Nigeria's 2023 elections similarly highlights the growing influence of social media platforms in mediating political information and voter perceptions (Aina & Afolaranmi, 2025). These developments indicate that propaganda has become deeply embedded within contemporary electoral communication processes rather than serving merely as a supplementary campaign tool.

Public opinion, understood as the aggregate of individual attitudes toward matters of public concern, occupies a constitutive role in democratic theory (Lippmann, 1922; Price, 1992). Habermas (1989) locates the legitimacy of democratic governance in the communicative rationality of the public sphere, where opinion formation is expected to occur through open, reasoned, and inclusive deliberation. The empirical reality of electoral communication in Nigeria diverges substantially from this normative ideal. The political communication environment is characterised by unequal information access, media concentration, state interference in broadcasting, digital disinformation, and the systematic mobilisation of propaganda by well-resourced political actors (McNair, 2018).

While the literature has addressed aspects of political communication, media framing, social media influence, and democratic challenges in Nigeria's Fourth Republic, the specific conceptual relationship between electoral propaganda and public opinion formation has received comparatively limited systematic attention. Existing scholarship has generated important empirical insights into campaign communication, electoral behaviour, digital media influence, and propaganda practices in particular election cycles (Okolie et al., 2021; Anaukwu & Obiozo, 2025). Moreover, recent work has increasingly examined the role of social media in shaping political attitudes and electoral outcomes in Nigeria (Aina & Afolaranmi, 2025), while broader analyses have explored the implications of digital communication for public political opinion between 2015 and 2023 (Onwuta, 2026). However, these studies generally focus on specific elections, platforms, or measurable communication effects. Less attention has been devoted to developing a comprehensive conceptual explanation of how electoral propaganda operates as a sustained system of public opinion construction across Nigeria's Fourth Republic. This limitation is particularly significant in contemporary information environments characterised by what Bennett and Livingston (2018) describe as a disinformation order, where political actors increasingly compete to influence public understanding through strategically managed information flows. This paper seeks to address that gap by providing a theoretically grounded examination of how electoral propaganda operates to construct public opinion in Nigeria's democratic context. The study contributes to the political communication literature in Africa by situating electoral propaganda within a theoretically integrated framework that combines Agenda-Setting Theory, the Propaganda Model, and the Spiral of Silence to explain the interaction between media structures, influence strategies, and citizen responses in emerging democracies. It is limited to Nigeria's Fourth Republic from 1999 to the present and employs a conceptual, library-based methodology drawing on peer-reviewed scholarship and credible secondary sources rather than primary data collection.

Specifically, the study pursues three objectives: (i) it examines the structural mechanisms through which electoral propaganda operates in Nigeria's Fourth Republic. (ii) it analyses the role of digital communication technologies and emerging artificial intelligence applications in transforming contemporary propaganda practices. (iii) it evaluates the implications of propaganda-driven public opinion formation for democratic consolidation and civic engagement in Nigeria. Through these objectives, the study provides a holistic account of the evolving relationship between electoral propaganda, media influence, and democratic politics in contemporary Nigeria.
## Theoretical Integration and Discussion

This study is anchored in three complementary theoretical traditions: Agenda-Setting Theory, the Propaganda Model, and the Spiral of Silence. These theories function not as independent frameworks but as analytically integrated lenses that illuminate distinct but interrelated dimensions of the propaganda and public opinion relationship in Nigeria's electoral context. Agenda-Setting operates at the media-public interface, explaining which issues receive salience. The Propaganda Model operates at the structural level, explaining why media systems reproduce elite-serving narratives. The Spiral of Silence operates at the individual and social level, explaining how manufactured opinion climates are internalised and reproduced through conformity dynamics. These perspectives provide a multilevel explanation of propaganda, linking institutional communication structures, media agenda construction, and citizen responses. Their continued relevance is particularly evident in digitally networked communication environments where elite influence increasingly operates through both traditional media institutions and algorithmically mediated platforms (Howard & Woolley, 2016).

Agenda-Setting Theory, developed by McCombs and Shaw (1972) through their landmark study of the 1968 United States presidential election, proposes that mass media exert significant influence over public opinion not by telling people what to think but by shaping which issues and actors receive public attention. The second level of the theory, introduced by McCombs, Shaw and Weaver (1997), focuses on attribute salience, arguing that media influence public perceptions not only by determining which issues become prominent but also by emphasising particular attributes of those issues and political actors In Nigeria's electoral context, second-level agenda-setting is observable in the systematic foregrounding of candidate attributes such as ethnic identity and religious affiliation by state-aligned media, while corruption records and policy failures receive diminished attention. The agenda-setting function thereby serves as a primary vehicle through which electoral propaganda directs public evaluative attention toward propaganda-friendly narratives. In contemporary digital environments, agenda-setting extends beyond conventional news organisations to include social media platforms, influencers, and algorithmic recommendation systems that shape the visibility and circulation of political content. As a result, political actors are increasingly able to influence public salience structures through coordinated online communication strategies that amplify selected issues while marginalising others (Woolley & Howard, 2018).

Attribute framing translates into concrete electoral outcomes through its operation on ethno-regional and religious identity dimensions. Okolie, Enyiazu and Nnamani (2021) document how both major parties in the 2015 presidential election constructed propaganda campaigns around ethnic and religious identity attributes that systematically displaced policy and governance performance as the primary evaluative criteria available to voters. By framing elections as contests between ethnic or religious communities rather than alternative governance programmes, propaganda substitutes identity loyalty for deliberative judgment, producing evaluations that are structurally resistant to counter argument because they are anchored in identity rather than evidence. The persistence of such identity-centred framing demonstrates that agenda-setting effects in Nigeria often operate through culturally resonant narratives that shape not only what citizens think about but also the criteria by which political actors are judged.

Herman and Chomsky's (1988) Propaganda Model identifies five institutional filters through which news content passes before reaching the public: media ownership concentration, dependence on advertising revenue, reliance on elite information sources, flak from powerful interests, and dominant ideological frameworks. Applied to Nigeria's electoral environment, these filters reveal the structural dependencies that render the media system susceptible to propaganda. Nigerian media organisations depend substantially on government advertising revenue, operate within proprietorship structures aligned with partisan interests, and function in a regulatory environment in which licences and accreditation can be deployed as instruments of pressure (RSF, 2024). These conditions create powerful institutional incentives for media organisations to reproduce propaganda-aligned narratives and disincentivise independent, adversarial electoral journalism. Contemporary developments suggest that these structural filters now extend beyond conventional media organisations. Digital platforms, targeted advertising systems, data analytics, and organised social media manipulation campaigns increasingly function as additional channels through which political actors influence information visibility and narrative dominance (Bradshaw, Bailey, & Howard, 2021; Woolley & Howard, 2018). Rather than replacing Herman and Chomsky's original framework, these developments illustrate how its underlying logic can be adapted to understand propaganda in hybrid media systems characterised by interactions between legacy and digital communication infrastructures.

Noelle-Neumann's (1984) Spiral of Silence Theory explains how propaganda-constructed majority opinion climates suppress public expression of dissenting views. Individuals who perceive their views to be minority positions tend to remain publicly silent out of fear of social isolation and sanction, creating a feedback loop in which the dominant opinion appears to grow ever stronger while dissenting perspectives recede. In Nigeria's electoral context, the spiral mechanism has particular explanatory power. Electoral propaganda is frequently designed not merely to persuade voters but to construct the social perception of overwhelming consensus around a candidate or party. Orchestrated rallies, manufactured endorsements, inflated crowd estimates, fabricated polling results, and coordinated social media endorsements collectively trigger this spiral, creating an information environment in which opposition views appear socially deviant or futile. This mechanism is especially effective in Nigeria's high-context social culture, where public deviance from perceived community consensus carries significant interpersonal costs and where communal identity frameworks tend to override individual political judgment. Social media environments may intensify this process because visible indicators of popularity, including likes, shares, comments, trending topics, and coordinated online endorsements, create powerful signals regarding the perceived distribution of public opinion. These signals can reinforce conformity pressures even when they are artificially generated through organised digital influence operations (Howard & Woolley, 2016).

These three theoretical traditions explain the full arc of propaganda's influence on public opinion: structural filters determine what information enters the public sphere; agenda-setting determines which issues and attributes within that information receive salience; and the spiral of silence determines how citizens respond to the manufactured opinion climates that result. The integrated framework reveals that propaganda in Nigeria does not merely influence pre-existing public opinion but actively constructs the informational and social conditions within which opinion formation occurs, a distinction with significant theoretical and practical implications. Importantly, the emergence of computational propaganda, artificial intelligence-assisted content generation, and organised disinformation networks does not invalidate these theories; rather, it demonstrates their continuing utility in explaining how contemporary technologies amplify long-standing mechanisms of political influence. The digital transformation of propaganda has altered the speed, scale, and precision of opinion manipulation, but its effectiveness continues to depend on agenda control, structural information asymmetries, and perceptions of social consensus.
## Methodology

This study uses a qualitative conceptual design based on library-based documentary analysis. Instead of collecting primary data, it interrogates theoretical frameworks to build explanatory accounts of complex social phenomena. The method involves the systematic identification, retrieval, critical evaluation, and thematic synthesis of peer-reviewed journal articles, scholarly books, policy documents, and credible institutional reports relevant to electoral propaganda, political communication, public opinion formation, disinformation, democratic governance, and digital media. The documentary corpus was assembled from academic databases and scholarly search platforms, with emphasis placed on literature addressing Nigeria's Fourth Republic while also incorporating foundational works and comparative studies that provide theoretical insight into propaganda and opinion formation. The literature matrix therefore combined classical texts in political communication with contemporary scholarship on electoral communication, social media influence, and democratic participation. By adopting a conceptual documentary approach, the study shifts attention from election-specific measurements towards a broader examination of the structural and communicative processes through which propaganda shapes public opinion across successive electoral cycles.

The analysis applies thematic content analysis and conceptual synthesis, adapting Braun and Clarke (2006) framework to conceptual inquiry. Documents were examined for recurring patterns relating to propaganda strategies, media influence, information control, digital disinformation, public opinion formation, civic engagement, and democratic outcomes. Themes were generated both deductively from Agenda-Setting Theory, the Propaganda Model, and the Spiral of Silence, and inductively from patterns that emerged across the reviewed literature. Through iterative comparison and synthesis, related concepts were organised into broader thematic categories that illuminate the structural, technological, and democratic dimensions of electoral propaganda in Nigeria. This approach ensures that the analysis remains theoretically grounded while remaining attentive to the documented realities of Nigeria's evolving electoral communication environment.
## Thematic Synthesis of Electoral Propaganda
## Structural Machinery and Media Capture

Electoral propaganda in Nigeria's Fourth Republic is not an improvised or incidental feature of democratic competition. It is structurally organised through dedicated party communication apparatuses, government information management infrastructure, and contracted digital influence networks that operate across traditional and social media platforms. Understanding this structural architecture is essential to understanding how propaganda achieves its opinion-constructing effects at electoral scale.

The incumbent advantage in electoral communication represents perhaps the most enduring structural feature of Nigeria's Fourth Republic propaganda environment. State-controlled broadcast institutions have historically provided disproportionately favourable coverage to ruling party candidates, effectively deploying public communication resources as instruments of partisan electoral propaganda. Government information and communication ministries routinely engage in narrative control, strategic framing, press access management, and the coordination of official messaging in ways that systematically blur the boundary between legitimate public information and partisan propaganda. The National Broadcasting Commission (NBC) has been implicated in this dynamic, with its regulatory decisions at times aligning with incumbent political interests rather than public interest broadcasting principles (RSF, 2024). This pattern reflects broader concerns regarding the vulnerability of public communication institutions to political influence, particularly where regulatory autonomy is weak and media accountability mechanisms remain underdeveloped.

The proprietorship model of Nigerian media transforms private broadcasting and press institutions from independent information providers into extensions of partisan communication networks. Media ownership structures are especially consequential during election periods because proprietors frequently possess direct political interests or maintain close relationships with political elites, creating incentives for selective coverage and agenda promotion. In their systematic content analysis of 288 national newspaper editions from the 2019 campaign cycle, Obukoadata, Okon, and Obogo (2024) provide empirical support for this shift. They demonstrate that name-calling and bandwagon techniques were the most heavily deployed propaganda devices, appearing prominently on front and inside pages. These findings validate the propaganda model's predictions regarding elite narrative reproduction while mirroring the classic persuasion strategies detailed by Jowett and O'Donnell (2015). Ultimately, this pervasive coverage confirms that newspaper-based propaganda operates as a structured, sustained communication strategy rather than an incidental editorial phenomenon.

The dependence of private Nigerian media on government advertising revenue compounds the structural propaganda vulnerability identified by Herman and Chomsky's (1988) Propaganda Model. Beyond advertising dependence, access to political elites, government information channels, and campaign advertising contracts may also shape editorial priorities during election periods, reinforcing incentives to privilege politically dominant narratives over critical scrutiny.

Government advertising budgets, allocated at federal, state, and local levels, function as both reward for favourable editorial treatment and implicit sanction for critical coverage, producing the systematic editorial self-censorship that the Propaganda Model identifies as constitutive of propaganda-susceptible media systems. While the Propaganda Model was developed for advanced capitalist democracies, its analytical core translates effectively to postcolonial contexts where state-media dependencies are more pronounced and institutional checks on media capture correspondingly weaker.

The disinformation supply chain constitutes a further structural component of Nigeria's electoral propaganda machinery. Fabricated content, including false polling figures, manipulated images, fake endorsements, manufactured scandals, and invented policy statements, is produced, packaged to appear credible, and injected into information channels ranging from encrypted WhatsApp group networks to mainstream broadcast media. The effectiveness of such content often derives from its strategic adaptation to existing political grievances, identity affiliations, and public anxieties, enabling propaganda messages to appear plausible even when unsupported by verifiable evidence. Apuke and Omar (2020) characterise this supply chain as a systemic threat to democratic decision-making, noting that the motivations driving fake news production in Nigeria include explicit partisan intent to distort voter choice. In the 2023 election cycle, Anaukwu and Obiozo (2025) document how disinformation campaigns exploited social media platforms to spread false narratives about candidates and voting procedures, contributing to measurable public confusion about the electoral process.

These developments indicate that contemporary electoral propaganda increasingly operates through interconnected media ecosystems in which misinformation can move rapidly between online platforms, interpersonal networks, and traditional news outlets.
## Digital and AI-Driven Transformation of Propaganda

The 2015 Nigerian general election marked a structural shift in electoral propaganda practice, as both the ruling Peoples Democratic Party and the opposition All Progressives Congress deployed digital war rooms, paid social media influencers, and WhatsApp chain message campaigns at scale. Okolie, Enyiazu and Nnamani (2021) document how international political consultancy firms were contracted to design and execute propaganda strategies in this election, deploying emotionally charged narratives around corruption, security failure, and human rights abuses to construct evaluative frames favourable to the opposition candidate. The structural normalisation of contracted propaganda services marked a qualitative shift in Nigerian electoral communication, transforming propaganda from an opportunistic campaign tactic into a planned, professionally managed communication function. This professionalisation mirrors a broader international trend towards organised social media manipulation, whereby political actors employ coordinated digital communication networks, influencers, targeted advertising, and automated accounts to shape public discourse (Bradshaw, Bailey, & Howard, 2021).

The 2019 and 2023 election cycles witnessed a significant intensification and sophistication of digital propaganda operations. This development reflects a broader global transition towards what Howard and Woolley (2016) describe as computational propaganda, in which algorithms, automation, and digitally mediated influence systems are deployed to shape online political communication and public opinion at scale. WhatsApp's encrypted peer-to-peer architecture has emerged as particularly consequential: content circulates through pre-existing social trust networks, acquiring interpersonal credibility endorsement at each transfer point while remaining immune to external fact-checking or platform moderation. The 2023 election also introduced new dimensions of propaganda weaponisation, including the documented deployment of manipulated audio recordings, deepfake videos, and, for the first time in Nigeria's recent electoral history, the co-optation of credible fact-checkers' reputations by political actors seeking to lend authority to propaganda content (Olaniran and Diepeveen, 2023).

The growing role of artificial intelligence in electoral propaganda represents the most significant recent development in this domain. Anaukwu and Obiozo (2025) argue that AI-assisted misinformation, like deepfake content and synthetic political narratives, significantly shaped voter perceptions and amplified false electoral claims during the 2023 presidential election. Jain and Mitra (2025) demonstrate that AI-driven tools including sentiment analysis, deepfakes, and personalised messaging have fundamentally altered the political communication landscape by enabling highly tailored propaganda content at scales previously unachievable. Wack, Ehrett, Linvill and Warren (2025), in a study published in PNAS Nexus, provide direct empirical evidence from a state-backed disinformation campaign that generative AI adoption enabled substantial increases in disinformation production volume without loss of persuasive impact. The Dubawa fact-checking organisation (2025) has documented a trajectory of AI-enhanced electoral propaganda in Nigeria extending into the preparations for the 2027 election cycle, with fabricated video and audio content depicting senior political figures already circulating at scale.

Facebook's micro-targeting architecture enables propaganda to be delivered to highly specific demographic, geographic, and interest-defined audience segments with precision unavailable through broadcast media. Such practices are characteristic of computational propaganda strategies, which combine social media platforms, algorithmic systems, and audience data analytics to influence political attitudes and behaviour with unprecedented precision (Woolley & Howard, 2018). These architectural affordances are deliberately exploited by political actors, and Apuke and Omar (2020) find that citizens relying primarily on social media for political information are measurably more susceptible to propaganda-driven opinion distortion. The broader African context illuminates these dynamics: a comparative analysis of electoral disinformation across Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa between 2017 and 2023 demonstrates how digital tools including algorithms, deepfakes, and bots have amplified propaganda potential to an unprecedented degree (Alberts, 2025; Woolley & Howard, 2019). In Nigeria's context, where digital platform oversight capacity remains underdeveloped relative to the scale of political disinformation activity, AI-enhanced propaganda presents a particular governance challenge for which the existing regulatory framework offers no meaningful response.
## Implications for Democratic Consolidation and Civic Engagement

The systematic operation of electoral propaganda in Nigeria's Fourth Republic carries profound implications for democratic consolidation and civic engagement. Consolidation theory, as articulated by Linz and Stepan (1996), holds that a foundational prerequisite of consolidated democracy is a communication environment enabling citizens to form genuinely informed opinions that translate into meaningful electoral choices. Propaganda-saturated electoral environments systematically subvert this prerequisite by replacing deliberative information with strategically constructed narratives.

In contemporary digital environments, this challenge extends beyond traditional propaganda to include coordinated disinformation campaigns that distort public understanding of political realities and weaken the informational foundations required for democratic participation (Bennett & Livingston, 2018).

Gyimah-Boadi (2015) identifies the manipulation of electoral communication, including propaganda, media capture, and disinformation, as a primary mechanism through which nominally democratic governments erode substantive democratic quality without formally abandoning democratic procedures. The 2023 Nigerian election provides a concentrated recent illustration of these dynamics. Madueke and Enyiazu (2025) find that INEC's institutional constraints, including corruption, non-adherence to procedural rules, and lack of independence, created conditions in which the manipulation of the information environment around electoral administration compounded pre-existing integrity deficits, with disinformation campaigns exploiting and amplifying institutional vulnerabilities to maximise public confusion and minimise accountability. Bradshaw, Bailey, and Howard (2021) show similar concern on how coordinated digital campaigns can diminish trust in electoral institutions while creating uncertainty about the legitimacy of democratic outcomes.

A corrosive secondary effect of propaganda-saturated environments is the erosion of public trust in democratic institutions and information systems (Bennett & Livingston, 2018). Apuke and Omar (2020) find that repeated exposure to politically motivated disinformation produces not heightened critical discernment but generalised information cynicism, a disposition characterised by wholesale distrust of all political communication. This cynicism is paradoxically functional for propaganda operations because it undermines the credibility of fact-checking and investigative journalism that might otherwise constrain disinformation, creating an epistemic environment in which all claims are treated with equivalent scepticism regardless of their evidential grounding. Howard and Woolley (2016) argue that digital propaganda systems increasingly operate through algorithms, automated accounts, and networked influence structures that amplify selected narratives while obscuring the sources of manipulation. Under such conditions, citizens may find it increasingly difficult to distinguish between authentic political discourse and strategically engineered information flows.

The polarising consequences of identity-based electoral propaganda pose a further structural challenge in Nigeria's context of pronounced ethnic and religious diversity. By activating ethno-religious identity frames as the dominant evaluative lens for electoral competition, propaganda systematically deepens social cleavages that consolidation theory identifies as primary threats to democratic stability. The 2023 Lagos governorship elections illustrate the ongoing potency of this mechanism, with specific narratives deployed to amplify ethnic and political differences that escalated into post-election violence and institutional controversy (Ademosu et al., 2026). Digital communication technologies frequently intensify these dynamics by enabling divisive narratives to circulate rapidly within ideologically homogeneous online networks, thereby reinforcing existing social and political divisions rather than facilitating democratic deliberation (Woolley & Howard, 2018).

The long-term civic engagement implications are equally consequential. Communication environments that consistently construct false realities, suppress critical perspectives, and manufacture social consensus habituate citizens to passive reception of political narratives rather than democratic deliberation. Across successive election cycles, the result is an electorate participating formally in democratic processes while being systematically denied the informational conditions necessary for substantive self-governance. As artificial intelligence tools become increasingly accessible, the capacity to generate persuasive synthetic content at scale may further complicate democratic communication by accelerating the production and circulation of misleading political information (Wack et al., 2025). Strengthening democratic resilience will therefore require not only institutional reform but also sustained investment in media literacy, fact-checking capacity, and transparent regulation of digital political communication.
## Conclusion

Electoral propaganda in Nigeria's Fourth Republic constitutes a structurally organised and institutionally embedded system of strategic communication that actively shapes the conditions under which public opinion is formed. Drawing on Agenda-Setting Theory, the Propaganda Model, and the Spiral of Silence, this study demonstrates that propaganda operates through interconnected structural, communicative, and social mechanisms that influence how citizens interpret political realities, evaluate candidates, and participate in democratic processes. The analysis further shows that the digital transformation of electoral communication has expanded the reach and sophistication of propaganda through social media networks, organised disinformation campaigns, computational propaganda, and emerging artificial intelligence applications. By integrating insights from political communication, democratic theory, and contemporary scholarship on digital influence, the study contributes a conceptual framework for understanding how electoral propaganda continues to shape public opinion and democratic governance across Nigeria's Fourth Republic. The findings suggest the need for a multi-level response involving institutions, media organisations, technology platforms, and citizens. Strengthening the independence and accountability of media regulatory institutions, promoting transparency in digital political communication, supporting fact-checking and disinformation-monitoring initiatives, and expanding media and information literacy programmes are essential for protecting democratic discourse. Given the increasing use of artificial intelligence and digitally mediated influence strategies in electoral politics, future research should continue to examine the implications of computational and AI-enabled propaganda for electoral integrity, civic engagement, and democratic consolidation in Nigeria and other emerging democracies.

title: Setting the 2027 Agenda: Re-Examining the Discourse on Good Governance and the Nigerian Broadcast Media
abstract: This study is a conceptual work that analysed the place of Nigerian broadcast media in the context of discourses on democracy, good governances and elections. The paper leveraged on numerous related literatures to provide context, re-examine the broadcast media landscape and also advance the position that the broadcast media, despite its contemporary challenges that include proliferation of digital platforms, poor resources and pressure from different groups, still remain relevant and continue to provide effective platform for critical discourse on political matters. The paper utilises the tenets of democratic participant theory to explain good governance and the role of the media Methodologically, the paper relied on secondary data and observation of the radio and television programmes as well as broadcast schedules of selected media stations to examine past experiences and current efforts by Nigerian broadcast media in engaging the public through intentional programme contents to set agenda for the 2027 elections and expectations for good governance. Thus, findings from the analysis revealed that despite the proliferation of media channels that include digital media platforms, which all contribute significantly to political discourse and good governance, the broadcast media as popular traditional media channels continue to retain and consolidate on its traditional role in political mobilisation and participation in the contemporary time. Therefore, the study concludes that the role of broadcast media is imperative in promoting good governance by holding government accountable to people and ensuring transparency and justice in any democratic setting like Nigeria through its efforts to provide a platform and various forums for political debates, discussions and conversations through interviews, current affairs and discussion programmes in both national and local broadcast stations. In view of this, it is recommended that broadcast stations should strengthen their programmes on political matters to be accessible and participatory and the regulatory body such as the National Broadcasting Commission should also continue to formulate and strengthen policies that would continue to guide the broadcast media in their dealings with political matters.

bodyParagraphs: ## Introduction

As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general elections, questions of good governance are likely to occupy a central place in political and public discourse (including the media). Issues such as accountability, transparency, responsiveness, service delivery, citizens' participation and respect for the rule of law remain important to how governance is discussed and evaluated. In this context, the broadcast media occupies a significant position in shaping public conversations, providing platforms for political actors and citizens, and bringing governance issues to wider audiences. According to Akingbohungbe (2025) good governance remains a critical ingredient for the growth, unity, and transformation of any nation; and in a country like Nigeria, where it is blessed with human and natural resources, the struggle for good governance has continued to be at the centre stage of national debates. It is obvious that institutions, laws, and leadership play central roles in governance, the media, both traditional (television, radio, newspaper and magazine) and digital are also powerful catalysts for shaping democratic outcomes and ensuring governmental accountability. This is largely achieved through intentional and sustained contents by media organisations including the broadcast media (television and radio).

According to Malam (2022), broadcasting is one of such endeavours that are inseparable from politics. This is because through the broadcast media, broadcasting has become a tool that is used for mobilisation and bringing about change. Broadcast media as communication channels have for many years provided a platform for political discourse. Observably, various television and radio stations in Nigeria have introduced programmes in their broadcast schedules that are often designed to increase political mobilisation, participation and track governance. Such programmes can include current affairs, discussion programmes among others that target electorates as well as sensitize the public on good governance. Citizens can only demand for accountability, fair election and justice when they are informed, aware and participate in decision-making processes that can ultimately bring about good governance. This position aligns with the perspectives of some scholars such as McQuail (2010), who notes that in politics, the mass media provides an arena for debate and also set channels for making policies, candidates, relevant facts and ideas widely known as well as providing politicians, interest groups and agents of government with means of publicity influence.

Paletz (2008) also posits that the media are indispensable to democracy, a political system predicated on the consent of the governed. Paletz further argues that the media expresses political contents in four different ways that occasionally overlap, which include explicit and intentional contents such as debates, adverts and commentary; explicit and unintentional contents; implicit and intentional contents as well as implicit and unintentional contents. The explicit and intentional contents on broadcast media such as debates, adverts and commentaries are usually programmed to achieve a particular goal. Thus, these intentional programmes, particularly those related to politics and good governance can set an agenda and subtly aid in forming public opinions on critical issues. Baym (2013) on the other hand notes that one form of political media is the public-affairs interview. As much as political media have changed, the one-on-one interview remains a primary mode of political engagement.

Thus, the media including the broadcast media play a significant role at different phases in political change, particularly during elections. Yusuf, Abubakar and Adamu (2025) note that the role of the media during election periods can be examined across three broad phases: the pre-election phase, the election phase and the post-election phase. In each of these stages, the responsibilities of the media assume different dimensions and objectives. This is largely because the media function as critical actors within the democratic process and therefore play significant roles in shaping political communication, public awareness and setting agenda during the electoral cycle.

The pre-election phase is particularly important because it lays the foundation for informed political participation. This phase is often characterised by intense political party activities such as candidate nominations, campaign mobilisation, policy articulation and coalition building. Within this period, the mainstream media become highly active as political developments generate a steady flow of newsworthy events and issues for public dissemination. For media organisations, it is also a period of increased commercial activity as political actors purchase airtime and advertising space to communicate their messages to the electorate. Baym (2010) notes that politicians have wider televisual resources at their disposal to make arguments, influence opinions, and build constituencies. Likewise, contemporary citizens, in their efforts to engage with, and perhaps find pleasure in, the political domain, are drawing on any number of programs and generic configurations that crisscross categories of news and entertainment, and politics and pop culture. It is apparent that public discourse is no longer contained, nor constrained, by the high-modernist institutions and discursive structures once narrowly assumed to constitute the legitimate arena for the exercise of representative politics.

Beyond the commercial opportunities, the pre-election period places a significant democratic responsibility on the media. Through the wide range of political content produced and disseminated during this time, the media provide civic and voter education by informing citizens about electoral procedures, voter registration requirements, the rights and responsibilities of voters and the importance of peaceful participation in the democratic process. By doing so, the media helps prepare citizens for meaningful engagement in the electoral process.

Interestingly, the Nigerian government in a bid to ensure good governance in the country had in, the 1999 Nigerian constitution, Section 16 (1) a, b, c, and d, and Section 16 (2) rooted some of the principles of good governance as possible criteria for governance in the country. These provisions seem ineffective despite enormous financial resources, and huge potentials of the country, including the social and economic policies that have been implemented by successive administrations. Good governance continues to be elusive to Nigeria. Therefore, it becomes imperative to recognise the effort of media organisations particularly the broadcast media in complementing efforts towards achieving good governance through its effort to mobilise, sensitize and create awareness about government policies and programmes.

Effective and efficient governance is integral to any country's wellbeing. The concept of governance is contextualised in this paper as the exercise of power or authority (political, economic, administrative or otherwise) to manage a country's resources and affairs. It comprises the mechanisms, processes and institutions through which citizens and groups articulate their interests, exercise their legal rights, meet their obligations and mediate their differences.

The main strategy of having effective and efficient governance is to relate to the functioning of the public sector focused on accountability and scrutiny and the performance of the public sector on the connection between policy and implementation. It provides a concept that allows the public to discuss the role of government in coping with public issues and the contribution that other players may make. It opens one's mind to the possibility that groups in society other than the government (for example, 'communities' or the 'voluntary sector') may have to play a stronger role in addressing problems.

This paper is interested in discussing the 2027 Nigeria's general election and how the broadcast can help in setting the agenda for the public through its content. At present, political parties are intensifying their preparations for the 2027 General Elections, with candidates emerging for various elective positions across the country. Candidates of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) and opposition parties have increasingly utilised the media to present their programmes, policy positions and development plans to Nigerians and their respective constituencies. This growing presence of political actors in the broadcast media provides an important context for examining the nature and substance of political broadcast programmes and the extent to which they engage with issues of good governance. With the electoral cycle already underway and political campaigns subject to the timetable and regulations issued by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), the media is expected to play a significant role in shaping public discourse leading to the 2027 elections.

While the Frankfurt School for example have the view that media contents are negative because in their context the Nazi, Germans used radio, newspapers, films and television to disseminate propaganda and were pivotal in the spread of capitalist ideology, this paper argues that media contents are a mixture of positive and negative. The paper is segmented into the following sections. First, it provides an excursion on Nigerian Broadcast Media and the past experience on good governance in relations to the elections. The section limits discourse to Kano broadcasts and political programmes as well as the discourse on media at the national level. This paper is useful as it provides a basis for examining political broadcast programmes in relation to their engagement with issues of good governance. It advocates a shift from personality centred political discourse towards issue based and governance centred communication, with greater emphasis on accountability, transparency, public participation and citizens' concerns.
## Contextualising Broadcast media and its Role in Governance

On 5 March 2026, the international broadcast network Al Jazeera aired one of its regular programmes, Head-to-Head with Mehdi Hasan, featuring Nigeria's Presidential Adviser on Communication and Policy, Daniel Bwala. The interview attracted considerable attention within Nigeria's media and political circles and remained a subject of public discourse across both mainstream and digital platforms. Commentators, political actors and citizens reflected on the issues raised during the exchange, particularly those relating to governance, accountability and the broader dynamics of political communication in democratic societies.

However, the prominence of this interview also raises important questions about the role of Nigerian based broadcasters in shaping conversations on governance within the country. While Nigerian broadcast media organisations such as Channels Television, African Independent Television (AIT), Arise News, News Central TV, TVC News and the public owned Nigerian Television Authority regularly host programmes that provide platforms for public office holders and public affairs analysts to discuss national issues, the interview in question originated from an international broadcaster.

In the buildup to the 2027 general elections, issues surrounding the removal and possible reinstatement of petrol subsidy have once again become prominent in the Nigerian media. The debate was recently reignited following the renewed position of Atiku Abubakar, presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), that a form of petrol subsidy should be restored. The proposal generated a response from the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, which challenged him to explain its legal, fiscal and operational implications, including its proposed cost, source of funding and mechanism for ensuring that consumers benefit. Such debates are important governance issues that should receive sustained attention in political broadcast programmes. Rather than merely reporting exchanges between political actors, broadcasters have an opportunity to interrogate the substance of competing positions and provide citizens with the information required to understand their implications. Questions concerning the economic consequences of subsidy removal, the proposed mechanism for its restoration, the cost to public finances, accountability for subsidy expenditure from the time of removal to date, and its likely effects on fuel prices and the wider cost of living warrant thorough public discussion.

The fuel subsidy debate is one among many other issues that demonstrate the broader role of the broadcast media in setting the governance agenda for the 2027 elections. This development calls for reflection on the extent to which Nigerian broadcast media are proactively creating platforms that rigorously interrogate governance issues and stimulate substantive public debate. It raises a fundamental question about whether the broadcast media are adequately setting the agenda for governance conversations as the country approaches the 2027 general elections. Consequently, there is a need to re-examine the role of Nigerian broadcast media in promoting accountability, stimulating informed political discourse and strengthening democratic engagement during the electoral cycle.
## Nigerian Broadcast Media and Good Governance: The Past Experiences

Mass media are critical stakeholders in ensuring the accountability of government to the governed through providing information for the citizens to hold those in authority accountable. According to Curran (2002), they help in promoting what is right in the society and also serve as platforms for articulating citizens' voices and preference for government to use in policy formulation. Regardless of format or nature (broadcast, print or online), media has a significant role in boosting good governance. The roles of the media in good governance can be underscored under eight (8) perspectives which include participation, transparency, responsiveness, equity and inclusiveness. According to UNESCO (2005), participation is a crucial element for good governance. The media enables participation in two ways; as a facilitator providing platforms for the citizens to have accurate and sufficient information that help citizens make rational and informed decisions and take the right course of action beneficial to them: As a feedback mechanism, the media provide the means for the citizens to register their feelings and express their assent and dissent concerning issues. The media as the primary intermediaries of information supply the information that other sectors of the society need to participate effectively.

Among the various elements of good governance, transparency is widely recognised as a core principle (Bellver & Kaufmann, 2005). The media can play a key role in increasing government accountability to the general public by explaining government policies and actions in this manner; what is to be done, how and why an action has to take place, who is involved and by what standards decisions are made, and in this way government actions and inactions are exposed to the glare of the general public. It is perhaps in the area of engendering transparency in the society that the Nigerian media continue to be acknowledged (Olutokun & Seteolu, 2001; Jibo & Okoosi-Simbine, 2003). Good governance also requires that institutions and processes try to serve all stakeholders within a reasonable timeframe, by responding to the grievances, needs and aspirations of the citizens. As mentioned earlier, the media act as a feedback mechanism where the publics are given the opportunity to bring their plight to the notice of the State. The media often do this through various media campaigns and programmes that serve to remind the State of their obligations to the public. Moreover, the wellbeing of society depends on ensuring that all members have a uniform stake in it which requires all groups, particularly the most vulnerable, to have opportunities to improve and/or maintain their wellbeing. The media's role in this regard is very simple- giving balanced and fair coverage to all issues in a manner that diverse voices and opinions will be represented. It is perhaps in this function that the Nigerian media have been greatly faulted. The Nigerian media have been accused of prejudice in reporting and treating issues of public concern.

Arguably, the broadcast media terrain in Nigeria has evolved into a highly competitive and influential sector that plays a significant role in shaping governance discourse. Malam (2022) argues that the emergence of private radio and television stations following the deregulation of the broadcast sector has contributed to the dissemination of diverse political views and opinions. By the existence of broadcast media (private and public), they have contributed to an emerging liberal democratic space that promotes free flow of contending political views which seems to be absent in the days of public ownership monopoly of the broadcast media. Through news bulletins, political talk shows and public affairs programmes, broadcast media have become central platforms for interrogating public policies, scrutinising political actors and facilitating citizen participation in governance. Over the years, radio and television stations across the country have hosted programmes that enable citizens, political elites and policy experts to debate issues of national importance. In this regard, broadcast media have contributed to strengthening democratic culture by promoting public engagement with governance processes.

This section examines past experiences of Nigerian broadcast media in advancing conversations on good governance from two perspectives. The first focuses on programmes aired on broadcast media with national outlook, while the second part examines the role of political programmes by FM radio stations in Kano State. The choice of Kano is deliberate, as the state can be regarded as a major centre of political activity in Northern Nigeria. Kano also has a large concentration of broadcast media organisations, making it an appropriate setting for examining the nature and extent of political broadcasting and the interrogation of good governance issues in the lead up to the 2027 general elections.
## Good Governance Discourse at the National Level

## Nigerian broadcast media also contribute to governance discourse through nationally televised political programmes. Television networks often host high profile discussions that bring together political leaders, government officials, opposition figures and policy analysts to deliberate on national issues. For instance, programmes such as Politics Today and Daily Politics on Channels Television and Trust Television have become influential platforms for discussing governance issues in Nigeria. Through interviews, panel discussions and policy analysis, these programmes examine government policies, electoral developments, legislative activities and public administration challenges daily. They provide viewers with insights into the workings of government while also creating opportunities for public scrutiny of political actors.

It should be noted that the broadcast media at the national level have the capacity to make a significant contribution to the interrogation of governance issues. The Nigerian Television Authority (NTA), as the national public broadcaster, is particularly positioned to provide a platform for sustained discussion of public policies, government performance and issues affecting citizens. However, concerns about government influence and control over the public broadcaster raise questions about the extent to which it can effectively perform its role in tracking good governance. Olaiya, Apeoko and Ayeni (2013) argue that the media must be guaranteed freedom and independence in the discharge of their professional responsibilities. The degree of media independence is closely associated with its capacity to scrutinise public affairs, hold political leaders accountable and serve the public interest.

Broadcast programmes related to politics can therefore serve as important mechanisms of accountability by questioning political leaders, seeking explanations for government actions and subjecting policy proposals to public scrutiny. Through such engagements, the media contribute to transparency and informed public debates, while providing citizens with opportunities to assess competing political claims and governance positions. These programmes also demonstrate the capacity of broadcast media to shape national conversations by determining which governance issues receive sustained public attention. The effectiveness of this role, however, depends largely on the extent to which broadcasters can operate with professional autonomy and provide critical, balanced and evidence-based interrogation of political and governance issues.
## Broadcast Media and Good Governance: The Kano Experience

Programmes on good governance are usually tied to politics. Political programming on FM radio stations in Kano State demonstrates the vibrant nature of broadcast media engagement with governance issues at the sub national level. Radio remains one of the most accessible media platforms in northern parts of Nigeria, largely because of its affordability, linguistic inclusiveness and ability to reach audiences across urban and rural communities. Thus, FM radio stations in Kano provide important platforms for citizens to discuss political developments, express their opinions and question public authorities.

Political programmes across FM stations in Kano are diverse in format and orientation. They include public discussions, policy debates, audience phone in segments and interviews with political actors. These programmes provide opportunities for citizens to articulate their views on governance, public policies and political leadership. As noted by Siraj (2016), almost all FM radio stations in Kano broadcast political programmes that focus on governance and public affairs. Some of the notable programmes include:

The programmes highlighted in Table 1 provide platforms for discussing public policies, electoral processes, governance challenges and socio-economic issues affecting citizens. Through such engagements, radio stations facilitate political participation and contribute to democratic accountability. Citizens visit these stations and are provided with opportunities to access airtime to express their views, raise concerns and comment on issues relating to good governance in Kano State and Nigeria more broadly. Observably, the stations allocate varying amounts of airtime depending on the nature of the programme, the issue under discussion and, in some instances, the ability of individuals or organisations to pay for airtime. This commercial dimension may influence citizens' access to broadcast platforms and the extent to which different voices are represented in public discourse.

Nevertheless, the programmes provide an important avenue through which citizens can question public officials, express dissatisfaction with government policies and draw attention to issues affecting their communities. An important feature of these programmes is the provision of a right of reply, particularly where allegations are made against government agencies, public institutions or political office holders. Such opportunities can promote fairness and balance by allowing individuals or institutions that are the subject of criticism or allegations to respond. In this regard, political broadcast programmes can serve as platforms for public scrutiny, dialogue and accountability, thereby strengthening the role of radio in promoting good governance and democratic engagement. A number of individuals, including Dan Bilki Commander, Alhaji Nagoda, Ali Baba and others, regularly appear as guests on these radio programmes. Their recurrent participation provides opportunities for sustained discussion of public policies, governance challenges and issues affecting citizens even though it is viewed by others as broadcast political thuggery because of their utterances. While the presence of these individuals does not, in itself, establish that the programmes promote good governance, their engagements can contribute to keeping governance related issues within the public domain.

Another example is the Hausa television series Kwana Casa'in, produced and broadcast by Arewa24, a Hausa satellite television station in Kano, with support from the MacArthur Foundation. The series uses fictional narratives to portray political and socio-economic realities, including corruption, abuse of public office and other governance challenges. Through its dramatic representation of these issues, the programme provides an alternative form of political communication through which audiences can reflect on the consequences of corrupt practices and the responsibilities of political office holders.

The multiplicity of political programmes across different broadcast stations reflects the pluralistic nature of the Nigerian broadcast media environment. These programmes are not necessarily monolithic in their perspective; rather, they provide spaces for diverse political interests, ideological positions and analytical viewpoints. Such diversity creates opportunities for governance issues to be debated from different perspectives and enables citizens to encounter competing interpretations of political policies and government performance. In this sense, the plurality of political broadcast programmes can contribute to a more expansive public sphere in which citizens engage with governance issues, scrutinise political claims and participate in democratic discourse.
## Good Governance Agenda and Broadcast Media in Nigeria

As Nigeria prepares for another round of elections in 2027, the broadcast media can reflect on its past and present challenges as well its potentials to add value to the political activities in the country. The role of the broadcast media in these activities should be targeted towards holding everyone responsible and accountable for good governance before and after elections; either as electorates or political candidates. The aftermath of every election comes with the expectation for good governance. Good governance provides transparency, accountability and social and physical developments. Abraham (2021) argues that the role of the media in promoting good governance is clear. All aspects of good governance are facilitated by a strong and independent mediascape within a society. Only when journalists are free to monitor, investigate and criticize the public administration's policies and actions can good governance take hold. Thus, the author identified two key activities that can promote good governance; active participation and civic forum for political debates, which can both be facilitated by the broadcast media. It is important for Nigerian broadcast media to resist pressure from political parties, political candidates, pressure groups and even electorates in discharging their duties and also insist on freedom of expression and the role of the mass media as enshrined in the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria as amended. This can further be consolidated when journalists adhere strictly to journalism ethical standards.

The broadcast media can contribute significantly to the promotion of good governance and the development of a fair and just political system, particularly as Nigeria approaches another electoral cycle in 2027. To fulfil this responsibility, broadcasters need to recognise and utilise the distinctive potentials of radio and television. Ogah and Abari (2023) identify eight potentials that make broadcasting a unique medium: flexibility, omnipresence, voracity, regularity, anonymity, heterogeneity, mode of transmission and immediacy. These characteristics provide broadcast media with the capacity to reach diverse audiences, disseminate information rapidly, facilitate continuous public discussion and provide platforms for citizens and political actors to engage in issues of public concern.

This potential becomes particularly significant during election periods. In Nigeria, the organisation of political debates involving presidential and other candidates has become an important feature of communicating politics and interrogating good governance. Such debates provide broadcast media with opportunities to set the agenda by determining the issues presented to candidates and the questions through which their policy positions are examined. Beyond providing candidates with an opportunity to communicate their programmes, electoral debates can enable broadcasters to subject competing policy proposals to public scrutiny and encourage candidates to address issues of governance, accountability and citizens' welfare.

Consequently, the effectiveness of electoral debates should not be measured merely by the number of candidates given airtime or the size of the audience reached. Greater attention should be given to the issues selected for discussion, the depth of questioning, the opportunity provided for candidates to substantiate their claims and the extent to which citizens' governance concerns are reflected in the debates.
## Good Governance and Media: Democratic Media Participant Theory

Central to this discourse on good governance is the media democratic theory. The media in all its forms provides an obvious conduit for democratic participation and education. The theory is an extension by McQuail in 1987. Democratic Participant Theory is often seen as a development of Social Responsibility Theory, although it is more accurately described as a response that extends its ideas. While Social Responsibility Theory emphasises ethical media practice and service to the public, Democratic Participant Theory places stronger focus on the active involvement of citizens in media processes.

The theory proposes that the media should support and promote the views and opinions of individuals regarding governance, leadership, and public accountability. It highlights the importance of equal and unrestricted access to media, regardless of status, wealth, or social position. Participation in decision making within society and involvement in communication activities should not be limited to elites but should be open to all citizens.

A key principle of the theory is the decentralisation of media power. It encourages the growth of community and small-scale media platforms so that diverse voices can be heard. In this regard, governments are expected to identify, train, and provide funding for smaller media organisations, while still preserving their independence. According to Baran and Davis (2012), Democratic Participant Theory supports cultural pluralism at the grassroots level. Media should be used to stimulate and empower diverse groups within society, enabling them to represent their own interests and perspectives. The theory also emphasises that audiences should not remain passive consumers of media content. Instead, individuals should actively create, share, and influence media messages. This ensures a more inclusive and participatory communication environment.

Good governance rests on principles such as transparency, accountability, inclusiveness, responsiveness, and the rule of law. Democratic Participant Theory strengthens these principles by positioning the media not merely as an information channel, but as an arena for citizen engagement. When individuals can access media platforms freely and express their views on governance, leadership, and policy, transparency is enhanced. Government actions become more visible and open to public scrutiny, reducing the likelihood of secrecy and abuse of power. The emphasis on active citizen involvement directly supports accountability. When people participate in media processes by questioning decisions, debating policies, and sharing local experiences, leaders are compelled to justify their actions. This continuous interaction between citizens and those in authority creates a system where public officials remain answerable to the people. In this sense, Democratic Participant Theory transforms the media into a mechanism through which accountability is demanded and enforced.
## Conclusion

The obvious potentials of broadcast media have continued to make these channels of communication unique among the various media channels that include the digital media platforms. As traditional media channels that have gained popularity among audiences since its emergence and development, particularly in Nigeria, the broadcast media remain relevant, active and widely accessed by the audiences in the contemporary times. This positioned the broadcast media at the centre of political discourse as it regards its role in political mobilisation, participation and promotion of good governance. Numerous programme contents on international and national television and radio stations that include interviews, current affairs and discussions are becoming engaging and popular because of the political contents that include issues around good governance. National television stations such as Channels Television, TVC, and Arise TV have been demonstrating capacity in terms of providing platforms and forums for political discourse and conversations. Equally, local or broadcast stations operating at sub-government levels such as Freedom Radio, Pyramid FM and Rahma Radio in a place like Kano also broadcast programmes that encourage political participation and promote good governance.

Thus, it is argued here that despite the challenges facing the Nigerian broadcast stations, their effort in consolidating democracy and promoting good governance such as transparency, accountability, fairness and justice cannot be ignored especially as the country approaches the 2027 general elections and the expectations of good governance appear to be growing higher. The efforts of the Nigerian broadcast media in recent time suggest that the broadcast media are consolidating on their traditional role of serving the people with focused content to promote good governance.
